This research proposes a 2-phase WSN data collection method, starting with dividing the monitoring area into a hierarchical grid system. Next, cluster head nodes are chosen via a probability process in this grid. The cluster heads create virtual backbones and use multi-hop routing to send data to the sink node. This ensures efficient energy usage and multiple collection paths. A new algorithm estimates the link quality in reverse, providing the sink node with information about link quality, which can be used for data restoration. This estimation technique reduces the need for extra collection rounds, thereby saving energy.

In the field of computer vision, context plays a crucial role in identifying objects, and humans naturally make use of background information to distinguish between target objects and non-targets. However, current deep learning-based object detectors fall short in capturing context-related features. Context-aware object detectors build on background information to improve the representation of target objects, but their sophisticated implementation has limited success. This paper introduces a newly crafted context-aware data set, ContextObjects, which is 10 times more expansive than existing object data sets and contains a rich diversity of scene objects in various contexts. Through thorough experimentation, it is demonstrated that context-aware object detection deeply depends on background information, and context-aware data sets significantly outperform generic training data in terms of performance. Furthermore, it provides a context-aware baseline object detector, which incorporates contextual background details to enhance the target object representation, utilizing the Rich Feature Hierarchies module.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system that includes a small parameter lambda and an external force. The given system, which is of nonhomogeneous type, features a critical growth term and an external force in a given domain in R^2. By applying a variational approach in conjunction with a linking method, we are able to establish the existence of a solution with at least two nontrivial components when parameter lambda takes on a finite value. Additionally, we examine how the solution behaves in relation to the Dirac measure as the parameter approaches an infinite value.

We establish refined upper bounds for the probability of rare events in systems of independently behaving binary elements, taking into account dependencies between the elements. These upper bounds are significant for applications in statistical physics and machine learning, where they help analyze the typical behavior of large, independent but potentially dependent systems of binary variables. Notably, our upper bounds provide the necessary conditions to prove sharp concentration phenomena in Ising models on various graphs, including self-interacting paths on self-avoiding walks on integer lattices and trees under measure defined by Edwards model.

Let $p$ be an odd prime and consider the ring of power series in two variables with coefficients in $\Zbar\Zbar_p(\Zbar_p(\Zbar_p[[t]]))$. We have established that this ring possesses a tamely ramified $p$-adic field extension in which its Witt-Salticulin ring is computable.

This study investigates the spin-dependent dihadron production asymmetry in the SIDIS process when both the quark and the nucleon are longitudinally polarized. To explain our findings, we consider the leading-order contribution from the interference between a quark handness-dependent asymmetry in the quark-quark correlation and a spin-dependent asymmetry in the hadron formation process. Our calculations reveal that the cosφR dependence of the spin-spin asymmetry is primarily driven by the interference of the scalar part of the quark-quark correlation with the Hessian and the pseudoscalar part of the quark-quark correlation with the booson effect. Moreover, the contribution from the scalar part of the quark-quark correlation can be separated from the Hessian and the booson effect through the analysis of the hadron charge dependence, whereas the cosφR asymmetry is mainly contributed by the interference of the scalar part of the quark-quark correlation and the Hessian and the pseudoscalar part of the quark-quark correlation can be probed by analyzing the hadron charge dependence, whereas the cosφR asymmetry can be influenced by a different interference term. To investigate this, we consider the interference between a quark handness-dependent asymmetry in the quark-quark correlation and the hadron formation process, as well as the interference between the scalar part of the quark-quark correlation and the Hessian and the pseudoscalar part of the quark-quark

E. B. Fock created a unique, conformally related coordinate system in 1930s, which was particularly useful for simplifying the metric of a linearized, expanding universe. This coordinate system is now recognized as a key feature of the de Sitter universe. Fock's work was integral to the development of a coordinate system used in the de Sitter and Bertotti's investigations into static, expanding regions of the universe. Fock's first publication in general relativity included the derivation of the de Sitter universe as a vacuum solution to the Einstein field equations. However, Fock's own conclusions about this solution, initially presented in his first book on the subject, were somewhat ambiguous and likely influenced by the views of his contemporary, A. Einstein, who strongly opposed these findings.

This research focuses on translating symplectic maps from one submanifold to another within the same or a different ambient space, given that these underlying spaces are equipped with differential forms that yield non-zero values on 2-forms when applied to pairs of vector fields. A particular method of translation is explored, known as the Legendre transformation, under various conditions. A key aspect of this method involves determining the necessary and applicable conditions for this transformation to maintain its symplectic properties either in a neighborhood of the diagonal in R^n or in a neighborhood of the graph of a given function between two distinct manifolds. Furthermore, this research seeks to extend a previously proven method, which only functioned in Euclidean spaces, to include situations involving several variables and situations where the differential forms in question have more general characteristics.

This study proposes a novel entity recommendation method on the Wikipedia platform, rooted in entity-document bipartite graphs. Unlike previous approaches that utilized pairwise or multi-pairing Wikipedia entities and pages, our method incorporates a layered graph representation to integrate both entity background knowledge and cross-entity interaction information. By applying entropy-based pooling and a learnable non-linear transformation, we convert both document and entity representations into layered graphs. Additionally, we introduce a co-representation learning module to embed entities within both document and neighboring entity spaces. Experimental evaluations on Wikipedia and extended to Yahoo! Knowledge Graph confirm our method's efficacy.

Accepting previously rejected or unmatched kidneys offers significant benefits in transplantation, though there's no established standard for optimal acceptance. We formulate and solve a stochastic optimal control problem to determine the best course of action, considering a patient's growing rejection risk. The ideal standard should also be applicable to blood transfusions and organ donations in a broader context. Our solution can be implemented using various methods, and our findings suggest the patient should accept an unmatched kidney as their rejection risk reaches a threshold. The concept of optimal acceptance can be understood through theoretical analysis, simulation results, and real-world examples.

Implicit ties in speech patterns can convey shared knowledge between speakers on challenging topics such as romance, friendship, and professional relationships. Current models of implicit ties fall into two categories: explicit strategies that involve direct communication, like talking about mutual connections or shared experiences, and unconscious phenomena that arise naturally during collaborative discussions. Research into implicit ties has revealed the influence of key factors such as the ease with which speech is processed, the presence of shared vocabulary, and the exchange of subtle non-verbal cues. This paper provides an overview of research surrounding implicit ties in speech and highlights notable implicit ties phenomena.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely used in subsequent tasks, relate to the semantic significance of words, with a specific emphasis on understanding financial regulatory documents. To assess the coherence of these embeddings, we employ the Loughran-McDonald sentiment dictionary, renowned for its reliability and influence in financial NLP research. Furthermore, we evaluate word2vec models applied to SEC filings, with a mathematical analysis highlighting both the capabilities and constraints of such models. To facilitate a thorough understanding, we establish a precise mapping between the word2vec loss function and probabilistic language generation, leading to valuable insights for future modeling approaches.

Y. Sun, J. Wang, and R. Zhang pioneered a novel method to optimize integrated data and energy transfer systems using multiple transmitters and receivers along with multiple frequency transmission channels. They demonstrated that their proposed system greatly enhances system performance by utilizing multiple antennas, multiple frequency channels, and a new underutilized resource called wideband waveforming. To maintain consistency with industry standards and facilitate practical implementation, this research paper investigates creating equivalent performance gains using conventional multiple-input single-output and multiple-input multiple-output wideband OFDM systems. By establishing theoretical equivalent relationships and providing numerical validations, this paper offers valuable design insights for achieving balanced data and power transfer through widely available wireless communication technologies.

This research introduces a new method for modeling the interaction between fluids with different temperatures that freeze or melt, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, we develop a numerical solution using the level-set technique to track the contact line and the embedded boundary method to model the crack. This method effectively handles complex scenarios, including pinching, self-touching boundaries, and pinned contact lines, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through various tests, solving the Stefan problem and considering surface tension effects.

A quantum logical framework has been developed to address the basic structure of human language, utilizing Schrödinger's formalism. This approach diverges from traditional classical logical models and is based on a quantum version of Tarski's semantic theory. Building upon existing work in quantum logic, the model is expanded to incorporate linguistic statements that express negation and modality, which occur frequently in human language. To accomplish this, a technique known as "putting a spin" is introduced. This method involves applying phase rotation and square root transformations to language propositions, drawing on the interpretation of the Bloch sphere. As a result, new quantum states are created to represent negation and modality, and these are explored from both mathematical and semantic perspectives. This development marks an initial step in formulating a quantum interpretation of language within the Tarskian framework and paves the way for a quantum semantic interpretation of Lodash.

Deep learning-based policy recommendations for games often employ zone diagrams that visually explain ideal equilibria. These zone diagrams also facilitate efficient sample usage in reinforcement learning by identifying sample-effective learning algorithms. This research introduces a way to project abstract game states onto the diagram's underlying space, enabling the first projectable state-space maps and a novel algorithm able to learn optimal equilibria efficiently using a limited number of samples. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness on the Batting game, achieving optimal value functions with fewer than one million interactions by leveraging an ideal zoning map, or interacting directly with the game environment in less than 250,000 interactions. The method's potential for facilitating cooperative learning in games is also discussed.

A dynamic model known as the Holten network evolves alongside an epidemic process, where the nodes' connections are swapped at a specific rate to track the spread of an infectious agent. As this tracking occurs, we monitor the epidemic's density and the clusterness of the network's fractal structure. When a certain threshold is met and a triadic cycle forms between neighboring nodes, the middle node recovers immediately. Without delay, and assuming a rapid tracking process, we find that increasing the network's cycle structure leads to a abrupt drop in epidemic density. The rate of this decrease can be calculated using an adjustable parameter that represents the efficiency of a preventive measure. The resulting system exhibits two distinct states and an unstable equilibrium between them. Delays in the network's cycle formation cause the middle node to lose a connection before the cycle is formed. This results in the middle node losing connectivity as the cycle is formed and leads to a change in the network's structure, leading to the middle node becoming infected again.

This research explores the interconnections between Cotton flow and both the structural and geometric properties of a nearly Kenmotsu 3-h-Manifold. Specifically, we identify conditions under which a manifold becomes invariant under the flow, and we establish that invariant manifolds will ultimately converge to a state of being Kenmotsu manifolds. Additionally, we establish necessary conditions for the existence of cotton solitons in relation to the 1-eigenspace of the tensor representing the manifold's conformal structure.

Partonic structure hadrons is crucial for precision measurements in high-energy physics experiments, particularly in processes involving deep inelastic scattering, particle production in proton collisions and the overall momentum distribution within the hadons described by the momentum sum rule. In recent years, with the advancement of global analyses combining data from various experiments, especially with more accurate measurements from electron-proton collisions at HERA and a new dataset from CMS in pp collisions at LHC, the need for a robust and transparent theoretical framework has become evident. This framework is now a prerequisite for incorporating the previous achievements of PDF fitting into the high-precision physics environment of the High-Luminosity LHC era. Furthermore, with the potential for establishing charged lepton beams with energies up to 65 GeV at FCC-ee in the future, even tighter constraints on the internal structure of hadrons could be imposed through processes such as neutral current and charged current reactions. As a consequence of these advancements, there is a growing demand for publicly available code that transparently implements numerical and statistical algorithms for global PDF fitting while ensuring the incorporation of state-of-the-art theoretical predictions consistent with next-to-next-to-leading order calculations including various migration effects, making sure the code is compatible with popular fitting libraries such as Coppela and EiCDF in order to meet these challenges.

To accelerate the convergence of policy optimization in reinforcement learning, a common practice is to combine data from various time periods in training. Although experience replay is a well-known technique, its underlying rationale remains unclear. By analyzing the algorithm through variance theory, this research reveals that the primary advantage of experience replay lies in reducing variance. Based on this finding, the paper proposes two innovative experience replay methods, the Batch Rehearsal Policy Optimization and the Variance Diminution Based Policy Optimization, which are simpler to implement but outperform the standard approach. To further minimize variance, the paper suggests utilizing online data and addressing the gradient estimation noise. The proposed methods demonstrate superior performance through evaluations in both continuous control and card games.

I present libcommute, a C++11/14/17 template library for performing operator algebra
calculations with customized numerical types, operator representations, and graph structures.
It includes a set of core functions and can be integrated with downstream projects,
including my Python wrapper libcommote and the Python operator algebra DSL pycommute.
pycommute is ideal for constructing Hamiltonians, and both libcommute and pycommute are
suitable for performing exact diagonalization with both classical and quantum computers.

We analyzed the electronic and superconducting gap structure of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)As$_{2}$ using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, focusing on various energy regions around the Fermi level. To reveal both coherent quasiparticle bands and the superconducting gap structure, we utilized our high-energy-resolution setup in conjunction with ultraviolet and soft-x-ray radiation at photon energies between 12 and 120 eet. Our measurements indicate an isotropic superconducting gap on the hole-like band near the $\Gamma$ point, with a maximum size of 3.5 meV, and observe nested electron-like bands and a nested hole-like band, the latter matching well with the nested electron-like bands in terms of Fermi velocity and binding energy. These findings suggest electron-electron interactions may be present near the hole-like band, which connects to the electron-like bands through a bandwidth transfer analysis and indicates holes and electrons weakly interact with one another.

Two different approaches have been employed to apply the supersymmetry technique to matrix variables, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization method. We demonstrate the equivalence of these two methods, and utilize the superbosonization method to derive the Berezin identity. Furthermore, this method is applied to calculate the average polynomial of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble matrices.

Initial findings from a measurement of the long-lived top quark decay product's angular distribution have yielded results consistent with the predicted polarization from a specific process outside of top quark pair production. To achieve this, a specialized technique has been utilized that focuses on the decay of the top quark and its antiparticle, respectively, and data were analyzed within various intervals of an impact parameter and photon transverse momentum. Additionally, a more comprehensive utilization of spin information in top quark events has been investigated by utilizing machine learning techniques and resulted in enhanced signal purity. These improvements have ultimately been applied to the polarization measurement and also facilitated a more in-depth study of the difference between the top quark and antitop quark interactions, ultimately supporting the standard model predictions with a high level of confidence.

Evaluating the impact of thickness and defect disorder on the conductive layer of LaNiO$_3$ within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices was conducted using $\beta$-detected NMR with spin-polarized $^8$Li. By varying the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness from 3 unit cells upwards, our study reveals that the conductive layer remains in a deeply polarized state with a broad resonance, while near the interface, there exists a partially undoped region with a distinct resonance. As the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness increases, the undoped region exhibits a unique evolution of resonance depth and width, displaying hysteresis as both the LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ layers grow.

In our effort to investigate advanced systems that engage in conversations, we are dealing with numerous unmanaged choices in the dialogue tree, affecting both the system and human participants. To tackle this problem, we are presenting a new dataset called MultiTalk, a management platform consisting of over 4500 node expansions managed sessions between human users. Notably, the dataset encompasses a wide range of topics in conversations, as well as human participants' responses. We are also introducing the concept of conversation set management tools, which provide the capability to experiment with diverse human-computer dialogue sessions. We propose two baseline systems that utilize the capabilities of the dataset, first, a simple rule-based system that showcases the dataset's potential, and second, a machine learning-based model trained to predict human responses. The results of the experiment demonstrate the value of the dataset in training high-performing systems that engage in diverse conversations, as well as the potential for future research to utilize the capabilities of the dataset to achieve even better performance.

This research analyzes and models the throughput of an wireless communication system, consisting of a single source and multiple destinations in a large-scale environment. In this system, an intelligent surface aids transmission by reflecting signals through a coherent space division multiple access approach. We account for correlated signal fading and a practical model of the surface that divides its elements into excited and passive sections, where only the former receive and transmit signals. By applying large-system analysis and deriving an integral equation, we can determine the average throughput of the system and evaluate how it is affected by phase-shift design, correlation, and the number of active elements on the surface. Our results show that increasing the number of active elements improves throughput up to a certain point, where additional surface elements contribute minimally to performance gains.

We introduce MG-Fast, an efficient tool for simulating N-body particles in theories of modified gravity. MG-Fast allows researchers to replicate the results of a vast number of simulations with different parameters by scaling specific quantities, significantly reducing computational time. This method involves creating a single high-resolution simulation in reduced units and then adjusting the scaling factors to produce the desired output. Our approach works with various theories such as f(R), D6R, and Hubble-parametrized models, and can even account for dynamic functions and cosmological evolution. The integrity of these simulations has been verified by comparing their outcomes to high-resolution simulations for specific cases. MG-Fast provides high-quality density fields and can be accessed via its publicly available Python interface and accompanying documentation.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a model for chordal Gaussian free fields in the upper half-plane, characterized by a family of driving processes in the upper half-plane that influence the Gaussian free field, with corresponding SLE curves representing the g-level lines. This framework establishes an equivalence between the driving processes and the SLE curves. This equivalence enables the construction of models analogous to two-dimensional gravity, where polygons are bounded by these lines. Specifically, considering a one-component log-gas on the interval $[0,1]$ with interactions proportional to $\kappa$, we obtain an equivalent model to $\kappa$-CFF coupled with one $\kappa$-SLE in the upper half-plane, where the boundary of a polygon formed by two i.i.d. $\kappa$-Bessel processes and two independent monotone $\kappa$-SLEs in the upper half-plane, with driving processes being increasing functions of a Brownian motion. Additionally, we derive formulas for the probability that this polygon has a non-empty interior and the expected area of its interior.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source derivative designed as a collaborative workspace for'research-in-action'. Its primary function is to facilitate structured collaboration between experts and individuals with less technical knowledge, by integrating and sharing knowledge within a shared knowledge base (SKB). The WorkingWiki template can be easily deployed using 'MediaWiki Template Installer', which also supports the popular 'Semantic MediaWiki' extension. Researchers who utilize WorkingWiki have the ability to customize 'SMWQL' queries and visually present their data through 'Semantic MediaWiki Client Tools', effectively turning their project into a dynamic, interactive SKB. We demonstrate the installed Template's features through the 'WorkingGeoNet Wiki' project, a sub-project of GeoNet, which focuses on New Zealand's geological hazard monitoring.

This study investigates the combustion response of a turbulent jet flame in a combustion chamber as it transitions from a low-fluctuation state to a highly active state when subjected to acoustic forcing. To simulate the active flame state accurately, the research utilizes an active flame modelling technique that adjusts the injection rate of the turbulent jet to maintain a desired state. By integrating this approach with linear stability theory and the equivalence between linearized Navier-Stokes and Lagrangian frameworks, the combustion dynamics can be simplified. The resulting model employs linearized equations of state and flame speed adjustments as linearized flame models. The research findings show that the active flame state exhibits a significant amplification of pressure fluctuations at the combustion chamber's fundamental mode resonance when the injection rate adjustment gain reaches a critical threshold. The gain parameter's value directly controls the system's stability, while the highly active flame state can be characterized as an unstable limit cycle within a linearized framework. To achieve this state accurately, the research suggests utilizing more complex flame models that account for flame surface area and local mixture fraction fluctuations. Furthermore, the results indicate that the highly active flame state utilizes the turbulent jet flame's ability to modulate the turbulent kinetic energy within the combustion chamber.

We propose a novel method for identifying topological phases in stars through the use of invariant circle maps, which are sensitive to both frequency and stellar structure. This approach builds upon previously developed invariants for stellar topological phases by incorporating a more comprehensive framework. Our theory is validated using a model similar to Lorenz oscillators, representing mixing dynamics in stars. Additionally, we apply our method to analyze the mixing properties in realistic stars, discovering a range of stars with similar mixing behaviors and characteristics that correlate with specific stellar parameters.

A new universal method has been developed to classify dynamic phenomena in networks of spiking neurons, specifically distinguishing between synchronized and chaotic states of travelling waveforms known as chimeras. This method is unaffected by factors like the measure of synchronization used or the type of interactions between the neurons. It builds upon a previous theory of dynamic synchronization by distinguishing between states of dynamic order and disordered states, including tripersists. In addition to classifying waveforms, this method can determine the structure of synchronized clusters by distinguishing between coherent states and chaotic dynamics within those clusters. We applied this method to investigate the impact of noise on waveforms and cluster structures in an oscillatory network, discovering that a certain type of noise can enhance chaos and disrupt the travelling waveforms and cluster coherence.

Our new variant of the 2D Ising model is based on a 2 by 2 by 2 list of interaction values, which vary across neighboring site pairs on a 3D cubic lattice. We use the mapping to convert this into a 2D Ising model with 4 distinct interaction values, which then correspond to cluster types. Monte Carlo simulations reveal that the system exhibits an explosive transition at high temperatures, where it suddenly shifts from a disordered state to an interlocked multi-cluster low temperature state. These simulation outcomes are complemented by precise mathematical derivations of the model's entropy and energy properties in their extreme high and low temperature limits.

We investigate the impact of ultralight dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay, Neutrino DM halo forming a background that may interfere with experimental signals. The frequency of halo particles at Earth's location depends on ultralight DM properties and the position within the galaxy, leading to oscillating modulations in the Neutrino DM flux. This could provide insight into the mass and decay constants of DM particles through analysis of neutrino data. In addition, we consider the effects of Neutrino DM interactions on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the Cosmic Microwave Background, which place stringent constraints on the neutrino-DM interaction strength. The level of these interactions also influences the structure formation of dark matter halos, potentially providing further constraints. However, we find that in regions of high matter density, such as the galactic center, neutrino reactions can be so intense that halos transition to mixed phases of neutrino gas and dark matter clumps, affecting structure formation in those areas.

The isotropic flux of ultra-high energy photons may originate from a process 
called synchrotron self-termination, which occurs within solar magnetic fields. 
To understand this process, we created a model that accounts for the interaction 
of ultra-high energy cosmic ray protons with cosmic microwave background, 
resulting in the emission of ultra-high energy photons and neutral pions. These 
photons then diffuse within the solar magnetic field until they escape or get 
absorbed in synchrotron radiation. Our analysis reveals that processes 
involving solar magnetic fields can explain the observed ultra-high energy 
photons flux limits established by the HiRes and the Auger experiments. Our 
model also indicates that if a significant portion of the ultra-high energy 
cosmic ray composition is made up of neutral pions, the observed ultra-high 
energy photon flux limits would be easily accounted for. Furthermore, our 
model naturally predicts the presence of an ultra-high energy neutron flux 
around $10^{9} GeV$.

Nonlocal gravity theory offers an alternative explanation for phenomena attributed to dark matter and dark energy. In this study, we derive the fundamental equations of motion, known as the nonlocal Poisson equation, directly from a specific nonlocal gravitational action. This derivation reveals a frame-dependent nonlocal term that needs to be accounted for. We also investigate the implications of this alternative gravitational equation on matter distribution, particularly in scenarios of stationary equilibrium, and compare the results with those from the standard local equation. We find that for regions where the nonlocal term is significant, notable deviations from expected density profiles occur. These outcomes are verified through numerical simulations using a nonlocal solver, both with and without considering the frame-dependent term. We explore the nonlocal equation's consequences for galaxy rotation curves and the cosmic expansion, finding sufficient evidence of frame dependence in rotating galaxies but negligible effects in the cosmic expansion.

Conflicting updates pose a significant challenge in replicated storage systems, leading to divergence across copies and hindering real-time collaboration. Existing solutions, like Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), address this issue but often come with performance and flexibility limitations. We propose an adaptable design framework for conflict-free data structures that prioritably delivers functional equivalence, replica state consistency, and efficient operation performance. Our framework provides a set of design principles and examples, potentially guiding developers in creating customized, high-performance CRDTs that meet specific application needs.

Functional genomics data can offer useful insights into the biological functions related to certain genomic regions, which can inform our understanding of the genetic basis of complex traits and diseases. A novel statistical method is presented that integrates functional genomics data with results from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) across the entire genome. This method, known as Genomic Control, standardizes the variance of a score derived from comparing GWAS and functional genomics data, thereby producing a modified p-value. It is then used to identify variants, genomic regions, and network motifs that are significantly enriched for associations with specific traits and diseases. The method was tested using 18 human traits and diseases as pilot studies, with results showcasing its effectiveness in revealing biological patterns related to muscle strength, obesity, and Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, the score can be controlled to facilitate regional or biological-enriched association testing, which was further explored through case studies on grip strength, body mass, and Alzheimer's disease.

This study discusses the significance and technical aspects of using minor collision events in hadron physics experiments, with a focus on improving physics capabilities, and explores how this approach can be employed to detect heavy particles or study rare phenomena in searches using leptons or jets at hadron colliders.

A well-known characteristic of low-mass X-ray binaries is their quiescent periods, typically measured by the time interval between outbursts. This time varies greatly among different sources and is often irregular. As a result, predicting the time of next outburst based on historical outburst patterns is a difficult task. Our analysis of outburst periods for 11 sources in the vicinity of the Galactic Centre reveals the significant role of accretion disk precession in explaining their irregular recurrence times. Notable among these sources are XTE J1739-285, which exhibits a precession period of approximately 1.1 years that aligns with its past outburst observations, and XRF 1736-345, for which a shorter axis precession period of about 4 years fits its outburst data better than its commonly accepted 16-year period. Our study also implies a minimum distance of at least 0.03 parsecs for X-ray binaries near the Galactic Centre, otherwise, a close approach to the supermassive black hole would occur within their typical outburst period. Estimating the total number of such X-ray binaries within a minimum radius of 0.15 parsecs, we find there should be a minimum of eight such X-ray binaries that do not emit detectable X-rays from the vicinity of the supermassive black hole. Our findings also suggest a possible explanation for the apparent overabundance of soft gamma

Wide stellar pairs are highly effective in testing diverse theoretical gravity concepts, particularly those that may be expanded into modified theories. We investigate the size distribution of wide stellar pairs, discovering a notable proportion of pairs with separations greater than 1000 astronomical units. Notable research projects such as the Pan-STARRS1 Three-Pi Catalog, which contains over 1,100 such wide pairs, provide a rich data set for analysis. Careful examination, including the study of multiple astrophysical phenomena, reveals that most known influences on wide pair dynamics do not account for the observed stability of these systems. We further present an in-depth analysis of their dynamics, utilizing a model that accounts for observed phenomena and demonstrates that the majority of wide pairs remain stable, as predicted by both Newton's gravity and General Relativity.

Radio observations of large-scale structures in the universe using low-frequency arrays have been hindered by radio sources that are compact and faint. These sources can compromise the sensitivity of the observations and reduce the achievable baseline. To characterize the properties of these sources in a reliable manner, researchers need to account for their spectral behavior and the variation in their brightness across different parts of the sky. This study investigates the relationships between various properties of a sample of 1159 compact faint radio sources as a function of their angular size through a statistical analysis method called stacking. By converting flux values into natural logarithms to ensure the validity of this analysis, we discovered significant correlations between several properties of the sources as they relate to their angular size. Specifically, as the sources become smaller, their polarization percentage increases, their color becomes more reddish, and their morphological complexity also becomes more pronounced. To better understand these relationships, the study employs simple theoretical models with limited parameters to describe the sources as mini radiotestbeds containing one or more components with different characteristics. These models successfully capture the key features of the observed data and provide a framework for interpreting the sources in a physically meaningful way. Additionally, a new source of large public data is introduced to address the limitation of previous datasets, which were often contaminated by marginal detections and lacked polarization information.

This research investigates the impact of starquakes on shock wave propagation in nearby systems. We examine how the dynamic behavior and heating of the surrounding medium, as well as the development of shock waves, are influenced by the star's oscillatory motion. We focus on the performance of 1D radiation-hydrodynamic simulations in a stellar seismological context, addressing the issue of numerical dissipation on sub-seismological scales. The simulated scenarios are categorized based on the ratio of the stellar oscillation frequency to the rate of the sound wave passing through the stellar surface. The results reveal a significant increase in the stellar envelope's temperature due to sound wave heating. The presence of a shock wave is heavily dependent on the stellar size and the surrounding medium, with the stellar squaring effect on wave morphology being a dominant factor in the development of the shock wave. The outcomes of the simulations are then used to infer the potential for starquakes to facilitate the propagation of sound waves in systems with active magnetic activity, such as young stars, and to assess the feasibility of utilizing starquake-induced seismic activity for dating the age of such systems.

This paper explores three algebras or non-mathematical structures whose representations or elements seem to link to classical algebraic geometry, and for each, there's a associated "moment map" that produces an interesting variety. These are: first, a pair of opposite subalgebras within the complexified Kac-Vergne Lie algebra whose elements commute, associated with the Grassmannian; second, the skew group algebra of $SL_2(\mathbb{C})$ and the integers, associated with the spherical variety $SL_2^{!1}$; and lastly, the Gelfand-Ziglin algebra, associated with the flag manifold. In each case, we identify an integer point in the image of a moment map from an algebra to a flag manifold or other spherical variety. To do this, we derive a geometrically interpreted formula for a specific integer - linked to algebraic geometry and representation theory - by applying a method of geometric integration that utilizes the language of D-modules. This approach may have broader applications in geometry and physics, with connections to the Carnot upper half-plane and Chern-Simons theory on this algebra.

We develop a theoretical framework to examine the impact of acoustic phonons on solid materials, deriving specific changes in electronic density functional theory within the perturbation of phonon displacement. This framework enables the calculation of the acoustic electron-phonon interactions, spin-phonon coupling, and the associated adiabatic potential for electrons and phonons. Notably, we discover that the electron-phonon coupling constant can be expressed through the electronic momentum dipole and subsequently obtain the form of the spin-phonon coupling, which arises from the interaction between the spin magnetic moment and the electronic orbital induced by strain field. Furthermore, the spin-phonon coupling can be expressed in terms of the materials' elastic properties, Young's modulus, and the magnetic moment. Based on this framework, we also investigate the spin-phonon coupling in typical materials, such as Cu, Ni, and HoO2, and show that its magnitude is approximately 10-12 eV/A~{-}1~s~{1}~ and HoO2 exhibits the strongest coupling.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes serve as an overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, with a focus on its core concepts, and will also introduce some recent major breakthroughs within the field. Given their informal nature, a basic familiarity with quivers and algebras is assumed.

Conversational interactions between humans lead to a diverse range of language
structures and meanings, in stark contrast to single-turn conversations which
can be examined through binary yes/no answers to nuanced questions.  To better
capture the complexity of human language in response to semantically varied
inputs, we introduce a new benchmark for Natural Language Generation (NLG)评估
known as Semantic Variety in Dialogue (SVID).  The proposed SVID benchmark
consists of 4,800 noun-verb pair combinations generated by humans, resulting in
5,880 unique combinations per participant, across eight different languages.  This
new benchmark enables evaluation of NLG models on their ability to generalize
to novel combinations of concepts, rather than merely memorizing specific
combinations.  To begin addressing this challenge of semantic generalization,
we develop a simple baseline model that achieves satisfactory performance on
evaluation metrics known as BLEU and ROUGE, while exhibiting considerable room
for improvement.

Automated driving systems depend on predicting pedestrians' intentions to avoid accidents.  However, interpreting partial information from video frames is a complex task due to the limited field of view and reliance on safety cameras.  To address this challenge, our approach uses a set of video clips captured during lane changes to classify hazardous actions of pedestrians.  By combining the segmentation masks of detected pedestrians with analysis of the clip's content, our method achieves higher accuracy than using clips alone.  We propose a two-stage network that first transfers segmentation masks using an encoder-decoder module and then classifies the adapted clips through a temporal convolutional network.  This design allows for the use of fewer clip frames and accounts for the static information in the images.  Our method extracts key features from the clips and masks to capture the context of the scene and the object interactions.  To train the network, we created HAZVID, a new dataset with annotated HMI labels for safety-critical pedestrian actions during vehicle lane changes, and it will be made publicly available for research purposes.

The potential existence of rotating brown dwarfs and black dwarfs as ultimate merging planets has long been debated. This study seeks to establish the mass-shedding limits of rotating objects by simulating them as fluid bodies subject to rotation forces, accounting for possible non-steady states and differential fluid rotation. Starting with different initial conditions, one-dimensional simulations gradually lead to mass ejection at the mass-shedding limit. Notably, even rapidly rotating brown dwarfs can exist, filling an extensive region of the effective temperature versus mass diagram. This finding implies that rotating brown dwarfs represent a substantial portion of the parameter space available.

In complex particle physics experiments, particularly in amplitude analyses, intricate instrumental and physical influences are captured in the data in an uninterpretable manner in the measured angles and decay distances. To isolate and understand these effects at a fundamental level, one would need a comprehensive detector simulation coupled with a detailed particle flux model. However, such an approach proves to be computationally costly. As an efficient workaround, practitioners employ simplified effective models designed to replicate the observed experimental distortions. In this study, we introduce the first generic effective model that can serve any amplitude analysis conducted by the LHCb collaboration, utilizing Bayesian methods to fit the model's intrinsic effective parameters directly from experimental data. The resulting models are computationally minimal, typically involving less than 10 parameters per reaction and process, and their impact on decay data is modeled through a computationally efficient matrix. To validate the effectiveness of these simplified effective models, we demonstrate their utility in estimating bias in multivariate amplitude analyses and accurately estimating statistical uncertainties in mass measurements, achieving an accuracy within 1-3 standard deviations of the theoretical values.

A significant number of high-energy cosmical phenomena are associated with Long Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), and their Afterglows have long provided strong evidence for this association. The theory behind this connection dates back to the 1990s, when the fireball model was first proposed. Over the past 20 years, numerous observations and data collections have significantly progressed, fueling both theoretical and practical research and development projects focused on Grand Extragalactic Afterglow (GREBA) models. While traditional fireball models have often relied on the simplifying assumption of monochromatic radiation, these models have been observed to deviate from actual data in significant ways. As a result, alternative models have been put forward, often incorporating multiple components or extending into cosmological effects, but they lack a universally accepted standard model due to the complexity of afterglow dynamics. This study puts forward a novel, comprehensive afterglow model that lacks complex extensions, and demonstrates a notable correlation between the afterglow flux values and time duration across the X-ray, optical, and infrared spectral ranges, based on a dataset of 148 bursts from the GALEX Afterglow Database. The theoretical framework proposes multiple theoretical flux evolution functions and displays a strong correlation coefficient of 0.71, in contrast to the existing power-law models.
