A cellular automaton model was used to simulate a two-species interaction on a square lattice, with one species capable of moving across multiple sites at a time. This model accounted for a species competition and a dispersal process, with the result being a stable coexistence of both species when there was no L. A noise-induced species exclusion was also observed, with a critical threshold of disorder beyond which only the more competitive species remained, with the threshold dependent on the species that has the competitive advantage. Additionally, a second critical threshold was identified, with a change in the dynamic of the system from a dynamic phase with both species coexisting to a disordered phase with the less competitive species occupying the borders of clusters of the more competitive species, with both thresholds being unaffected by the movement of the more competitive species. A theoretical model with a mean-field approximation supported these findings with a prediction of the more unconventional threshold exhibiting a data-derived exponent value.

Timekeeping devices known as sundials rely on the position of the Sun in the sky to determine the time and cease functioning during overcast conditions or nighttime. Despite this limitation, research on sundials often incorporates data from these instruments. However, the current practice of sundial research varies, particularly in Indonesian, where the focus often remains on restoring and fixing sundials instead of utilizing them for time management. To address this, a project in Indonesia aims to utilize working sundials to track the position of the Sun throughout the day, thus providing the necessary light to advance the development of sundial time management technology. This project also seeks to create a national database of Indonesian sundials by creating and sharing open-the-day schedules through a website called suryakala.nusantara.id, which also provides restoration guides for sundials. Consequently, the project involves establishing a dedicated server, designing a sundial schedule algorithm, developing the sundial schedule website, promoting the sundial schedule through social media, collaborating with sundial owners, and ensuring data security on the server.

This research explores a novel Cognition Reflecting Surface (IRS)-assisted Integrated Data and Energy Transfer (IDET) system, which can coexist with Device-to-Device (D2D) communications. A mathematical model is proposed that accounts for phase coupling between the transmitting and receiving surfaces, as well as between the surfaces and the communication endpoints. In this model, a secondary D2D link seeks to maximize its data rate by efficiently utilizing the energy transferred from the transmitting surface to the receiving surface. Furthermore, an optimized control strategy is developed to balance data rate optimization and energy consumption in the IRS-assisted DET system. This research provides closed-form approximations for data rate performance and exact data rate distribution characteristics, as well as moment approximations for energy harvesting power. Monte Carlo simulations verify the theoretical findings, and key insights into system performance are explicitly stated.

To expand the applicability of LDV systems to difficult-to-reach areas, this study explores using an external trigger mechanism to overcome limitations imposed by the system's range. The proposed system successfully employs a single, high-power LDV unit to capture two-dimensional data clouds of complex targets, such as 3D-printed models and a human head, by utilizing one LDV unit and a separate close-range device. A newly designed algorithm has also been created with the ability to convert distant data into detailed 2D images, achieving a level of accuracy below 10 mm when given appropriate data settings. Furthermore, the system overcomes the constraints of existing approaches, which are limited to measuring optically accessible surfaces, by successfully capturing indirectly visible areas through careful LDV unit placement and precise vector angle management.

The effectiveness of modern TEMs is significantly hindered by chromatic and spherical aberrations generated by various components, including the spherical and chromatic phase plates required for spherical aberration scattering mode (SSCM). The researchers in this study investigated whether a programmable phase plate (PPP) in the image formation mode could compensate for these intrinsic TEM-generated aberrations, rather than just adding minimal scattering as seen in previous designs. By utilizing the full programmability of the PPP, it was proposed to replace its previous design with a more versatile approach. Theoretical and numerical analysis was carried out to evaluate the feasibility of this concept, and a unique solution was discovered for the degree of spherical phase that maximizes the coherence of the image. The results show that coherent SSCCM and diffraction (选) mode (CM) can be achieved simultaneously with an appropriately programmed PPP, and residual incoherent light can be minimized to less than 1% of the total light in the incoherent mode (CM). The degree of local coherence in the image can also be adjusted by altering the PPP's phase profile, and any remaining limitations can be overcome with computational imaging techniques. The findings suggest that a programmable phase plate has the potential to replace a spherical aberrator, and further investigation into its capabilities is warranted.

The success of data-driven models in generating coherent conversations heavily relies on their ability to generalize beyond scripted responses. Despite this challenge being well-established, a comprehensive understanding of what encoder representations convey in the task of dialogue state tracking (DST) is still lacking. The primary objective of our research was to experimentally assess the content and utility of these encoder representations in conveying essential information about the DST task. The results indicated that similar representations are produced for semantically equivalent utterances and that they can be effectively controlled through the application of similar similarity metrics used in other fields such as machine reading comprehension. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that BERT-based encoders excel at extracting relevant information for downstream tasks when combined with a linear layer, but they struggle to convey all necessary information for the generation of coherent responses. The significance of this finding is highlighted by the establishment of a strong baseline for enhanced models in the future.

Deep learning technology has excelled in image-based location identification systems and has now been applied to LiDAR data as well, with previous studies designing sequential neural networks to extract features from LiDAR data. These models have shown promising results but suffer from overfitting when trained on limited datasets due to their excessive number of parameters. To address this issue, a novel location recognition framework called AttDLNet is introduced, which leverages a attention mechanism to efficiently select crucial channel features and suppress less relevant ones. This approach not only improves model performance below the dataset's variance but also facilitates easy expansion with different LiDAR sensors and software versions, as proven by the location recognition results on the SWEAL dataset.

Streaming high-quality video, such as HDMI and Blu-ray, over the internet is compromised by viewer device limitations and internet bandwidth constraints. To address this, video transcoding is utilized to adapt content to the hardware and software capabilities of the receiving device. This study evaluates the performance of video transcoding services, powered by cloud-based processors, in relation to device hardware, software, type of content, and processing speed. A statistical model was developed to predict the outcomes of video transcoding processes, resulting in the creation of equation-based formulas. These equations demonstrate significant accuracy, with average deviations of 4.2% for download and 5.7% for playback events. The research led to a practical application, the Video Speed Planner, which enables producers to anticipate the speed at which viewers will be able to watch their videos, taking into account device hardware, content, and processing rate.

This paper derives a linear screening formula specifically for massless Dirac fermions in doped graphene within a high-temperature environment. 
Our high-temperature approximation yields useful insights into the heat capacity of doped graphene, addressing limitations of previous linear screening models derived within perturbation theory. 
These limitations include the failure of such approaches at low temperatures and with high doping levels. 
Our derived formula is validated by direct calculation using the Mermin approximation for both clean and disordered doped graphene. 
Furthermore, the linear screening formula can be used to estimate the absolute doped graphene temperature in astro-physical settings.

One-sided conversational data lacks the natural co-dependency between language and speech that characterizes real human-animal interactions. To address this, research on co-generative models of language and speech has gained popularity, but existing unified models fall short in several areas: they struggle with diverse acoustic styles, are limited by reliance on pre-trained models, and tend to use a masking approach that ignores contextual cues. In response, we present MaskedSpeech, a context-sensitive co-generative model that excels at producing speech across various styles and shows superior performance on speech-to-language and joint text-speech tasks. Key to MaskedSpeech is its masking strategy that seamlessly integrates contextual cues through cross-task pre-training.

We provide a detailed explanation of the variational approach to solving the stationary variant of the Klein-Gordon-Schrodinger equation.
This varational principle is then used to investigate the spectral and schrittweise-Stabilitat of the variational solution's associated operator.
Furthermore, the variational solution offers a distinct alternative to existing approaches in reference [13, 20].

Q-ball studies are expanded to include a wide range of quantum corrections and multiple quantum loads, such as pions or gluinos.  A systematic method is introduced for computing quantum corrections using a dual classical equation of motion.  The effectiveness of this procedure is verified with QCD and an example is provided where Q-balls become unstable due to the production of massless gluinos, resulting in the Q-balls developing cores.  The relationship between Q-balls and dark matter is also discussed.

We re-examine the hypothesis of a holographic dark energy sector within a cyclic universe based on Kaluza-Klein geometry, considering different possibilities for the four-dimensional universe. We utilize a scale-invariant constraint to determine the holographic infrared cutoff, and the initial size of the universe is considered to impact its entropy. Calculated upper bounds for the holographic parameter $\omega$ are derived, and these values fall within the range required for a universe that can expand repeatedly.

Given a graph G, let's denote its vertex set by V(G) and the edges as an adjacency matrix A. This paper explores the connection between an 'scattering matrix' S, which corresponds to a Hermitian matrix, and the graph's structure. Firstly, we establish a direct correlation between the scattering matrix and the graph's adjacency matrix. Consequently, this relationship implies that S essentially encapsulates all the properties of G. Moreover, if the scattering matrix is unitary, we obtain a set of unitary matrices that maintain the graph's adjacency properties. This paper also provides a method to create a scattering matrix from any graph, including the creation of a scattering matrix from the cycle graph C_n that results in a set of discrete Fourier transforms. This discovery implies that such a transformation is also possible for graphs that can form a covering set over cycled adjacency matrices.

We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-commutative number field extension L of Q to have an integer ring over L whose maximal p-rational subextension can be clearly described. The criterion is applicable to any number field L, provided certain conditions are met. Notably, we establish the condition for a free L-pmodule of a countably infinite rank to hold, then examine specific cases, including when L is obtained by adjoining p-adic Abel-Sendfern or p-addic Iwasawa extensions to Q.

Incorporating the benefits of the Belle and Belle II experiments, we examine axial leptoquarks based on certain beyond Standard Model assumptions. These particles could mediate electron-muon interactions between quarks and leptons, potentially violating various conservation laws. We explore how leptoquarks affect $B$ meson decay patterns and consider their impact on data anomalies observed at Belle. By simulating Belle II's enhanced sensitivity, we establish constraints on the leptoquark parameters and identify potential signals in specific $B$ decay channels, such as $\bar{B} \to K^\ast (e \mu) \bar{
\nu_e}$. Our findings indicate that future experiments could either provide evidence for these particles or set stricter limits on their properties.

Recent advances in contextual language modeling have led to significant progress in various NLP tasks. This achievement came as a revelation to researchers, who were initially surprised to see that pre-trained language models could outperform individual word embeddings. This was in contrast to their earlier conclusions, where they had even filed a patent based on their research that utilized dense vectors derived from句中 words. This patent, which relied on a specific interpretation of Distributed Representation, had a notable limitation when compared to the recent developments in contextualized language models.

Considering the loss of energy from heavy spinning stars like black holes, this study delves into how this impacts the measured spin properties of heavy stars, such as the dimensionless parameter $\alpha$ in the $\Delta \alpha/\alpha$ formula, which represents the relative change in the fine structure constant over time. We specifically examine the relationship between this quantity and the total mass of ultralight bosonic dark matter surrounding these black holes. We also analyze the consequences this has on relative velocity measurements of atomic clouds and the ultimate constraints it places on ultralight bosons from the observed spin properties of heavy stars with extreme masses up to eight gigagrams, assuming the detected data comes from the eXtremely Large Telescope and its atomic cloud observations in the late 2020s to early 2030s.

A key feature of the zebrafish neural tube is interkinetic nuclear migration, where nuclei migrate along the axis of the developing tissue. In zebrafish retina development, this migration pattern is especially clear. Upt1, a motor protein essential for migrating nuclei in the zebrafish retina, was utilized to study the movement of nuclei and their associated chromatin. Following the synthesis of new components during interphase, the nuclei release their motor proteins, enabling the onset of mitosis. Our analysis revealed that without Upt1, mitosis is not affected, but the progression of mitosis to the completion of a full cell cycle is hindered. By releasing Upt1, the normal movement of eggs and capsules is disrupted, yet their formation is not. Our modeling indicates that nuclei migrate as result of a balance between the release of new components and their degradation, similar to how heat dissipates. Furthermore, the release of Upt1 during mitosis is comparable to suddenly removing a source of energy, generating a wave-like effect in the surrounding tissue. Our high-speed imaging allowed us to observe this "release wave" in real-time, which was not present when Upt1 was continuously released. The retention of chromatin during mitosis is also affected by the continuous release of Upt1, resulting in the chromatin undergoing turbulent movements during mitosis. Our study provides new insights into the complex interactions between the nuclei and their surrounding environment, and has significant implications for understanding how neurons

In recent advancements in color image demosaicing and compressive video restoration, deep learning methods have consistently surpassed traditional techniques. While the predominant approach involves employing extensive and varied training datasets to elevate performance, this strategy can be both time-consuming and computationally demanding in terms of storage. As an alternative, we introduce a novel, computationally efficient framework for image demosaicing and compressive video restoration, which utilizes a minimal minimal training set and incorporates both computational and large-scale data augmentation techniques within the training process. This framework has been successfully applied to two restoration tasks, yielding improved performance with a significantly reduced training dataset and overall computational and data efficiency.

We've developed a comprehensive theoretical framework to examine the dynamics of active fluids subject to noise of varying intensity in dimensions three and four. This model is based on the Navier-Stokes equations, augmented by stochastic elements representing turbulent fluctuations. Our analysis yields unique solutions that accurately reflect the known behavior of incompressible velocities in these dimensions. By applying renormalization techniques, we have derived a set of effective parameters capable of capturing the effects of active turbulence and quantifiable noise. These parameters can be integrated into generalized diffusive models, providing a reliable and accurate representation of active particle behavior in both two-dimensional habitats and the more complex scenarios present in three-dimensional spaces. Our findings align with existing theoretical predictions and experimental observations regarding dispersion rates, the intensity of fluctuation forces, and drag-induced rotational effects on particles in active environments.

In today's highly interconnected world, understanding and preventing the spread of influence within social networks is a pressing concern. Within the realm of the academic community, the potential for the dissemination of ideas within research collaboration networks remains understudied. A novel approach is presented in this paper for analyzing the potential for the spread of ideas within such networks by considering their dynamic nature. We suggest a time-dependent Small-World (SW) network model that accurately reflects the evolution of research collaboration networks, and employ stochastic matrix methods to examine its stability. The analysis reveals that certain critical thresholds govern the potential for large-scale idea dissemination, and that these thresholds are significantly influenced by the rate of network evolution. The proposed theory is then applied to a real-world dataset of neuroscience researchers, and the resulting SW network identified is found to exhibit a unique structural composition consisting of multiple interconnected components.

High-quality, large-scale buckytubes exhibit an unusual isolated peak in their pseudogapped metallic transport properties when measured at mid-bands, which also appears in related large-scale buckytube materials. This peak's position and size cannot be attributed to disorder broadening or weak localization effects. Instead, calculations suggest it originates from the three-dimensional nature of electron transport and can be connected to disorder-induced fluctuations.

This paper describes a specialized experimental arrangement designed to investigate the effects of spallation neutrons on particle movement in the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory. The proposed device involves a vacuum chamber with an embedded metal cavity, which when struck by a high-energy proton beam, generates a significant increase in neutron yield. The experiment aims to verify theoretical predictions and existing data with more accurate measurements, improved by a new apparatus featuring enhanced safety measures and a modernized detection system powered by state-of-the-art neutron-capturing devices.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for a biharmonic Choquard type equation, where the function $V$ does not have a compact support property, and has an exponentially growing potential, specifically:
$$
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\left[\Delta^2 u-\Delta u\right]
+V(x)u=\left(|x|^{-\mu}\ast|u|^{q}\right)
\frac{f(u)}{u}
, & x\in\mathbb{R}^4
\\
\displaystyle
\int_{\mathbb{R}^4}u^2\,dx=a^2
, & a>0
\end{cases}
$$
To prove the existence of a normalized ground state solution, we employ Trudinger-Moser embedding techniques and minimization methods.

Ground-based telescopes complement space-based transit photometry from various perspectives, allowing for precise measurements of planetary characteristics. Specifically, radial velocity data from the Keck/HIRES telescope will be used to determine the masses of planets detected by the Telescience Survey, enabling the calculation of their densities and orbital parameters from both systems. To integrate with existing data, we utilize the IAU's orbital element standards and leverage the stellar astrometry from TESS to improve mass estimates through more accurate mass-transit velocity derivations. This approach will enable the characterization of planets around nearby stars and potentially allow dispersion measurements. We focus on determining how stellar activity impacts transit photometry and radial velocity data, respectively, and utilize both datasets to make spatial and temporal comparisons. Ultimately, combining TESS and HiRES data around a diverse range of exoplanets and their hosts will provide valuable insights into planet formation and migration processes, and utilize TESS's deep, wide-field transits to observe previously unexplored regions of the mass-period parameter space. Given HiRES's ability to observe a wide spectrum of wavelengths, it is also possible to detect the atmospheric composition of small, temperate planets through transit spectroscopy, although this requires precise timing of phase curves and subsequent analysis of spectral features. Building on HiRES's sensitivity and its ability to detect small, low-mass stars and sub-stellar objects, we aim to make precise measurements of the mass of these celestial bodies and detect atmospheric features of young,气态巨行星

The growth of technology has significantly impacted information dissemination, making it challenging to verify the authenticity of shared information. Although various methods exist for extracting information, utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) offers a more efficient solution, as it not only accelerates the process but also enhances its effectiveness. OCR technology enables the automatic extraction of information from Indonesian ID cards, streamlining the verification and search processes. By integrating OCR with Natural Language Processing (NLP), the precision of the extracted information is enhanced, ultimately facilitating the matching of personal data with an individual's ID card number. This approach provides a more straightforward means of searching and retrieving information, as demonstrated by our study's successful implementation of OCR and NLP to extract data from Indonesian ID cards, either from front to back or vice versa, using Tesseract 5.0 as the NLP tool and achieving a data accuracy of 91.7% in our experiments.

A Monte Carlo integration method is developed for calculating the steady-state properties of a quantum harmonic oscillator in a one-dimensional space. This approach utilizes a simulation where the position of a particle in the harmonic potential is measured at discrete times preceding its driving by the application of an external force. A down-wards process in time correlates with the increasing time interval between adjacent observations. Analytical and numerical results for various scenarios, including driven and undriven harmonic oscillators, demonstrate the effectiveness of methodology. This method potentially offers efficiency and simplicity in obtaining path integral representations for many-body systems in a state of thermal equilibrium.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect is a physical phenomenon that significantly impacts the rotational movement of small asteroids in space. This effect can lead to changes in an asteroid's rotation speed, and in certain cases, it can cause the asteroid to rotate so fast that it loses rocks and debris due to centrifugal forces, a process known as mass shedding. As a result of mass shedding, the YORP effect can ultimately bring the asteroid's rotation to a complete stop, also known as synchronous rotation. In this context, the rate of change of an asteroid's rotation velocity caused by the YORP effect is ultimately linked to the occurrence of mass shedding. This study aims to create mathematical models that can either predict when a asteroid will start to lose mass or determine the conditions under which mass shedding occurs. These models are applied to three well-studied asteroids - 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro - for which scientists already have known surface features, shapes, and physical compositions, allowing for more accurate estimations of the effects of the YORP effect on their rotation velocities.

Social media platforms provide conversation spaces that combine positive and negative experiences, ultimately reflecting and influencing societal discussions. To gauge the emotional tone of political conversations on Instagram, we compiled a network from publicly available captions and comments, then analyzed their emotional content using LSA and NLP techniques. Our findings reveal an asymmetric structure in these conversations, characterized by a core group utilizing sophisticated language within a narrow semantic domain, along with multiple distinct communities expressing basic emotions. Furthermore, removing influential users can significantly alter the connectivity of the network, while removing users with extensive networks may inadvertently amplify underlying emotional patterns, warranting caution in drawing conclusions from influential sources on social media platforms.

We show that collections of homeomorphisms of a plane, unit disk, or annulus that are continuous with respect to the non-Archimedean metric on the boundary are also continuous in the sense of Roelcke, using a simplified version of Beardon's theorem. This implies the supremum of the non-Archimedean diameters is compact, and thus has a non-Archimedean diameter supremum. We extend this result to finitely handled annuli by using a compactness property of non-Archimedean diameters of homeomorphisms with bounded distortion. Additionally, we discuss how this relates to collections of quasisymmetric and quasiisometric homeomorphisms.

Accurate characterization of M-dwarf stars is crucial for a wide range of scientific studies, including exoplanets, stellar atmospheres and population analyses. M-dwarf stars in the field are often observed with near-infrared spectroscopy, which can provide a range of diagnostics. However, this method is limited to certain wavelengths and does provide only bulk properties of the stars. As a result, a more comprehensive approach is required to fully characterize these stars, particularly in other spectral ranges such as the ultraviolet. Field M-dwarf stars are frequently found with chromospheres and coronae, which can significantly impact the stars' ultraviolet flux. To address this, we used the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS) to examine how well standard stellar atmosphere models match M-dwarf stars across a wide range of parameters, including color, surface gravity, temperature and magnetic activity levels. We found that the stars with the MUSS sample generally match the expectations of standard stellar atmosphere models, although some discrepancies were observed and some trends identified. We also discovered differences in the fit of the MUSS sample stars based on their color and activity levels, which led to the development of two separate groups of stars and their respective luminosity functions. These two "activity-temperature" based groups can be used to improve the MUSS sample stars' temperature estimates, resulting in more accurate absolute magnitudes and distances. Traditional wire surfaces are prone to unintended ripple formation when exposed to rain, which can disrupt their intended operation. To mitigate this issue, a novel wire dual-meta surface has been developed offering ripple ripple scattering capabilities. When exposed to rain, its two distinct layers scatters the ripples in opposite directions, effectively cancelling each other out and preventing the ripple formation. To achieve this, a specific wire arrangement with varying spacials is used to ensure optimal performance. By tuning this wire design, high rain ripple scattering efficiency is achieved across a wide frequency range and under different rain conditions. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed method's ability to maintain low rain ripple scattering efficiency when exposed to heavy rain, allowing it to be utilized in a wide array of optical applications.

In database theory, the task of computing conjunctive query answers is known to be efficiently solved for certain types of queries, but complex self-joined queries present an obstacle. Although it is generally accepted that this complexity arises from the explosive growth of subquery components during evaluation, there is still much that remains unclear. This research fills these knowledge gaps by providing several efficient algorithms for specific scenarios and a randomized algorithm in the case of three-way self-joins. Additionally, it offers a connection to Dyck path problems in the context of self-joined queries with three ways.

The concept of regular methods was first introduced by Alpern and B\'{e}rardiu in their 1985 paper, with a formal definition however being a relatively recent development initiated by Chatterjee, Meel, and Singh around 2014. Building upon earlier work by McNaughton (1966) and Harju and Karhum\"{a}ki (1988), they provided a regular method for Naive Parity Game solving which was subsequently refined by Chatterjee, Meel, and Singh (2014) to match the optimal time complexity achieved by Eyraud-B\'{e}rard and Gastin (2007). In our research, we have utilized automated tools to generate a regular synthesis for the Naive Parity Strategy based on its circuit implementation, utilizing only basic operations such as finite state transducers, projections, and boolean functions, as demonstrated in the preceding study. This has enabled us to generalize the result to include both even and odd values, with a full extension of the method being provided for inclusively ordered trees in a subsequent paper. Our work however leaves several promising research directions unresolved, including the extension of the method to include more complex games such as those involving priority games on infinite words.

Using LHCb data collected at $\sqrt{s}=7\, {\rm TeV}$ and $\sqrt{s}=8\, {\rm TeV}$, a observation is made of the $B^+ \to J/\psi K^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0}$ decay, and the branching fraction of the $B^0 \to K^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0}$ decay is determined, thereby constraining standard model parameters related to these processes.

Recent advances in machine learning techniques for supervised and semi-supervised classification have significant potential in analyzing time series data and identifying dynamic patterns within. In this study, we apply a machine learning-based phase reconstruction method to investigate a time series generated from the Lorenz system, and demonstrate how this approach can lead to the discovery of previously unknown dynamics in complex systems. By utilizing only a limited number of known attractor states for training, we achieve successful reconstruction of the system's phase space and detect an additional, hidden attractor that requires extensive data to manifest. Furthermore, we investigate the affect of noise on this attractor and utilize this method to analyze an experimentally ambiguous dynamic by combining it with careful design of an external perturbation, resulting in a similar outcome to a known multi-scroll attractor.

This research offers an unbiased estimation approach for the mean absolute deviation from the median in a exponential distribution. A associated variance estimation method is also introduced. The research implications are explored, along with application examples and supplementary data provided for comprehensive understanding.

To optimize control systems subject to constraints, we utilize a approach that involves solving a sequence of problems based on the reachable states from a given point. This strategy is effective for obtaining a solution to the optimal control problem through a succession of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. We improve this approach by reformulating it using a Cauchy-type variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation for the reachable states, which enables us to simplify the computation of a key parameter and achieve convergence to the optimal control system. This method offers significant computational advantages over traditional approaches, as it avoids the need to estimate a difficult-to-calculate value function.

Many real-world tasks rely on icons and pictograms that convey information through subtle visual changes. One effective strategy is to remove a part of an icon and expect the brain to infer its meaning.然而, consistently presenting icons with the same part removed may lead to suboptimal recognition. Our study introduces a new, innovative approach called "modulated periodic activations" (MPA) to determine the optimal timing for removing different features. Firstly, we developed a unique training method that automatically determines the ideal timing by leveraging properties of periodic functions. Secondly, we discovered that MPA neural networks excel at conveying a wide range of functions without needing to predetermine which parts to remove. Moreover, these achievements can be achieved with a relatively small amount of training data.

The brain's ventral temporal region processes complex visual information, including the distinguishing features of living things, a capability thought to stem from specialized cells located in the posterior part of this area. These cells, often referred to as the "animacy center," have been widely studied, but their true nature remains a topic of debate. Some researchers argue that they should be called the "non-animacy center" due to their higher sensitivity to inanimate objects over living things. Recent studies have attempted to map the distribution of animacy-sensitive cells across the entire ventral temporal cortex, but they were limited to areas that respond to visual forms rather than flat images. Our new research expands these findings by identifying a broader pattern of animacy-sensitive neurons across all parts of the human ventral temporal cortex. This detailed map supports the hypothesis of a specialized animacy region located in the posterior part of this area, while also highlighting a co-existing pattern of neurons sensitive to inanimate objects in the middle and front sections of the ventral temporal cortex. Our results further suggest that there are distinct clusters of neurons sensitive to both animals and inanimate objects in specific areas such as LTCC, MTV, and dmSTV. Our findings indicate that the ventral temporal cortex contains a sophisticated system of neurons organized by the type of living things depicted, supported by our additional analysis of unique long connection patterns and distinctive structural features.

The conjecture of PGL(2,C)-unique ergodicity for GL(3,R) Maass newforms remains an open question in mathematics. A crucial aspect of this question involves understanding the average size of |f|^2 in various contexts. In this study, we've made significant progress by averageing |f|^2 across a family of newforms with bounded weight and deriving a nearly optimal bound. The achieved bound is up to a logarithmic factor better than what unique ergodicity would suggest. Furthermore, this result allows us to derive a strong constraint on possible GL(3,R) Landau-Siegel zeros. The possible location for the s-pole of a Dirichlet L-series is now limited to a specific region in the complex plane. This series expands on previous research by achieving a more favorable bound, improving the previous result by shifting the relevant parameter from 2 to 43/19. Additionally, this study derives an average lower bound for the third moment of GL(2,C) automorphic L-series in the critical region. The achieved bound indicates a possible shift in the central critical region for this family of L-series.

We have adapted Chriqui-Martínez and Moiseev's classical relational Hoare logic to accommodate quantum programs, introducing a novel framework for verifying quantum procedures against classical specifications. Our approach incorporates expectations into both classical and quantum logic, enabling the precise analysis of quantum programs through preconditions, postconditions, and intermediate expectations. Our logic includes an inductive rule that facilitates correctable errors via Ada invariant checking, an essential feature for the reliable induction on quantum loops. Our approach is illustrated through multiple examples, including correctable quantum Gibbs sampling and correct quantum phase estimation, for which we have also provided a correctness proof. Our work provides a robust foundation for the correct induction on quantum loops through the adaptation of the relational paradigm.

The transmission of contagious diseases often hinges on a few key individuals known as super-spreaders, who are responsible for a significant portion of cases. The proposed intervention strategy includes deliberately isolating super-spreaders to substantially reduce the rate of disease spread, based on research into log-normal variation in transmission. Theoretically, a minimal number of isolated cases can lead to a notable reduction in infections. However, a more comprehensive mathematical model is needed to assess the efficacy of this approach under diverse conditions. The system of random Ricker maps developed as part of this model provides such an evaluation. It reveals that while the super-spreader intervention strategy may not always be successful, under typical circumstances it can indeed reduce the rate of infections.

Let G be a group acting on a topological vector space over the complex numbers. For a given element, we examine the subspace consisting of those that are eigenvectors with a corresponding eigenvalue also being an eigenvector for another group element. The collection of these subspaces forms a closed decomposition within the original space. Moreover, this collection becomes orbitally closed when any finite collection of G acts results in the closure being the sum of its components. Specifically this holds true when the underlying group consists of continuous linear operators whose components are of the form GLn (for a given n). this property is utilized to demonstrate the cyclicity of certain collections of such operators that exhibit a cyclic behavior under a certain collection.

The primary function of vector magnetograms is providing information about the magnetic field in the Sun's visible surface. These magnetograms are essential for the development of reliable models and forecasts of solar activity. However, the quality and accuracy of these models and forecasts are compromised by inconsistencies in vector magnetogram data. While previous studies have successfully addressed some of these inconsistencies for scalar magnetic field information, the correction of bias in vector magnetic field data remains a significant challenge. A new framework is introduced to allocate and reduce the uncertainty and bias inherent in vector magnetic field data, focusing on the application of the Minimum Ensemble Spread Data Assimal (ENSEF) technique to the interpolation of magnetograms. Although ENSEF has been extensively utilized in numerical weather prediction, its employment in solar physics is a novel approach. The results of the study indicate that the ENSEF method can effectively reduce spread and bias in vector magnetic field data, with the potential to enhance the data's quality and accuracy. The findings of the study are further illustrated by the application of the ENSEF technique to magnetograms acquired on 10/11/2018, with a comparison to the traditional smoothing method revealing the superior performance of the ENSEF approach in achieving a more balanced trade-off between the reduction of spread and bias in vector magnetic field data. The research also highlights the critical importance of addressing the inherent uncertainty and bias in vector magnetic field data for the improvement of the physical understanding of the solar atmosphere and the development of reliable models

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 446 young stellar clusters in 36 galaxies from the LEGUS sample. The analysis encompasses a wide range of halo radii for these clusters, the half-light radii in specific colors or de Vaucouleurs radii for some, and the dispersion radii for others. The errors associated with these measurements are also included. In doing so, the largest half-light radii found were 0.3 parsecs, the largest de Vaucouleurs radii were 0.2 parsecs, and the largest dispersion radii were 0.3 parsecs. The measurements of these radii in relation to the masses of these stars reveal that more massive stars tend to have larger radii. The masses of the stars within these clusters are influenced by multiple radii measures, the mass of their central stars and surrounding dark matter are correlated with certain radii, and the distributions of these radii vary significantly across the mass ranges of these stars. Additionally, the measurements of these radii in relation to the ages of these clusters and their environments are explored. The results indicate that the stars with high masses have larger radii than those with low masses, older clusters tend to have larger radii, and the dynamic interactions between cluster members and their surrounding environments have a significant impact on the size of these clusters. The analysis also includes a discussion on how the dynamic processes within these clusters may contribute to the formation of massive

We present a new, uncomplicated way to calculate the decay of hadrons decaying into two photons, specifically $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$. The new method avoids the issues with fake signals caused by virtual photons turning into quark loops.  By using an effective theory where quark currents are replaced by color dipole operators separated by a long distance, we can accurately estimate the decay width of $\eta_c$. The calculation relies on Higgs-like operators which have been simulated using lattice QCD,  and the estimated decay width $\Gamma(\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma)$ is 22.7(5.5) febt. The result is in line with the experimental evidence. The method may also be used to estimate the decay width of $\eta_b\rightarrow 2\gamma$. The corresponding calculation gives the estimated decay width $\Gamma(\eta_b\rightarrow 2\gamma)$ as 2.44(0.53) ast. The result is in line with the experimental evidence. The new lattice calculation of the hadron matrix element $\langle \eta_c| \mathcal{O}(T) \mathcal{J}(0) |0 \rangle$ is 0.084(18) geV$^5$ and $\langle \eta_b| \mathcal{O}(T) \mathcal{J}(0) |0 \rangle$ is 6.6(1

A prominent computational obstacle in modeling $d$-dimensional systems by the Hubbard model is the sign problem, whose severity increases exponentially with system size, dimension, and beta (the inverse of temperature). We propose a potential solution to this issue by introducing a dual-network architecture that leverages complex-valued neural networks and employs a variational approach to mitigate the sign problem's impact. Our method yields significant performance gains over standard sampling techniques in multiple test scenarios, including $1$-dimensional models at finite temperatures, $2$-dimensional models even when $T$ approaches $0$, and $1$-dimensional models doped with extra electrons, all while maintaining comparable computational costs.

All integers $n$ that can be written as the sum of two distinct powerful numbers share a common characteristic, where the maximum exponent $\omega(n)$ equals the number of prime factors of $n$. Let $B$ be a given real value and define $n \llangle B$ when it satisfies the condition $\omega(n)/\Omega(n) \geq 1 - B^{-1}$. The count of integers $n \leq x$ meeting the criteria $n \llangle B$ and having at most $B$ prime factors, denoted by $\pi_B(x; \llangle B)$, grows in proportion to $\rho_B(x)$, with the proportionality constant being 1. Additionally, the count of integers $n \leq x$ meeting the criteria $n \llangle B$, having exactly $j$ prime factors, and satisfying $n \geq c_B x (\log x)^{j-1}$, meets the condition, with $c_B$ representing a constant dependent on $B$. However, it is observed that the function $\rho_B(x)$ closely resembles $x \rho(x/D_B)$, and for most values of $B$, the parameter $D_B$ is significantly less than $1/B$, although its exact relationship to $1/B$ remains an open area of study.

Given any non-erasing free monoid homomorphism σ and subshift X that has topological entropy, there's a corresponding transformed system σ(X) equipped with a measure μ such that the topological entropy of X equals that of Y, and for which σ actually maps Y exactly to X while preserving topological entropy. Conversely, if a free group endomorphism φ isn't an inner automorphism and a sequence has sublinear complexity, the transformed sequence φ(s) will have linear complexity. On the other hand, if the sequence s has lineable complexity and 1-based, the transformed sequence φ(s) will have sublinear complexity.

In our research, we focus on creating models capable of adapting seamlessly to new tasks within the same domain, leveraging previously acquired knowledge without retraining. We challenge existing models, which rely on overfitting to distinguish between tasks. Instead, we propose an alternative approach, based on disentangling factors of variation and utilizing auxiliary mechanisms like clustering and mutual adaptation. We call this proposed method UTCOGA. This framework facilitates separating task-related and irrelevant information, enhances the model's ability to generalize across tasks by incorporating an self-supervised loss, and enables it to cluster accurately based on implicit task information. We show superior results on benchmarks, including MultiArXiv and BAblysh with the following improvements: 7.84, 5.84, and 3.44 on MultiArXiv, and 5.44, 3.44, and 78% BS on BAblysh, respectively.

This paper presents an innovative artificial intelligence framework known as 
M-ar-K-Fast, capable of performing real-time, unsupervised dimensionality 
reduction on time series data stream without requiring prior knowledge. By leveraging 
online and dynamic statistical methods along with an adaptable kernel, this system 
leverages new feature extraction techniques to provide timely and meaningful insights. 
By automating the selection of optimal lag values and incorporating historical data, 
M-ar-K-Fast efficiently manages high-dimensional data streams and mitigates issues of 
concept drift and seasonality. Finally, by integrating state-of-the-art clustering 
algorithms, this framework effectively identifies patterns and structures within the 
data, ensuring robust and reliable results.

The software development sector, particularly game development, is experiencing a surge in investment and demand. Despite its prosperity, requirements engineering (RE) in this field receives less attention than it should. To rectify this gap, our research explores current RE practices within the game industry during its early stages. Through an ANOVA-driven statistical investigation involving 132 game developers and managers, our study reveals the prevalence and application of various RE methods. The results indicate a widespread use of informal techniques, including ad-hoc processes and existing management methods, in game development organizations. Furthermore, our exploratory factor analysis uncovers three primary drivers motivating RE adoption within this sector: product complexity management, clear role definition, and enhanced team communication. To promote RE integration, our research outlines several implications for both industry practitioners and future scholars.

The realization of secure and private machine learning has gained significant momentum through the exploration of deep learning combined with differential privacy. Unfortunately, direct application of private training techniques to neural networks often hinders optimal performance due to the inability to effectively harness these methods' full potential. The difficulty of determining effective hyperparameters in such schemes poses a major obstacle, as the optimal values can vary greatly from those in non-private learning. The proposed framework addresses this challenge by formulating the selection of hyperparameters as an optimization problem that can be efficiently solved through a Bayesian approach, leveraging a small set of carefully chosen, easily computable performance metrics. The resulting model enables a rapid assessment of hyperparameter effectiveness, bypassing the need for extensive trials and significantly enhancing performance in multiple settings. Notably, this approach also facilitates the optimization of hyperparameters in existing private learning protocols for neural tangent kernels and multi-layer private tangent kernels, in addition to fully private stochastic gradient descent. The benefits of this method include a substantial improvement in performance over standard tangent kernel prediction, as well as the ability to optimize complex hyperparameters such as network architecture and step size, as demonstrated in experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

A research extension of word problems in groups is known as involutions, which focuses on determining whether two words equal each other under the condition that they both represent the same inverse. The objective of this study is to analyze the Boolean algebras formed by sets of involutions in specific groups, particularly in free groups and their two-generator variants. Researchers have successfully identified the Boolean structure of involutions in a free group of rank two. Furthermore, the team has developed an algorithm to decide the algebraic structure of involutions in a free group.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological understanding with its visible-infrared radiometer. The instrument will collect a vast amount of data over seven months of observation, allowing for precise measurements of the universe's expansion and geometric structure. The authors of this study developed a geometric model to analyze how correlated readout noise during the detector's readout process affects data analysis, based on the Euclid Near-Infrared Spectrometer requirements. The authors conclude that the noise will geometrically shift data points by up to 1x10^-3 on the Euclid NISP camera in one arcsecond units. While this impact is minimal for upcoming large-scale data analyses, it may be important for smaller sample studies and needs to be considered when performing detailed geometric assessments of the universe.

We applied the two-component model (TCM) approach, along with an alternative method using Gaussian Process regression, to a sample of 10489 metallicity stars from the APOGEE-DR16 dataset. Our goal was to identify distinct sequences in the Cephenya diagram that correspond to different chemical populations. Findings showed that the TCM approach consistently identified two main sequences, in line with the six metadata classifications of the stars. However, the two methods did not always match in their classification, differing in up to 50%. Discrepancies arose when stars possessed moderate to high metallicities, typically exceeding 0.0. By analyzing model residuals, we determined that the TCM approach most effectively captured the two main sequences when at least one of them was underpopulated, generally found in the disk thick and thin populations. In regions where populations were more balanced and had similar metallicities, stars scatter increased, likely due to non-TCM phenomena such as stellar evolution or stellar mixing. By leveraging the APOGEE-DR16 dataset, our analysis expanded the TCM application range for galaxies, while also providing a systematic framework to connect stellar populations and their distributions, potentially aiding future surveys conducted by the APOGEE-DES, NExUSS, and DUO programs.

During the COVID-19 pandemic in China, a severe outbreak of misinformation occurred on the internet. Despite available filtering techniques, many news platforms failed to effectively address the issue, leading to widespread dissemination of unverified information. A novel approach was proposed to address this problem by combining the spread model with the PageRank algorithm to both filter and measure the influence of online rumors. A comparative analysis demonstrated that this combined approach outperformed traditional methods in identifying the veracity of news. A new ranking system was introduced to classify and measure the influence of online rumors, outperforming the traditional PageRank algorithm. A weighted propagation model was devised to accelerate the speed of information transmission. A novel filter was proposed to automatically classify the content based on a combination of the spread model and the proposed approach. A novel measurement system was devised to both measure the influence of online rumors and both filter and rank the content based on a combination of the proposed approach. A novel multi-layered network model was devised to simulate the transmission transmission of misinformation. A simulation analysis demonstrated that this proposed approach could be an effective method for filtering and managing the transmission of unverified information. A theoretical analysis provided the underlying principles of the proposed method. A practical application showed that this proposed approach can be used to automatically filter and measure the influence of online rumors. A conclusion summarized the proposed method's ability to automatically filter and measure the influence of online rumors. A new instance of a remote, relatively close galaxy cluster known as Fornax is located at a redshift of 0.16 and comprises over 1300 bright stars per square arcsecond. Researchers believe observing the cluster in the ultraviolet spectrum may reveal previously undetected nebulae and ionized gas within some of the cluster's galaxies. Such observations could expose a significant amount of the cluster's missing baryonic mass, as well as offer insights into the history of star formation in these galaxies during their middle-aged star formation peak. A team of researchers has initiated a multi-wavelength study of the cluster, combining optical data with ultraviolet observations and deep X-ray imaging to study the global structure of the cluster as well as individual galaxies within it. A key aspect of this study involves analyzing planetary nebulae within the galaxies of the cluster, as these objects serve as reliable cosmic distance indicators and can provide valuable information about the history of star formation. However, detecting planetary nebulae in the ultraviolet spectrum represents a new and challenging area of exploration. To manage and analyze this new type of data, researchers have developed a specialized database of planetary nebulae and are seeking to discover additional examples of these objects within the cluster's galaxies, which would represent the first instance of such objects have been observed in a cluster of galaxies at this proximity.

Every second, a vast amount of data, such as social media postings, SMS messages, and Google searches, gets generated worldwide. To keep up with this rapidly evolving trend, a new, innovative system called LifeStream has been developed to efficiently process and analyze massive quantities of time-based data streams. LifeStream's architecture utilizes a unique set of buffers, known as time wheels, to seamlessly manage and link concurrent operations on these data streams. To further enhance performance, LifeStream incorporates highly optimized components, including custom-made operators written in C++, in-memory databases using hash tables, as well as a sophisticated system for load balancing and fault tolerance. In a benchmark test involving 10 different queries, LifeStream demonstrated exceptional speed, outperforming existing systems like TwitterStream by up to 52 times and Enchant by 3.2 times, while also exhibiting up to 52 times less query latency than TwitterStream.

This research paper delves into the concepts of Bertrand curves and their generalization, the (1, n)-Bertrand curves, along with their derivative, n-derivative curves, specifically focusing on timelike curves. We have established a new characterization method for timelike (1, n)-Berland curves using curvature functions and their derivatives, and derived the necessary conditions for spacelike curves to possess a specific property, and vice versa. Furthermore, our research reveals that a timelike curve can be considered a (1, n)-Bertrand curve if and only if it satisfies a set of curvature function relationships, and this relationship holds true for curves in higher-dimensional Minkowski space.

In classification tasks for machine learning, the choice of loss function appears insignificant in the fundamental design. Yet, the vast number of available loss functions raises concerns about the comparability of model performances. This study delves into the effect of different loss functions on the performance of a well-known architecture, ResNet, when applied to a prominent dataset, CIFAR-10. We examine various instances of the ResNet model and a range of loss functions, observing the resulting performance variations. The results reveal substantial discrepancies in models' accuracy due to the loss function, with some functions consistently outperforming others. This suggests the choice of loss function is more influential than previously thought and may need consideration in the comparison of model performances.

The stability of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations with a boundary feedback control, where the control is applied to a boundary that is not perpendicular to the flow, is analyzed. This study builds on previous research by Y. I. Karshon that proved exponential stability for a linear system with boundary control. Extending these results, we establish the exponential stability of the nonlinear equations under the same feedback mechanism.

This research employs a comprehensive thermomechanical model to simulate the
crystallization process in amorphous polymers, initiating from the glassy state.
We integrate the mechanical glassy stiffness into the rate-formulate Balmer-Prandtl-Einstein viscoelastic model and augment it with a driving force-based phase
field term to represent the sudden increase in stiffness. Experimental data from
uniaxial tension and compression tests, utilized to calibrate the constitutive
model, ensured mechanical consistency through the Saint-Venant principle.
Our mechanical glassy stiffness incorporation prevented spurious stresses typical
of over-constrained glassy models. Simulations of stress relaxation and
creep, followed by mechanical loading demonstrated accurate predictions when
compare to corresponding experiments. Moreover, our model successfully captured
structural and mechanical property evolution during strain-induced crystallization.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on spin-triplet Cooper pairs in a nelematic superconductor, a Pippard generalization of the Landau free energy was developed. The development of the Glorier equation of motion for the superconductor's order parameter under the simultaneous influence of finite momentum, magnetic fields, and nematic symmetry resulted in the calculation of magnetic susceptibility. The formulation of the susceptibility under the simultaneous influence of a finite critical velocity and an external magnetic field in the Ginzburg-Landau approximation was also demonstrated. A simple relationship was found between the magnetic susceptibility and the critical velocity in the limit of small momentum and strong nematic deformation, with the elasticity of the liquid crystal having negligible impact, where the susceptibility exhibits both node-dependent and s-wave like behavior.

Automated external instruction, or EFRA, enables autonomous systems to learn from simple yes/no feedback by generating diverse actions and receiving guidance on their optimal selection. While essential for mastering complex tasks, current EAF methods necessitate human input to pick the best action from multiple options. Our research seeks to minimize this human involvement by exploring ways to infer user preference from implicit signals. We introduce an innovative approach using unsupervised machine learning to convert user behavior into explicit feedback and present a generalized framework for examining this conversion in the context of robotic action acquisition. Furthermore, we outline a novel method to establish a reliable connection between user behavior and their ultimate goals.

High differential delay detection schemes are typically associated with improved frequency offset tolerance and better signal-to-noise ratio threshold performance, yet these benefits are offset by an increase in computational delay. A novel difference-delay detection structure has been developed in previous research, providing tolerance to frequency offset and carrier phase without sacrificing computational efficiency. This innovation enables conventional differential coherent detection to compete with state-of-the-art differential non-coherent detection methods. Building on this, the proposed innovation presents an enhanced differential delay detection structure, offering excellent frequency offset and carrier phase tolerance performance while matching the low computational delay of the conventional differential non-coherent detection method.

The occurrence rate of supernovae involving black-neutron star binaries is expected to exceed that of neutron star-nucleus mergers by an order of magnitude, potentially making the latter more visible as multi-messenger sources. The mass of the neutron star depends on the supernova explosion dynamics, which also influence whether a black hole or neutron star forms. Core-collapse simulations with realistic physical conditions reveal the role of stellar matter on the maximum neutron-star mass and event horizon maximum accreted mass, particularly for heavy-charged particles that reduce charge accumulation on the event horizon. Notably, stars with 20-35 solar masses will collapse into black holes after forming neutron stars with 2-3 solar masses, thus indicating that black-hole neutron-star mergers in the sensitive LIGO-Virgo range are feasible even with a 20 solar mass companion, thus suggesting the detectable parameter range for optimal black-hole neutron-star binary population and maximum neutron star mass limits, influenced by heavy nucleosynthesis and the stellar matter itself.

A previously reported finding suggests the quantum capacity of a channel influenced by the 4D spacetime structure decreases as the ambient temperature rises, eventually reaching the Hawking temperature associated with a black hole. In this temperature limit, the affected channel exhibits a steady-state transparency of approximately 0.86. To explore this outcome more closely, a more detailed model was then implemented. This model not only confirms the initial results but also reveals the presence of quantum correlations between the thermal populations and the quantum state within the channel. Ultimately, the quantum state's transparency can be fully recovered by discarding the thermal populations. A computational method was also used to investigate additional models and verify these theoretical concepts through laboratory simulations.

Disentangled rain generation and cleaning have been extensively studied, yet the interconnection between these tasks remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose a novel, unified framework that simultaneously generates realistic rain and removes it, by capturing the independent 'rain cause' and implicitly capturing the 'rain effect'. The cause represents the actual rain created in an input image, whereas the effect emerges as artificial rain added to a clean image. Our method utilizes latent space manipulation to achieve this disentanglement, utilizing entropy regularization to separate the cause and effect. The proposed approach not only yields realistic rain but also produces high-quality cleaned images with preserved high-frequency details. Our proposed model outperforms current standalone generating and cleaning methods in terms of quantitative and visual assessments.

The primary challenge in your current setup is the substantial human effort needed to train deep neural networks that excel at robotic tasks, as most methods rely on numerous human-labeled examples. In contrast, self-supervised learning can utilize vast amounts of unlabeled data to bypass this issue, but few techniques exist that combine human feedback with unlabeled data. This paper proposes a novel approach called Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VACR), which leverages human feedback to divide unlabeled data into clusters and trains a reward function through the evaluation of a few selected cluster representatives. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, three active learning scenarios were implemented and evaluated through both simulated and real-world experiments with real robots. The results confirmed the advantages of Visually Aided Cluster Ranking over conventional active learning methods and human-in-the-data systems.

A significant development in understanding continuum has been making use of models that utilize the concept of forcing. A model partnership, consisting of two such models, allows one to be obtained from the other through a specific type of generic extension. This concept enables the application of tools from integrating systems to model theory, leading to a more functional perspective on studying the continuum. In a joint study with S. Shelah, we explore model partnerships through the lens of set-theory. A model with specific accessibility properties, known as a precise model, is shown to be equivalent to any model that shares a model partnership with it. This, in turn, implies that any such model is E-equivalent to any other, provided they have the same language. A key application of this framework is in understanding the continuum problem, which we examine through the lens of stationary towers of forcing concepts. In this context, we introduce two concepts, a tower tower tower (TTT) and a tower tower (TT), representing closed ideals on $\omega_2$. If either of these concepts hold, it follows that $2^\omega = \aleph_2$. A more direct approach to obtaining similar results is also considered.

This study establishes regularity properties for the sequence of approximate solutions and a distinct smooth breakthrough result for a Q-curvature type problem on a fixed bounded domain in R^n. Additionally, sufficient conditions for both existence and nonexistence of bounded solutions are also demonstrated.

Assessing drug consumption risk before conducting clinical trials is a crucial step in creating effective medications.  The study explores how certain personality traits, specifically those outlined in the Five Factor Model, can help predict the likelihood of drug use misbehavior.  Researchers collected data from 470 individuals to examine the connection between the Five Factor Model and consumption assessment scores.  They found that neuroticism and conscientiousness are the most significant factors in predicting consumption risk, with other traits showing varying levels of influence.  Notably, the study discovered a clear, inverted triangular pattern of influence, allowing for the potential exclusion of histology and extradyadic scores from future studies.  These findings suggest that incorporating the Five Factor Model into consumption assessment processes is a promising approach to creating reliable risk evaluation systems for drug consumption.

The prevalence of machine learning models is now seen across nearly all sectors of the economy.  Unfortunately, these models, while effective, lack transparency in how they perform tasks and make decisions. Such opacity hinders collaboration between users and machines, as well as limits the ability to apply them in regulated industries such as healthcare and banking. To bridge this gap, we introduce ATOMIC, a general-purpose machine intelligence atlas that provides a structured framework for interpreting the functionality of machine learning systems through natural language descriptions. ATOMIC leverages existing resources, including natural language processing systems and massive language models, to generate precise, human-legible descriptions of complex models' behavior on particular inputs, facilitating human model comprehension. Furthermore, ATOMIC allows for the creation of these descriptions in Natural Language, enabling humans to communicate with machines about their models' performance.

The ultimate success of the cryptocurrency market hinges on the resolution of the liquidity crisis of 2020, a decision that can be influenced by the prediction of Bitcoin price trends using the HHL algorithm. Our research utilizes a hybrid quantum-classical approach, leveraging the HHL algorithm to solve a least squares regression problem, specifically to forecast the short-term direction of the Bitcoin price. By inputting relevant market data such as fear and greed indices, trading volumes, and fear index changes, our NISQ-HHL system was capable of producing forecast results that were surprising given the limitations of the hardware used. Furthermore, by incorporating random forests for a more robust analysis, our improved RFS-NISQ-HHL system was found to yield the best portfolio performance when evaluated through risk-adjusted return metrics such as Sharpe and Sortino ratios.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle sufficient quantities of matching text data, a novel multi-modal training method is proposed. This method employs a speech-text model with an internal mechanism that regulates the relative importance of information from both modalities. By utilizing this focused attention to both speech and text data, the model can effectively leverage both types of information. Experimental results indicate that this method yields significant improvements in performance compared to single-modal baselines and conventional cross-modal attention mechanisms. Furthermore, it leads to an optimal solution with considerably reduced training data requirements.

Fixed cross-section fluctuations are essential components of the fluctuation-flow correlation framework. Typically, one attribute within a specific range is used to define these fluctuations, and the range is simultaneously employed to identify regions with fixed values. This dual role creates a feedback mechanism where the same attribute can either suppress or enhance fluctuations, thereby influencing the range at which correlations are observed. The primary objective of the present investigation is to determine the optimal region size for detecting the fixed-cross-section signature in correlation functions, taking into account the suppression or enhancement of fluctuations within smaller or larger regions. The findings indicate the existence of a distinct peak in the region size correlation for region sizes smaller than a threshold, approximately 10 billion fermi, where the correlation of a specific region with its neighboring region is maximized. Region correlation analysis is also performed using Monte Carlo events to determine region sizes with fixed values of charged-particle cross-section fluctuations as a function of the region's dimensions and the overall event multiplicity.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$, it is shown that these first positions provide an unbiased and efficient estimation for the total number of elements in the parking distribution.

超导电性纳米线表现出量子相滑现象时, 利用栅极对其施加电压可以实现在超导态和绝缘态间的可逆转换. 我们在细的铌纳米线中观察到, 随着栅极电压的变化, 会触发量子相滑现象, 同时记录到的电流电压曲线会呈现清晰的锯齿状图案. 我们发现, 在关闭栅极电压时, 充放电过程中的平均电压呈现与温度无关的状态, 该电压不受细纳米线正常电阻的影响. 该结果无法用现有的量子相滑理论进行解释, 该现象可能是由于电荷库仑阻塞效应导致.

The discovery of T-dwarf stars became intriguing with the realization that they are predominantly composed of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. To gain more knowledge about the composition of these exoplanets and stellar objects, scientists analyzed the atmospheric composition of T-dwarf stars and planets. This analysis was previously hindered by a lack of an efficient spectral retrieval tool capable of processing multiple compositions simultaneously. The open-source code APOLLO was developed to accelerate this type of spectral analysis by leveraging GPU technology. Using APOLLO, researchers were able to accurately interpret the spectrum of T-dwarf stars in a matter of hours, leading to a significant breakthrough in the application of machine learning models to the interpretation of astronomical spectra.

Our study investigates the impact of virtual V-attraction and M-repulsion on the IEX effect in nucleons, which we incorporate into an effective Lagrangian and examine using the light-front holographic model, specifically in the deep inelastic scattering (DIS) regime. By deriving a new formula for the IEX structure function based on parton distribution functions (PDFs), we calculate the PDFs from a holographic quark-meson-glass effective theory (H-QMG) that includes color gluons. The results show a significant increase in the PDFs and the IEX structure function during the early stages of the quark-gluon fluid, with the impact declining over time. These findings may offer valuable insights into the characteristics of the quark-gluon fluid.

Dual representation models have been successfully applied in various domains to generate diverse and complementary outputs based on a single input, however, they have not been tested in the realm of video view prediction. In this study, we introduce a novel dual representation model for video view prediction that can produce both complementary and consistent images from video data, from an angle different from that captured in the video. Specifically, this proposed framework comprises three key modules: a video encoder that extracts relevant information from the video to represent it dually, a regenerator that produces images based on this representation, and a verifier which assesses the representation's capability to support both consistent and varied image generation. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of precision in image generation and the range of possible views that can be produced.

Wireless inter-level coupling has emerged as a versatile platform for studying deeply buried quantum systems, enabling coupling between adjacent energy levels. Toachar et. al. demonstrate the presence of inter-level coupling between adjacent confined electrons within a quantum dot, using a resonant microwave excitation to measure inter-level anti-crossing. By adjusting the gate voltage, they successfully swelled this inter-level interaction to approximately 250 MHz, providing evidence that adjacent electrons can interact with one another through capacitive coupling.

The Ω-baryon, which has been predicted for a long time, was experimentally confirmed in this study through analysis of data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC. By examining χc0 , χc2 , and JC/ψ0 states containing an s2s' system, researchers established that these predictions lie within or near the acceptable ranges derived from various theoretical frameworks. Additionally, by theoretically modeling the hadronic decays of the Ω-baryon resonances and comparing the predictions with available experimental data, a certain level of consistency was observed.

Airborne diseases spread easily in enclosed spaces like bus stops and public transportation, especially during peak hours. To model this, researchers used a simple well-mixed compartment model for a case study of measles transmission on a bus in Rio de Janeiro in 2016. They identified four key variables: the number of susceptible and infected people on the bus, the frequency of susceptible-infected encounters, and the probability of disease transmission during such encounters. They formulated an equation for R0, considering ventilation, temperature, humidity, and surface properties of the bus, as well as the frequency of susceptible-infected encounters. This study reveals that simply knowing the number of susceptible and infected people on the bus is not enough to predict disease spread. Instead, features that quantify susceptible-infected encounters are crucial. Changes in R0 can be attributed to changes in these encounter frequencies, as demonstrated with data from the field. The researchers propose using well-mixed framework models to inform public health strategies and reduce disease spread in crowded indoor spaces.

Building on my earlier calculations regarding quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence, I now investigate various possible ways to detect these effects. In the case of birefringence, the proposed detection methods involve analyzing the polarization changes of particle beams as they move through high-speed moving frames that experience the maximal birefringent effect. Proposed proposals include using gamma rays produced from accelerated protons in existing particle beam setups. For sub-nuclear frame birefringence, the suggested detection method suggests comparing the birefringent angles for different energy levels during the reconstruction of invariant masses in electron-positron beam data.
