This note outlines the method used by Eisenlohr and Farris to determine the transitivity of fully symmetric polyhedra. Their method employs an abstract form of the Sch\"afers cut construction to help establish the fact that any polyhedron $P$ is a sub-structure of another polyhedron $\hat{P}$ with higher symmetry, often as an orbit within $\hat{P}$. This method is then applied to prove that the tritruncated cubohexachoron is equivalent to $B_4$ and to demonstrate that the truncated tetrahedral polyhedron is a sub-structure of the tetrahedral polyhedron.

The concept of uncloneable encryption was first introduced three decades ago by Benaloh and Horowitz as a binary encryption method with one decade's technology gap between breaking and building. Building upon the initial idea, our research achieves a significant 50-year gap based on standard complexity assumptions. Our proposed scheme, an adaptively secure public-key encryption system, can be realized with as few as $\tilde O(\log^2 |{\mathsf{1msg}}|)$ key sizes, where the system is tailored for scenarios involving a single target message against an infinite number of distraction messages. This type of setting is frequently found in vote encryption and secret sharing applications. Our key innovation lies in utilizing the theoretical idea of learn-with-error subspaces, which, although interesting, has yet to be applied practically.

Physical layer security (PHL) relies on extracting a shared secret between legitimate parties from a unique characteristic of the communication channel that also distinguishes it from illegal listeners. This process involves two stages: first, legitimate parties measure and estimate the channel characteristics to generate a rough model, or "sketch," of it. In the second stage, one party transmits a carefully designed test signal through the channel, and the other party compares the received output with their own sketch to make a confirmation decision. Traditionally, both parties need to exchange encryption keys to communicate securely. In contrast, our study presents an innovative, keyless verification system that leverages the unique noise present in communication signals to achieve this. Our method utilizes an unsupervised learning algorithm to generate highly accurate, low-bit sketches of Gaussian noise channels, and a corresponding test classifier that uses these sketches for confirmation. Our results show that these sketch-based tests are highly effective, often outperforming similar methods that analyze the full signal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these tests can be customized to meet specific performance requirements by adjusting the size of the sketches.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of flattened $\sqrt q$ law and low-damped plasmons
occurs at higher densities. Additionally, our calculations revealed that
plasmon dispersion maintains $\sqrt q$ law in certain doped regions near the
K-points of the moiré superlattice, opening up the possibility of observing
flattened $\sqrt q$ law plasmons there.

This paper investigates the characteristics of almost conformal Ricci solitons when the underlying manifold is a Sasakian manifold. We demonstrate that on a Sasakian manifold, if a non-trivial almost conformal Ricci soliton has the conformal factor be a constant, then the potential function satisfies the Laplace equation. Furthermore, if the Ricci curvature is compatible with the Ricci soliton under these constant conditions, it must be equal to the potential function multiplied by -2. Additionally, we establish that on a Sasakian manifold, if a gradient Ricci soliton is equivalent to an h-CYM soliton, then it has to be a trivial soliton.

Stars and planets experiencing widespread wind activity and shaped磁层 by the wind-planet magnetic interaction can be found throughout the universe. The internal rotational energy of rapidly rotating oblique magnetic stars leads to massive wind mass ejection and intense electromagnetic radiation, vastly exceeding the solar output observed during the solar maximum. These characteristics, combined with massive stellar mass and磁 field, result in massive wind illumination and intense electromagnetic radiation in magnetic stars, often classifying them as luminous supranovae. In contrast, planetary magnetic fields preserve the wind particles until they reach the planetary poles, where they are funneled along magnetic field lines and released as intense pole-to-pole radiation in the case of magnetic stars. However, planetary magnetic fields typically suffice to stop the solar wind, unlike in massive stellar neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes, whose weak or absent magnetic fields allow wind particles to accrete and produce intense accretion disk or direct radiation. The extreme temperatures generated by this process can result in the acceleration of particles to intense gamma-ray emission, possibly contributing to the observed magnetar giant flare phenomenon.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect has the ability to generate strong spin-momentum entanglement across material boundaries, which thin layers with high spin-orbit coupling can induce in adjacent ferromagnets. As a result, this phenomenon has the potential to significantly enhance the magnetoelectric coupling in multilayer ferromagnets. In the current research, the magnetoelectric response of cobalt/bismuth cobalt multilayers is experimentally and theoretically analyzed to establish the role of magnetic interaction at the interface between layers and the impact of spin-diffusion length in normal metal. By theoretically modeling and experimentally using varying layer thicknesses, the spin-mixture at the ferromagnetic interface is mapped to understand its relationship with the overlying high spin-orbit coupling layer. In doing so, a optimal arrangement of layers is found where the magnetic interaction at the interface and the spin-hflip rate are balanced, thus maximizing the spin-mixture. In comparison to isolated high spin-orbit coupling layers, such engineered ferromagnetic multilayers offer a larger range for magnetoelectric control. In addition, different mechanisms contribute to the spin-mixture at the ferromagnetic interface, which is crucial for designing materials with enhanced magnetoelectric response.

This study presents solutions to the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation for a generalized Mie-type potential in multiple dimensions, utilizing the Jumarie type fractional derivative. By applying a recent transformation to simplify the equation, we obtain its reduced form. Several methods, including the generalized fractional variational iteration method, the fractional differential transformation method, and the Adomian modified decomposition method, are utilized to solve the transformed equation. These approaches yield excellent results, with results aligned and showcasing high precision through graphical representation. Additionally, this research offers a comprehensive overview of the fractional differential transformation method for solving such equations, demonstrating its effectiveness through comparative analysis of obtained solutions.

We analyze the effectiveness of regularization techniques in neural networks from a perspective of function smoothness. We demonstrate that certain regularization methods are equivalent to enforcing a constraint on the Lipschitz continuity of the neural network within the input space. Specifically, we prove that $TR$ and $TK$ norms represent the minimal Frobenius norms of the neural network's Jacobian matrices evaluated at training data points and a set of kernel matrices, respectively. Due to their connection with optimal transport, we further show that $TK$ is closely aligned with fairness principles, while both $TR$ and $TK$ contribute to enhancing the generalization capabilities of the network. We also establish that the minimal Frobenius norm solution for $TK$ can be obtained by inverting the regularized kernel matrix, which has implications for network generation. We define a family of neural network models, parameterized by a value $\alpha$, that interpolate between $TR$, $TK$, and standard least-squares regression. We conclude by presenting theoretical and empirical evidence of the benefits of both $TR$ and $TK$ in terms of fair and accurate predictions.

Recent research has highlighted the Basque language's suitability for studying
syntactic phenomena known as concords, due to its extensive concord changes
that reflect the syntax of noun phrases. As Basque's morphological richness may
pose a learning challenge, we investigated whether Bidirectional Long Short-Term
Memory (LSTM) networks can successfully capture the intricate concords feature.
Our experiments, comparing models with differing access to morphological
information, revealed that providing the target concords' canonical forms significantly enhances the models' performance.
Nevertheless, the LSTM networks struggled to reach the human accuracy level in
the more demanding classification tasks.
To gain insight, we examined the Basque concords' distribution, discovering that
lower-frequency concords correspond to more complex morphological categories,
whereas higher-frequency concords map to simpler categories.
This correlation between the concords' distribution and Basque's written form
may serve as a potential explanation for the limited LSTM networks' performance.

The James Webb Space Telescope's unique capabilities make planet detection through transit highly efficient, yet its transit timing relies heavily on precise orbital predictions. Traditional transit finding methods require sufficient data to pinpoint the orbit's orientation, otherwise, multiple transit observations may be unnecessary. Utilizing a global telescope network, we managed to fully HD80606 b's highly eccentric 110-day orbit, spotting the star at four different phases. We also observed the system twice, noting the broad and unusually loud HD80606 A's astrospheric radio emission during a peristellar passage. These new data have enabled us HD80606 B to accurately predict HD80606 B's future and upcoming JWST transit windows, although the primary 2024 transit window requires at least one more observation. In addition to supporting planet transit scheduling, our program also presents an outstanding opportunity to study the system, especially HD80606 A, with the JWST.

Table tennis competitions are highly demanding sports that require excellent balance in individuals. Engaging in such sports can offer individuals with mobility challenges an opportunity to enhance their balance through a therapeutic activity with numerous social advantages. To create new systems for balance therapy, we've applied data-driven methods to investigate the stability trajectories during table tennis games, accounting for the sport's intricate nature and straightforward rules. Our statistical analysis revealed notable differences in game dynamics across various underlying game states. Our findings will inform the design of balance therapy systems by suggesting deliberate game-modifying interventions to target specific stages of rehabilitation and encouraged us to create a prototype system incorporating these insights.

Our research offers a variational understanding of the phase-field approximation for breaking fluids, similar to the dynamic fracture model introduced by Bressans and Israel. This understanding is part of a broader study where we first prove that the relevant energies can be reformulated using a phase-field parameter, following an analogous reformulation for an intertial model by Desagulier and Monneau. In the case of small phase-field parameters, we demonstrate the existence of solutions that mirror the original solution, and these results are built upon the work of Monneau and Pharo for a related static problem.

We examine Drell-Yan production of heavy quark-antiquark pairs, specifically top-charm, at NLO in QCD using a virtuality-ordering scheme for parton showers. A study of rapidity and transverse momentum distributions for these pairs, along with NLO corrections to parton distribution functions, reveals significant impacts of the choice of scheme on these results. The accuracy of the top-quark mass is validated by comparing theoretical predictions with available experimental data, showing good agreement. A precise determination of the top-quark mass can be achieved with these models for colliders such as the LHC and the Electron-Ion Collider. Additionally, the resulting final-state showers for the top and charm quarks demonstrate the reliability of our NLO calculations.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage in pregnant women and increases cancer risk for frequent users. Reducing positron emission tomography (PET) doses by extending scan times allows for clearer functional and anatomical insights, yet this can lead to noisy images and increased motion artifacts. In this study, we propose a new neural network approach that utilizes transfer learning and dropout to create a robust model which inputs low-quality PET scans and healthy CT scans and generates detailed PET/CT merges for pregnant women. Our model calculates uncertainty measures to indicate confidence in its output data, resulting in a high-performing and reliable system that performs well on external datasets, outperforming comparable deep learning models and enabling the creation of dependable low-dose PET scans for pregnant women outside of the training population.

The growing amount of data generated by individuals, often without full awareness, can have a significant impact on their personal lives. A key aspect of the web 2.0 experience is user-generated content, which should be designed to adapt to each user's preferences and maintain their privacy. This involves balancing the customization of content with respect for each user's desire to control how their content is used. The research presented here outlines a potential framework for the web 3.0, centered on user-generated content that prioritizes personalization and the protection of each user's privacy. The proposed framework draws on the principles of belief desirability and the concept of the self, while also considering the influence of content on users and the role of metarepresentations in understanding how content can be used to convey meaningful information, potentially affecting other individuals. This, in turn, reflects an individual's self-image, as well as their understanding of themselves in relation to others.

Our analysis of centering theory within coreference resolution leads to the development of localized centering features, specifically designed to guide subsequent processing and predict coreferential relationships. By incorporating local centering forces into a BERT-based system, we introduce three distinct models that capture different aspects of this theory. In contrast to previous approaches focused on sentence-level processing, our method emphasizes the influence of recent history on local centering. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid model that integrates centering features with attention-based mechanisms to better align with the theoretical underpinnings of centering. Our experimental results demonstrate the explicit value of centering features in coreference resolution and indicate that combining such features with attention models yields superior performance compared to attention-alone systems.

We explore various parameterized approaches to solve the UPWARD PLANARITY problem, 
focusing on parameters relevant to embeddings of planar graphs. Specifically, we investigate 
parameters such as vertex count, edge count, and feedback vertex set size. 
For each parameter, we establish whether the problem is fixed-parameter tractable or APX-hard. 
Our findings reveal new results for both categories: the vertex count and edge count cases for 
fixed-parameter tractability, as well as the APX-hardness of the feedback vertex set size case, 
which was an open question prior to this research.

Software testing relies on accurate system configuration, a task that can be excessively time-consuming and manually inefficient, especially when dealing with complex, number-intensive requirements. Our proposed solution, a system setup tool, automatically generates the needed configuration by parsing text-based input files, ensuring consistency and speed across multiple tests. This setup system further streamlines manual processes by providing a guided, web-based interface for users to complete configuration steps. We showcase its efficiency through several examples of manually executed, repetitive config tasks now accomplished quickly and reliably through automated testing.

In this study, a novel class of operators in the transverse magnetic mode quantum Hall effect is introduced, characterized by extensive spatial distribution and intricate connections. The operators' time evolution, when subjected to an SU(2) spin Hamiltonian, exhibits varying rates of growth, with the most extensive local operators associated with the highest energy density. Notably, the connection and density of these operators can be manipulated through the adjustment of the space between charge impurities. The experiment in our model demonstrates distinguishable signatures in the Hall conductance at the beginning and the end of the quench process, which can be measured using a local probe current. These findings provide a means to detect the unique connections that emerge within these systems following a quench, and our work aligns with results from the time-dependent variational principle.

Recently, WiFi sensing has gained significant interest due to its potential for precise distance measurement, which is a fundamental input for orientation estimation in localization systems. In this project, our objective is to create accurate 2D distance maps in indoor spaces using the correlation between measured RSSI values and physical coordinates. To accomplish this goal, initial approaches involved training a set of supervised machine learning models to physically interpret the meaning of the measured signals. As a starting point for the project, the dataset consisted of 1D data collected in a corridor with dimensions of 9 meters by 3 meters. Three machine learning models were evaluated for their effectiveness: Linear Regression, Support Vector Regression, and Neural Networks. The results indicated that the Neural Network model achieved the most accurate distance estimation, with a mean squared error of 0.04 meters.

We suggest a scenario in which many stars and planets form a spherical shell surrounding a central black hole in galactic centers. In this configuration, often referred to as a Dyson Sphere, the inner surface of the shell is warmed by radiation emitted from the black hole. This system could serve as a natural habitable zone, providing living conditions suitable for life. Although forming such a structure would require immense luck due to the strong gravitational pull of the black hole, discovering it might be feasible through planet-based life detecting missions using radio and infrared signals. Furthermore, we explore how the formation and stability of such a system could be influenced by massive stars, which might be necessary to create the necessary conditions for the structure to exist.

Network monitoring is crucial in ensuring the proper functioning of network services. To detect discrepancies between actual and agreed-upon performance, traditional methods rely on a central system to manage and process data, which can be costly, a single point of failure, and inflexible. To address these issues, we propose an innovative, novel approach that utilizes peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to identify SLA breaches in a network. By combining the BERT multi-agent central control approach with the P2P protocol, we successfully tested and validated the effectiveness of this method, which can also be applied to other decentralized detection scenarios.

In the context of third-generation light sources and research devices, regenerative beam breakup instability (BBI) poses a significant threat to the performance of superconducting radio frequency cavities in energy recovery linacs. As we move towards producing light with higher brightness, the susceptibility to regenerative BBI in dd-coupled ERL systems increases. To mitigate this issue, altering the timing of when the radio frequency pulse is sent can stabilize the system by modifying the feedback loop gain. Our study reveals that optimizing the pulse filling pattern for both balanced and unbalanced systems can achieve stability with reduced power consumption and better system robustness. Furthermore, the ideal filling design exhibits stability limits that are up to three times better than conventional methods, significantly lowering the threshold for beam current instability in energy recovery linacs.

To detect scalable track-based information in high-luminosity hadron colliders like future CMS at HL-LHC, high-rate 3D scintillator sensors will serve as optimal pre-readout modules before the main silicon detectors. These rates necessitate precise measurements of track parameters, particularly total cross-sections, to effectively filter out background noise. In the study, the total cross-sections of neutrons were measured at various energies at the CMS interaction point using novel 3D scintillator sensors. The measurements were conducted as part of a test beam experiment in 2019, where the performance of the sensors was assessed. The results showed that the sensors can accurately measure track parameters with an efficiency of over 85% and low spatial resolution in the range of 5-15 micrometers.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking properties of particles change in response to surface forces and forces generated when they collide, in the context of what occurs in protoplanetary discs. The previous experiments were performed under conditions mimicking cold temperatures found in outer regions of astrophysical discs. The issue is that temperatures rise as you move closer to the central star. In these warmer environments, temperatures can actually mimic those experienced by early-stage planetary formations, or even present-day Earth conditions. The problem is that temperatures continue to increase even further, possibly reaching very hot temperatures of 300 degrees Celsius or above. The question is, how do these particles behave in these extremely hot environments? Can they stick together in these conditions, or are they actually being melted down, or even vaporized, as they should be according to theoretical models? The current experiments aim to replicate the temperature ranges typically associated with intermediate and inner regions of planetary discs. By doing so, the researchers are trying to understand the behavior of these particles in these very hot environments, or even present-day Earth conditions, in order to further inform theoretical models about how planetary formations occur.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a sophisticated variation of Supervised Local Linear Discriminant Analysis (LLDA) that addresses its limitations by utilizing a distance matrix to account for data non-linearity. As LFDA yields promising outcomes in fields such as pattern recognition and image compression, the `lfda` R package streamlines its application through an object-oriented interface and included visualization tools and non-linear extensions. Additionally, the package is featured in Swarnalekha Dey's book, where LFDA concepts and the package are thoroughly explained through diverse real-world case studies.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for developing safe and efficient human-machine collaboration, with the goal of enabling robots to learn from human demonstrations without extensive trial and error. However, straightforward imitation has significant limitations when it comes to handling safety constraints and obstacle avoidance in unstructured environments. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an Extended Kernelized Model Inverse Dynamics Controller that builds on previous work, incorporating nonlinear safety constraints and obstacle avoidance. This controller uses a kernel-based model of the system and a kernel-based inverse dynamics controller to track demonstrations while avoiding obstacles in task space. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through simulations of a robotic arm tracking a human demonstration while navigating around an obstacle and avoiding collisions.

To advance the precision of experimental measurements at large loop orders and lower orders, such six-gluon NLL results are essential. We have made significant progress by deriving a new expression for the six-particle scattering amplitude at the one-loop level, specifically the MELL stage. A key component of our derivation is the calculation of a specific interaction term between gluons, which we have determined in gauge theory using traditional methods. Our method involves utilizing both helicity and kinematic symmetries to simplify the problem. By leveraging the properties of naturalness, we were able to efficiently extend our initial ansatz to higher loop orders. Our final expression matches all previously reported results for quadruple-cut configurations in diagrams with central-emitted vertices. Additionally, our method is so precise that it can be applied to two-loop calculations.

Within the topological Rashba Hubbard model on a 2D square lattice, we examined how spin-orbit coupling and inter-site interaction influence the superfluid phase in the attraction regime. Utilizing a second-order self-consistent mean-field approach, we investigated this system at absolute zero and determined that it can be modeled as a Rashba variant of the extended Hubbard model with site-interaction. Our findings reveal that non-gapsing spiral order is prevalent among superfluid states and arises from strong spin-orbit coupling that prevents both kinds of exchange interactions from simultaneously reaching maximum values. Consequently, spiral order combines with topological properties to produce a novel spiral topological superfluid phase. The spiral topological superfluid is characterized by Majorana zero-modes at the system's edges within a non-trivial spiral band structure.

Using terahertz spectroscopy, we investigated how magnetic flux vortices move in a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductor and discovered an unusual transition as the density of flux increases. This transition, which occurs between single vortex behavior and a state of entangled vortex lines, most likely represents a phase transition where vortex loops form, and notably does so at a flux density corresponding to the $T_\textrm{c}$ onset in the $H-T$ phase diagram.

We investigate the statistical behavior of end groups in molten polymer brushes on substrates with complex geometries, particularly in highly stretched brushes. Our study reveals that in densely packed brushes, the movement of chain ends is constrained by "exclusion zones" in simpler geometries, but these constraints become infinite in certain geometries, known as "asymptotic confinement." As the density of monomers increases, the exclusion zones can match the full range of complex geometries, and we can describe this phenomenon using a novel, density-dependent parameter, $\sigma_\infty$. By utilizing the Asymptotic Scaling Theory, we derive a universal relationship between the size of these infinite exclusion areas and monomer density, validated by Monte Carlo simulations for various polymer chains.

A graph G is considered metrically unique可分辨 if a set of vertices can distinguish every other vertex by its unique distance profile. This property is associated with a minimum set of vertices known as the metric dimension of the graph. We investigate a variation of this concept, known as trimmed metric dimension, where only a subset of vertices needs to be uniquely identifiable. Although the general problem of finding this variation of the dimension is NP-complete, we focus on infinite families of graphs that have very large trimmed metric dimensions relative to their subgraphs. Specifically, we focus on paths and cycles.

Recent years have seen significant progress in using machine learning for both theoretical and observational aspects of astrophysics. With the 11-year dataset from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, researchers can utilize support vector machines to filter out variable sources and create enhanced all-sky maps that highlight changes over time. By analyzing daily, yearly, and reversed datasets, a random forest classifier has also been applied to identify transient sources and produce corresponding all-sky maps, revealing intriguing implications for observing gravitational wave events and the nature of neutron star pulsar mergers.

Integer programming problems, especially those involving matching and covering in graphs, can be efficiently approached by focusing on monarchies within the graph. A notable technique, the round-robin decomposition, breaks down graphs with monarchies into smaller parts through a series of one-on-one exchanges. This method ensures that optimal solutions to certain graph problems remain consistent with the graph's monarchy. A new variation, the extended round-robin approach, achieves better time and space performance while directly utilizing the graph's monarchy to identify high-quality solutions. This method is now used in state-of-the-art solvers, such as those solving challenging instances of the Traveling Salesman Problem.

Recent observations by the Pan-STARRS1, a 570-meter telescope located in Hawaii, have provided a wealth of data for the 10 million minor planets being tracked. Through the analysis of 3.5 million trusted Pan-STARRS1 observations in this wavelength range, researchers discovered 11285 candidates for binary asteroid systems, also referred to as "asters." To validate these potential asters, a thorough investigation was conducted by calculating the orbital characteristics of 9555 selected asters using the Tauris-Taylor method, resulting in the confirmation of 555 binary aster systems and the identification of 485 additional asters in the Main Belt as well as in near-Earth space. Furthermore, a database containing 12409 binary asteroid systems, dubbed the Pan-12409, was created and made accessible to the scientific community via the Astro-database System (ADS).

This research supplements the work of Auerbach, Ching, and Parhizkar (2019) by offering statistical justification for the inference in their study on economic social networks. The cited study estimates the coefficients in a specific type of regression model that has limitations, where the variables are defined by the connections within a social network. The model also accounts for the effects that occur between neighboring individuals within the network. Auerbach, Ching, and Parhizkar (2019) propose a new method for estimating the model and present evidence through simulations and real-world data, specifically using the 'Nine Cities Smoking Study'. This study establishes the statistical validity of the inference by verifying the consistency and normality of the estimation method's errors. The methodology is then utilized to estimate the impact of social smoking based on network data and existing literature.

This study introduces novel operators for integration and differentiation on a range of variables, taking into account changes in order. This innovation enables the development of a modified Leibniz rule for these operators. Additionally, the study introduces an operator-based definition for the Variable-Order Pulkit and Sharma Transform (VPST) and derives its core properties. Furthermore, the transform has been applied to solve differential equations, with detailed examples provided to illustrate its effectiveness.

The problem of detecting a signal that varies across an array of sensors is examined, with a focus on a scenario where the signal pattern changes over time within a low-dimensional subspace and the noise is Gaussian and unpredictable. Specifically, a test based on the recursive least-squares algorithm is analyzed to determine under what conditions this test can successfully identify when the signal is present or absent. Formulas are derived to show how the probability of errors evolves over time in response to varying levels of a control parameter used to filter out noise, with the analysis covering several applications including change detection in system states, the creation of adaptive filters when the signal pattern shifts, and variational Bayesian methods for inferring the dimensionality of the signal's subspace.

The development of advanced spectrographs, enabled by significant computational breakthroughs, has empowered researchers to make substantial progress in implementing high-precision representation systems. To streamline the interpretation of scientific observations, the associated spectrographs typically produce extensive spectral measurements captured on formatted disks. This advancement paves the way for the creation of user-friendly web applications, which enable the efficient analysis of complex data sets. As web platforms gain popularity for presenting and interpreting imaging and spectral data in scientific contexts, there is a heightened demand for user-friendly tools that facilitate effective data exploration. Furthermore, these tools enable the integration of vital aspects, such as unit conversion, spectral calibration, and data visualization, to optimize the overall user experience. Building upon the foundation of formatted disks, which encode imaging and spectral data in a compact and standardized manner, users can seamlessly access and visualize data without the need to perform time-consuming unpacking processes. To address the limitations of high-precision spectro-imagery formats, such as formatted disks, a comprehensive suite of web tools is presented, enabling the efficient exploration and analysis of complex data sets.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean began to form due to a break-up of the South Atlantic-Nubian Plate into multiple plates, and it is interesting to note the influence of pre-rift asthenospheric upwellings in the Southern Atlantic. The upwellings under West Africa and Equatorial Africa displayed different characteristics, with West Africa showing a large, concentrated upwelling and Equatorial Africa showing smaller, dispersed upwellings. The rifting process mirrored these upwellings, with West Africa experiencing a large, concentrated rift and Equatorial Africa showing a more distributed, complex rift system. Numerical modeling revealed that the behavior of plates above these upwellings was a key factor in determining the plate-break-up process, resulting in an asymmetric plate-break-up above West Africa and a more widespread, intricate pattern above Equatorial Africa. Observations of seismic upwellings and geological features supported the influence of sub-lithospheric dynamics in shaping the Southern Atlantic.

Information maximization is a well-established, unsupervised learning technique that naturally leads to a suitable loss function for self-supervised segmentation without requiring ground truth data. This research applies self-supervised learning techniques to the challenging task of segmenting medical images, a task for which large-scale annotation is particularly demanding. We develop an Information Maximization framework, incorporating both global and local information maximization, and evaluate it on two difficult medical datasets: the Medical Template Project (MeTPo) and the Actionable Baby Ultrasound (AbbaUS) dataset. Due to the tendency of Information Maximization to underperform at boundary regions critical for segmentation, a boundary-sensitive information maximization (BMI) loss is proposed. By placing greater emphasis on boundary regions and minimizing information maximization there, BMI enhances performance. Notably, BMI requires only a batch-normalization-based pre-training and no additional annotation, making it an efficient and effective solution for medical image segmentation.

In recent years, conversational agents have gained significant popularity.
Building upon this foundation, our goal is to create a conversational agent that can effectively interact with and lead other players through the world of Dungeons and Dragons.
To accomplish this, we collect dialogue data from actual games and train neural network models capable of engaging in conversation based on implicit objectives, ultimately learning how to guide others through the power of 'Theory-of-Mind'.
Our experiments reveal that models trained with this theory can successfully have meaningful discussions, but further improvement is necessary for them to efficiently lead other players through the game.

Despite significant progress in Lexical Semantic Change Detection, the task of Discovering New Concepts (NC) remains under-researched and lacks a comprehensive assessment. To address this gap, our work provides an in-depth exploration of the connection between change and discovery of new concepts. Additionally, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Task Learning Change-Discovery (MTLCD) to simultaneously tackle both tasks. To further enhance the research community's understanding, we establish a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating diverse models on the discovered NC. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the MTLCD framework in discovering NC concepts, leading to the introduction of a high-performing alternative. Overall, our work establishes a standardized benchmark for assessing the discovered NC concepts across multiple models, including the proposed MTLCD framework. The accompanying resources are available for download at the provided URL.

We suggest a novel way to define particle distribution functions that depend on transverse momentum, by drawing from the constituent quark model used in deep elastic scattering. This approach may also be applicable to bound states such as deep virtual Compton scattering and deep elastic scattering, and we demonstrate its connection to a quark model calculation.

The three-dimensional structure and knot type of a tangled one-dimensional object, or space curve, can be unraveled using specific measures of complexity. In contrast, the complex folding processes of proteins, particularly those containing knots, are influenced not just by the curve's geometry but also by the physical forces acting on the curve, including the tendency of adjacent segments to bond. As the curve becomes heated, disordered, and subsequently cooled, its behavior changes, and adding a limit to the angle between neighboring segments significantly impacts the formation of ordered structures. Our researchers utilized topological theory to analyze how heat affects the formation of this type of knot. They discovered that restricting the angle during the formation process of a (5_1) knot from a tangled state results in multiple distinct phases, whereas the (3_1) knot exhibits only one. Molecular dynamic simulations of (3_1) and (5_1) knot-formed proteins demonstrate that objects with similar topology can exhibit different dynamic properties while maintaining their stability. Additionally, binary mixing of these proteins reveals a unique phase that exhibits characteristics of two distinct structures, exhibiting a hysteresis effect dependent on the mixing parameters.

To address the anomaly in the Hubble constant, a new form of energy known as early dark energy (EDE) is suggested, which, surprisingly, can exist without being tied to a specific theory of physics. By analyzing how early dark energy influences the EDA parameter and considering cosmic observations from Planck, BOSS, and other experiments, this study examines the energy's density, equation of state, and associated sound horizon. Notably, it explores the effect of data combination and data analysis methods on EDE properties by applying profile likelihood to separate Planck data components. The results indicate that combining CMB anisotropy and lensing data reduces the free parameter range for EDE, whereas adding BAO measurements has a minimal impact. Furthermore, removing low-`l` temperature polarizations from the analysis significantly affects the EDE density and marks the beginning of a notable `l` range. This study demonstrates that profile likelihood enables a detailed understanding of how the EDE equation of state responds to separate data sets across different `l` ranges, thus providing a more in-depth comprehension of early dark energy.

We establish that the symplectic mapping category groups of a certain class of blowups, specifically over two-dimensional tori, are isomorphic to those of the underlying tori. A corresponding symmetry in symplectic geometry is demonstrated through our findings, where equal numbers of blowups at various points on a two-dimensional torus yield the same symplectic mapping category group. Furthermore, our main theorem allows us to reconstruct Gromov's result on the non-squeezing phenomenon from a broader framework. It also enables us to recover key features of the Hamiltonian flow associated with a specific setup on a two-dimensional torus, as well as part of the lasso theorem for Lagrangian submanifolds from our more general results.

A rigorous mathematical framework is developed to generalize the concept of spontaneous symmetry breaking in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. Our approach makes the abstract structure of a symmetry group explicit, utilizing Lie algebra elements to parameterize infinitesimal group transformations. This formalism leads to an expanded, precise definition of the spontaneous symmetry breaking, ultimately producing an exact expression for the mass of scalar particles in a relativistic quantum field theory, aligned with the standard mass-shell condition. A substantial body of examples is examined using this new framework to demonstrate the advantages it provides over previous, less precise definitions. In particular, the usual connection between massless particles and spontaneous symmetry breaking, often associated with the unbroken residual symmetry, appears overly restrictive, thus our approach is both more accurate and provides greater clarity. Furthermore, the framework is applied to examine the hypothetical Nambu-Goldstone bosons in a relativistic scalar theory without spontaneous symmetry breaking, yielding an inherently group-theoretic investigation of this scenario's nontrivial residual symmetry and its representations, which may also have broader implications beyond particle physics.

Recent advancements in learning from hypothetical examples have led state-of-the-art performance on various NLP tasks, yet some research suggests a significant portion of these examples becomes redundant. This proportion of unnecessary data is substantial and, in many instances, significantly so. In an effort to reduce this unnecessary portion, we propose an innovative hypothesis: it's more crucial to learn from hypothetical examples that contain phrasal hypotheses with significant impact, rather than trivial counterparts. To validate this, we introduce two notable contributions. Firstly, we present DISCO, an innovative hypothesis where a specialized model could guide a specialized teacher to filter out unnecessary hypothetical examples. This model could selectively filter out these examples and focus on those containing valuable phrasal hypotheses. Secondly, we provided a specialized teacher model and a corresponding evaluation benchmark comprising 3,222 hypothetical examples across nine distinct NLP tasks and two different hypotheses formats. This teacher model is capable of identifying these valuable examples in various contexts, resulting in substantial performance enhancements of up to 27.44% in our evaluations. Moreover, DISCO exhibits robust generalizability, achieving substantial performance improvements when applied to novel tasks and prompts, thereby confirming our initial hypothesis across multiple scenarios.
In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

In remote epitaxy, substrate dislocations do not affect the overgrowth layer and are thus preferred for producing high-quality thin films. Yet, realizing remote epitaxy is challenging due to the natural tendency for quasi-remote overgrowth modes and their hybrid variants that combine elements from remote epitaxy and their close relatives such as extrinsic dislocation-free epitaxy and van der Waals epitaxy. This dilemma can be addressed with ultrathin intermediate buffers, especially when considering the system of Heusler materials on the graphene/Al$_2$O$_3$ substrate. Utilizing the unique properties of this system and its lack of lattice compatibility with Heusler materials, it is possible to produce defect-free, strain-free films as薄 as 2 unit periods. Without an intermediate buffer, however, it is necessary for the Heusler materials to compete with the substrate for the underlying buffer and this results in mixed growth modes that combine remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $\mathbb{Z}_p^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m$-linear when it possesses a generator matrix that is structured in blocks of $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m$. In this paper, we focus on codes $\mathbb{Z}_p^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m$ where the prime number $p$ is either $2$ or an odd number. For these codes, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition to be $\mathbb{Z}_p^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m$-linear, along with methods to find the dimension parameter and kernel of such codes. Additionally, we establish two distinct criteria to be $\mathbb{Z}_p^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m$-linear codes.

A novel polymer plug formulation has been developed to prevent hydrocarbon wells from producing water.  The formulation will temporarily block the water-bearing zone, allowing the well to produce gas and oil.  The polymer's viscosity is designed to increase upon contact with oil, providing an additional barrier.  To maximize the plug's lifespan and prevent being mixed with incoming fluids, a special injection technique is used.  The goal of the optimization process is to find the perfect polymer viscosity profile, ensuring the plug remains intact for the longest possible time.  The model takes into account a complex series of events, including how the well interacts with the polymer plug, including a temporary period of violence as pressures adjust.  It also considers whether the polymer will separate into distinct layers, allowing the middle layer to provide an extra barrier.  The model includes various forms of friction as well.  Based on the adjusted conditions of the reservoir, a numerical method is used to solve the resulting equations.  The ultimate objective is to minimize cost by balancing the polymer's viscosity profile with its associated cost, ensuring the plug remains intact for at least a specified amount of time.  The ultimate goal of the study is clear, however, the precise formulation of the objective function was left to the reader's imagination.

Multi-label classification, where a single sample can belong to multiple categories simultaneously, is a common and challenging task in various real-world applications. Due to its nature, labeled data is scarce, necessitating the use of sophisticated models trained on unlabeled datasets via self-training. However, traditional self-training methods struggle in this setting as they rely on high-confidence single-label predictions, making them inadequate for the complex multi-label assignments underlying unlabeled datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel self-training algorithm called Single-to-Multi Label Self-Training (SMLST), which is capable of leveraging single-label labels to train robust models for multi-label classification. Specifically, SMLST identifies unlabeled samples that have been predicted with high confidence as belonging to the same label and then generates multi-label labels based on high-probability predictions for other labels. To prevent the model from becoming overconfident, SMLST selectively loses confidence in unlabeled samples with initial multi-label labels during training. Comparative experiments have demonstrated the superiority of the MLE and Cross-Entropy loss functions, and it has been concluded that both the training order of samples and the choice of loss function significantly impact the performance of the algorithm. Rivaling even the optimal performance achievable with full multi-label labeling, SMLST illustrates its effectiveness in addressing the scarcity of multi-label labeled data.

This research provides an upper limit for the total energy in time-fractional Allen-Cahn and damped wave equations, accounting for a specific range of the fractional exponent $\alpha$. By analyzing the fractional energy functional's behavior over time, we demonstrate that the energy decreases at a rate proportional to $(1-t^\alpha)$, and further establish that for a particular time $T<1$, the energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\beta}$ with the same proportionality constant. Additionally, within the equation $\frac{^\mathrm{C}D^{1-\alpha}u(T)}{^\mathrm{C}D^{1-\alpha}v(T)}$, we derive the relationship between Caputo derivatives, and apply similar techniques to parabolic and damped wave equations to obtain analogous results.

The GNS construction connects abstract states with concrete observables using pre-Hilbert spaces. We examine this process through the lens of category theory, and in particular how it relates to the way we see categories as pre-Hilbert spaces. We then discuss this in the context of the way we use C*-algebras as the building blocks for quantum mechanics.

We develop a new mathematical model to re-examine previously explored ideas about magnetically restricted disks in the energetic radio galaxies and quasars. The model shows that if the central black hole's magnetic fields are sufficient to satisfy the condition of the magnetic funnels, it can maintain stable, turbulent accretion, thus explaining the persistent high-energy emissions without contradiction. Furthermore, if the central black hole's mass is less than $10^{4.5}$ solar masses, this model can simultaneously account for the energetic and optical/UV emissions simultaneously, utilizing a unified approach by modifying the standard emission spectrum from a broadened disk. We observe that in high-energy gamma-rays, the standard emission spectrum from the disks behaves similarly to the observed emissions from nearby gamma-rays in the energy band of X-rays in a number of cases but also produces a number of exceptions where another emission-carrying structure above the high-energy gamma-rays is necessary. This could either be a faster-moving jet or another structure responsible for producing X-rays. Ultimately, this model can, under certain conditions where the energy of the radio photons is greater than that of the gamma-rays, account for the energy of the gamma-rays by accelerating electrons in the thick disk through another known mechanism called synchrotron self-Compton.

This research employs a unified statistical framework to analyze modern investment portfolios, leveraging cutting-edge tools from probability theory, statistics, and linear algebra. We utilize the proposed framework to investigate the key aspects of mean-variance portfolio investing, specifically the strategies for allocating returns to individual assets to maximize portfolio performance, an approach commonly seen in real-world portfolio management. By applying our model to real-world stock data, we explore the performance of portfolios managed through this strategy and demonstrate the versatility of our approach in solving previously challenging problems, including the estimation of portfolio risks in high-frequency trading.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and manual medical professional assessment combined with automated analysis using physical recording devices can effectively accomplish this. Multiple automated systems have been designed and utilized for condition diagnosis, with most relying on signal decomposition techniques like Fourier transformation. However, such methods may lead to inaccurate diagnosis, especially when confronted with data containing anomalies. This research introduces a novel approach, based on a deep learning network, capable of identifying normal and abnormal heart patterns without significant distortion, thereby building a robust framework for heart condition classification in scenarios involving noisy data.

With wearable devices accumulating health data, machine learning offers improved performance and privacy benefits when utilizing this data. However, sharing the trained model with other users can compromise privacy, making federated learning a more suitable alternative. FedTransfer, a novel federated transfer learning technique, combines the advantages of wearable devices and federated learning to share data across multiple devices while respecting user privacy. It allows for the transfer of health data from one device to another, but not from the same device. This paper introduces the FedTransfer framework, its operational principles, and potential applications in healthcare, along with challenges to be overcome.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher-order moments including skewness and kurtosis into a unified framework. By examining the objective functions and constraints, relationships between various methodologies can be identified. Specific approaches correspond to well-known methods under conditions of normal distribution, while others reflect the impact of non-normal distributions on portfolio selection. A case study using stock data with a non-normal distribution demonstrates the practical implications of incorporating skewness and kurtosis as constraints in portfolio optimization.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's transition to a non-stable cosmic epoch, potentially influencing the universe's ultimate fate. We Suggest a string vacuum must possess multiple distinct decay pathways, with the universe becoming dark energy dominated after each collapse and rebound. To address the coincidence problem, we Suggest that gravitational attractors may be the root cause of this phenomenon.

This study introduces three key algorithms designed to streamline software workflows,
which can be utilized in various areas such as software reverse engineering and deobfuscation.
To demonstrate their effectiveness, we created an exclusive software processing platform and
conducted an experiment focused on dismantling a highly deoptimized binary, produced from
an extensively obfuscated source code. Our method successfully reversed the deoptimized binary
and yielded a clean, optimized code, which was made available for download at the following link:
https://github.com/andrewbess/DrilWitchGo. Our contributions consist of developing a software
processing system composed of three distinct but complementary modules, which work in unison to
reverse software assets, despite challenges posed by data control loss and interlocking control
flows. Our approach utilizes a highly customizable framework, which allows for the development
of specialized Drulis transformations, thus enabling the preservation of semantic meaning,
highly interdependent program structures, and infinite recursion during the conversion of
abstract syntax trees from source to target languages.

This study tackles a classic optimal control problem, often referred to as the "investment-consumption problem," within the framework of stochastic calculus using semimartingales. The main innovation lies in its ability to address irregular cost functions that change over time, despite the limiting assumptions typically found in this area of study. The novel cost function in this paper significantly deviates from the standard framework, where costs are usually decreasing step functions with substantial penalties during transaction times. To prove the existence of optimal strategies in this complex scenario, a new approach to the value process is introduced, which may have broader implications for similar problems. The characterization of optimal strategies is proven through a specialized Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, and this characterization is further confirmed through a novel approach to the idealized case, specifically exploring the consequences of concave utility functions and convex switching costs. The implications of this work also provide insights into the idealized "dividend optimization problem." The innovative approach used in this study could potentially be applied to similar, more intricate financial models.

Research on the potential for scalar leptoquarks to be generated in pairs via the process of type C is typically initiated by examining whether they can be produced in C-type interactions. However, we find that due to the existence of competing interactions, pair production of type C is unlikely to be a reliable metric for assessing new physics capabilities, as pairs generated through C-type interactions face significant suppression from other more effective one-quark processes. Consequently, it is crucial to reassess any conclusions regarding New Physics parameters that are based on C-type pair production cross-sections.

Evaluating new hardware or chemical methods requires a reliable and efficient testing process. Using sequential designs with multivariate processes, this process can be optimized by pinpointing the best combination of factors quickly. Although standard models work well for shorter time sequences with lower dimensional inputs, they may not be as effective for more complex scenarios. By leveraging deep learning's flexible feature extraction capabilities, this research proposes a novel approach: a graph neural network model that integrates observations from a coalescing Brownian motion process. Initially applied to simple time sequences with low dimensional measurements, this model then becomes scalable, addressing more extensive sequences with higher dimensional measurements. When evaluated on both synthetic and real-world data, this graph learning approach shows significant improvements over the graph neural network with RBF kernels in terms of convergence speed and solution quality.

Photodissociation regions are characterized by low ionization levels and serve as an interface between a galaxy's molecular gas and neutral hydrogen. They are typically stimulated to very low temperatures by a process called "subthermal," which has significant implications. This phenomenon affects how photons below 4.9 micrometers are absorbed by a galaxy's molecular gas, leading to distinct differences in these emissions when compared to emissions above this wavelength from the same galaxy. This discrepancy can be utilized to calculate the total mass of a galaxy's molecular gas more accurately. Additionally, this process is essential in the study of active galactic nuclei because it significantly impacts the apparent cooling efficiency of their molecular gas. When correcting our observations for this, we can restore the apparent cooling power to levels comparable to those in normally stimulated regions. This has the potential to correct a previously observed correlation between a galaxy's active nuclear activity and its molecular gas reservoir, which actually persists even after correcting for this effect. Furthermore, we found that the mass of a galaxy's dust is directly proportional to its molecular gas mass, with a proportionality constant of approximately 0.017.

Our investigation proposes an intriguing duality between the weak interaction and heavy composite structures, yielding the muon $g-2$ anomaly of $\sim 7\sigma$ as well as explaining the $K$ and $B$ anomalies with remarkable simultaneity. The model's verification can be achieved through searches for contact interactions and single photon processes at the LHC, with potential confirmation from future colliders like the HL-LHC and the FCC.

Given the symmetric group $S_n$, a measure of distance between permutations $\sigma$ and $\tau$, denoted $d(\sigma, \tau)$, can be defined as the number of elements that differ, i.e., $d(\sigma, \tau) = |\{ i : \sigma(i) \neq \tau(i)\}|$. For any possible distance value $r$, we examine the set $B_r$, which consists of all permutations within a distance $r$ from a particular permutation $\sigma$. If $B_r$ is too large, it may be possible for two distinct permutations $\sigma$ and $\tau$ to have all their neighboring permutations ($B_{\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor}$) overlap, making it impossible to reliably reconstruct a permutation from its sequence of previous states, which is the fundamental issue we address. Our research reveals that the reconstruction threshold for the Hamming distance $d$ is in fact $\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$.

Research on musical instrument classification typically focuses on a limited number of instruments. To tackle this issue, this paper proposes a strategy that utilizes hierarchical relationships within a database to enable the recognition of a broader range of instruments. By training a model on just a handful of instruments and representing other instruments as combinations of those trained instruments, we can expand the model's classification capabilities. This approach utilizes a hierarchical structure, akin to the ISO 8825 standard, to organize the musical instrument database into a tree-like format. We propose an innovative network that incorporates this structure by integrating a hierarchical attention mechanism, which allows the model to assign varying levels of importance to different parts of the tree during classification. To test this approach, we conducted experiments on the MAIO dataset, and the results indicate that our proposed strategy significantly enhances accuracy in musical instrument classification.

In the knowledge-seeking process, questioners aim to acquire new information and present necessary background to enable a well-informed response. Despite progress, a significant barrier remains in accurately representing the context of a specialized topic, a topic that often demands in-depth domain expertise. Building upon this challenge, we introduce RASCB (Knowledge-Seeking Questions Answered in Research Papers), a novel dataset that contains a substantial collection of over 30,000 questions spanning 1,000 subdomains along with their corresponding answers extracted from academic papers. To compensate for the limitations of human-annotated data in evaluating large language models' ability to ask and seek knowledge effectively, we developed a comprehensive evaluation framework that compares the context of human-created questions to those of machine-generated ones. This framework systematically measures critical aspects including question clarity, ability to differentiate between inquiry and background, and ability to pinpoint information gaps.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. To precisely predict the signals these binaries produce, particularly in terms of frequency and phase, a substantial number of post-Newtonian (PN) terms need to be taken into consideration. As a result, this prediction can become computationally expensive and require manual selection of relevant PN terms. In order to streamline this process, we have developed a novel algorithm based on symbolic computation, which not only identifies the contributing PN terms but also cancels out terms that cancel out in summation. Furthermore, it eliminates terms with zero coefficients for specific binaries. By utilizing this algorithm, the necessary PN terms for predictions up to 3.5PN order have been determined, thereby enabling more accurate and efficient frequency-domain time-series conversions. Additionally, this algorithm has been made publicly available as an open-source tool, which accelerates such conversions by a factor of at least 10.

We establish a significant connection between the asymmetric simple exclusion process and its spatial characteristics by demonstrating the correspondence between the process's particle current and velocity systems previously analyzed in Grout, Quast, and Schumacher (2021). Building upon this connection, we establish the long-standing conjecture regarding the free energy distribution of the TASEP under half-way initial conditions as posed in Baik, Borodin, and Rost (2009). Additionally, our findings enable the derivation of explicit solutions for the one-point distribution of heights of ASEP domino tilings and the heights of ASEP queues, aligning with the results presented in O'Connell (2009a) and G\'oya (2017).

This paper offers an overview of mathematical modelling during an epidemic.
Various methods and comparisons are made between models that simulated human population dynamics during the current COVID-19 epidemic.
A key issue with modelling during an epidemic is choosing appropriate parameters, for which we examine relevant research and provide a key for model comparison.
This key is used to draw a comparison between models through simple simulations.
Such simulations can be applied to simple compartmental models and an agent-based model.
This paper also discusses statistical methods for analyzing and comparing model performance to real data.
A case study using open-source tools for comparing models to data is presented.
Various strategies for preventing the spread of epidemics are summarized, including their effect on model behaviour.
Relevant literature and model code used in this study are listed as reference materials.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and its description by a real-valued field. Using the Majorana model, we analyzed the characteristics of an ensemble of independent Majorana fermions. Our study involved computing key statistical functions including the density of states, Coulomb interaction energy, and density. Moreover, we investigated how the fermionic and real-valued aspects influence these functions within the context of the BCS theory of superconductivity. Notably, we found that the number of electrons in a superconductor is uncertain due to its delocalized electron wave function, which has implications for how the Coulomb interaction is handled in superconductors.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as informal tools to shorten lengthy terms,
but they pose significant challenges to noun phrase extraction systems,
translate-based info. retrieval systems, and machine readable translation platforms.
Despite their prevalence in various domains such as science, business, and public health,
current methods for identifying and resolving these acronyms are inconsistent,
inefficient, or non-existent. To address this gap, we have developed a web-based
platform called MadDog that provides a unified interface for finding acronym
resolutions across the internet. MadDog offers features like real-time suggestion,
batch processing, and a memory function to suggest previous searches, all via a
natural language query system. Additionally, we demonstrate MadDog's capabilities
through its successful deployment in an info. retrieval chatbot for COVID-related info.

We propose a method to convert spinless atoms into magnetic atom-pair entities with altered inter-pair connections, leveraging three-body recombination triggered by a monochromatic laser. In the process, the entanglement between the atom's and spinor internal states yields a single-species molecule. A key advantage of this conversion is that the atom-pair entanglement prevents spontaneous emission, which typically disrupts atomic state integrity. Furthermore, by controlling the converting laser, we can access both regime of two-body bicolor molecules and fully spin-polarized atoms. This capability offers potential for exploring non-linear dynamics, collective behaviors in magnetic spin-states, and stable long-duration entanglement.

Our proposed Convolutional DNA Storage (CoDNS) framework addresses a key limitation of existing DNA storage structures, which struggle to accommodate hierarchical relationships and update operations, commonly found in web pages and databases. By incorporating DNA index technology, CoDNS enables storage of hierarchical data and updates without requiring re-encoding of the entire dataset, which is attainable due to the self-descriptive nature of DNA addresses. By drawing on the error correction capabilities of DNA storage, we mitigate the risks introduced by the use of DNA addresses, which have shorter lengths than traditional error correction codes. By integrating a convolutional update mechanism, which is inspired by convolutional codes, CoDNS ensures robust error correction across both hierarchical data and update operations. Furthermore, CoDNS is shown to maintain operational efficiency by employing a binary tree structure that minimizes the impact of address lengths on operation performance.

Topological insulators represent a novel class of materials with exceptional properties for both fundamental research and applications, thanks to their robust, gap-filled surface states resulting from non-trivial topological invariants. Initially identified in conventional superconductors and magnetic insulators, these states have since been explored in various other materials, including topological crystalline insulators, anomalous Hall insulators, and anomalous Hall effects in topological semimetals. This paper provides an in-depth examination of nodal lines on the boundary of momentum space in topological insulators, focusing on their inherent characteristics and recent findings in topological semimetals across a range of systems, such as photonic crystals, elastic materials, and quantum mechanical systems. We particularly emphasize the distinctive features of nodal lines in crystalline topological insulators and their realizations in photonic and other types of systems.

A brain tumor is an abnormal growth inside the cranial cavity that can affect a person's thinking, movement, and overall quality of life. The rising rate of brain tumor incidents globally makes accurate diagnosis essential for successful treatment. In this study, a deep learning-based method called MAG-Net is proposed to accurately identify and classify brain tumors along with healthy brain tissue using MRI images. MAG-Net effectively uses information from MRI images across different sequences to improve performance and accurately segmentate and classify tumors into three categories: glioma, non-glioma, and healthy brain. The results obtained by MAG-Net in three experiments demonstrate an excellent balance between segmentation and classification performance, with a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.9309, 0.9181, and 0.9899 and a mean accuracy of 99.3%, 98.9%, and 99.9% respectively for paired tasks and a99.2% overall accuracy.

Differentiable programming frameworks like PyTorch and JAX have become a trend due to their ability to solve complex inverse problems by leveraging pre-trained models and vast datasets for self-supervised learning and domain adaptation. A key component in many such problems, particularly in tomography, is the shadow computation, which is typically performed using efficient numerical methods such as Sobol's quasi-Monte Carlo integration. However, these methods pose challenges when it comes to differentiating the computation with respect to model parameters, a requirement in optimization problems. This work proposes an algorithm that accurately calculates shadows in three dimensions at a high speed by utilizing adaptive matrix multiplication, a vital step in techniques like unsupervised learning and domain adaptation. The proposed method is seamlessly integrated into the JAX framework and 3DTomopy, a tomography reconstruction library, and has been demonstrated to serve as a reliable and transparent alternative to differentiable implementations of the Radon transform in joint optimization and inverse problem problems. By optimizing the computation of shadows and shadow differences, this proposed method can serve as a suitable alternative, and its benefits are showcased through its application in self-supervised learning and domain adaptation, particularly in the context of limited tomographic data and its performance is compared to other methods in simulated and real-world scenarios.

A deep learning-based interlacing removal technique has achieved high accuracy, but its computational demands hinder real-time performance in video. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed efficient models capable of processing high-frequency data at real-time speeds. However, these models struggle with low-frequency motion due to the limited available training data. In contrast, streaming applications frequently contain low-motion sequences. This research proposes a hybrid approach combining a deep learning-based algorithm with a traditional motion vector analysis method. By leveraging the strengths of both, the new system delivers superior results: the ability to handle both high and low motion while maintaining real-time performance. A comprehensive evaluation of the hybrid approach, along with its relative benefits and drawbacks, will be provided.

Researchers have successfully used the non-relativistic mean field model to measure the average square radius of the neutron distribution, a result that previously required experimental verification. In a comparative study, we used a simplified dimensional relativistic mean field model to evaluate both models. By making specific assumptions about meson exchanges, we were able to use the relativistic model to obtain average square radii of the neutron distribution in the range of 0.2 to 0.6 fm². This allowed us to confirm our previous results obtained with the non-relativistic mean field model. Furthermore, a direct relationship between the average square radius of the neutron distribution and the difference in the skins of the proton and neutron density distributions was established using both models, yielding the same average square radius range of 0.2 to 0.6 fm² in the case of conventional superfluid neutron stars. This direct relationship could potentially be utilized to determine the average square radius of the neutron distribution through astronomical measurements of parity-violating X-ray spectra.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks, supplying irrigation, and harnessing hydroelectric power. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed to model and forecast river flow velocities, their solutions require solving complex nonlinear partial differential equations, which can be time-consuming and difficult to solve, especially in real-time. In this study, we've developed a novel machine learning framework to predict river flow velocities based on the shape of a river, by utilizing a deep learning model that learns to directly output flow velocities. This model is trained on synthetic data and can be easily managed through a user-friendly interface, which allows for rapid and accurate predictions of river flow velocities. As a result, we've obtained hydroelectric power and irrigation irrigation water usage as explicit functions of river width, which can be computed almost instantly.

High dynamic range photography addresses the limitation of 2D digital images in capturing bright light sources within a scene with varying luminance levels. Traditional methods require a human to decide on the number and settings for photographic exposures, then align and blend them together. In contrast, our proposed methodology automatically determines the optimal exposure configuration for a given scene without human input. This algorithm first generates multiple possible configurations, each representing a different combination of exposure settings. It assesses each configuration's potential for successful capture, scoring them accordingly. Using these scores, it allocates computational resources efficiently to find the best configuration within a given time frame. Once the optimal configuration is determined, the system takes the exposed images and employs both fast and accurate techniques to blend them together, resulting in an output that maintains detail in both bright and dark areas of the scene without appearing unnatural.

Artificial Neural Networks are pushing the boundaries of performance in various prediction tasks but suffer from limited generalization capabilities and high sensitivity to overfitting. In contrast, humans achieve satisfactory prediction accuracy even with suboptimal data, primarily due to their ability to identify causal structures. This paper aims to introduce a framework that integrates causality with deep learning in order to develop more robust predictive models. The proposed framework covers both generative and structural models, explores the incorporation of coherence principles, and examines the use of expert knowledge in the form of Bayesian methods and generative models. Additionally, the authors will present their ongoing research through diverse research areas and potential organizational strategies.

Understanding how temperature behaves in reaction engineering processes, such as gas-solid fixed bed catalytic cracking, is challenging to measure accurately due to the difficulties in obtaining precise temperature readings. As a potential alternative, we utilize rapid magnetic resonance imaging (rMRI) to assess temperature distributions within a gas-solid fixed bed in real-time. By analyzing the changes in the transverse relaxation rate one ($\Delta R_2$) in rMRI data, we can successfully map out the temperature arrangement within the fixed bed. Furthermore, our findings indicate the existence of distinct temperature zones, revealing a cooler surface layer and varying temperature gradients within the bed.

In this work, we investigate the connection between the b-principle for complex structures and M. Tamanoi's proof of the Mumford conjecture, as well as A. Aougab and M. Longo's approach to generalizing the b-principle for moduli spaces of complex structures. Given M.
