This research reinterpreers the opportunity inequality measure using a probability space, which may be an real interval. By applying this opportunity space probability space framework, the opportunity inequality is demonstrated to satisfy characterizing properties, leading to the conclusion that the opportunity inequality index is a weighted average of quantile differences. Moreover, the continuity and rigidity of the index are obtained from this average form, resulting in the characterization of all indices that meet these criteria. When the weight function in the average is the density function, the connection between the w-quantile inequality and the opportunity inequality is further investigated. The relationship between the traditional inequality index, the Atkinson index, and the w-quantile inequality is also established, along with a strategy to redistribute incomes while maintaining the opportunity inequality.

For a specific type of group, we've developed a new mathematical object, referred to as a quantum blob, within an infinite-dimensional space, and have established a connection between its characterizations and a K-theory object, called BQK, associated with both finite and affine symmetric groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the quantum blob can influence the quantum K-theory of certain complex geometric structures, specifically flag manifolds and related spaces.

The widespread adoption of machine learning has brought substantial benefits, yet the potential for errors remains. One key aspect responsible for potential failures is data quality. Although numerous studies have outlined various critical quality dimensions, they often neglect to examine the interconnectedness of these qualities in relation to machine learning performance. The concept of data debuging, which aims to pinpoint performance-degrading issues within machine learning models, has been proposed. The development of the ShapleyML approach has enabled the attribution of model performance to specific inputs, setting the stage for a potential extension to shapleyML by incorporating domain knowledge. To address the computational complexities associated with machine learning pipeline analysis, a sampling-based method for estimating the Shapley value has been proposed. This leads to the introduction of DataDebugML, which facilitates the identification of data quality problems within machine learning pipelines. Through concrete examples, the quality of this system is demonstrated.

This study explores the connection between radio emissions and dynamical interactions in a one teraelectronvolt frequency in the MAVERIC survey's sample of radio transmissions from six Galactic globular clusters. Specifically, it examines 210 sources across six clusters observed with very large array telescopes at a one-eighth of a degree resolution. Statistical analysis reveals that approximately 50% of point-like sources in these clusters result from binary star collisions, while data from charted pulsars indicates that binary systems with radio emissions, featuring massive stars or compact remnants, are more prevalent than expected based on millisecond pulsar distributions in the Milky Way. These findings highlight the ability of binary systems to significantly contribute to one-treeth of a degree scale radio emissions in globular clusters.

We propose a novel method for reconstructing collapsed graphs using hypergraphs,
a higher-order representation, as guidance. Unlike previous approaches that merely
represent hyperedges as sequential pairs, our method retains a full description of
collapsed hyperedges in their redshift-space positions. This high-fidelity representation
allows us to extract additional features from the hypergraph, such as 'within-edge' information,
which we incorporate into our model through a novel loss function. Building upon this,
we propose GHRNet, a neural network that utilizes a novel training regimen to achieve
state-of-the-art results. In our experiments, GHRNet outperforms the current best method,
yielding a substantial improvement in recovery performance (0.46 FWD/0.49 BWD). In contrast,
existing reconstruction methods utilizing hypergraphs as guidance suffer from data leakage issues,
whereas our approach avoids this problem.

We employ an entropic measure to determine when a light output direction becomes dominant in a silicon microcavity system. Calculating this threshold involves comparing the entropic values of the system's overall light output with those of individual potential emission directions. This threshold determines when the system begins producing a highly directional light output. To verify this theoretical prediction, we utilize a phase-resolved near-field technique to map the emission patterns of the microcavity laser at various power levels.

We utilize thermal atomic rubidium-87 and demonstrate the potential of thermal atomic gases for nonlinear optical applications. By utilizing a technique known as super-radiance, we are able to utilize a thermal atomic gas and enhance the rate of photon emission from a weakly coupled laser, effectively using the thermal atoms collectively. The resulting photon correlations exhibit a shift towards super-bunching at increased pumping levels, a effect that is attributable to the collective interaction of the atoms and verified through numerical simulation and analytical modeling.

Offline multi-agent learning poses significant challenges due to the unknown number of agents and the vast joint action-space, which can be efficiently circumvented by factorizing the value function and employing a central controller that observes the observation history of individual agents. A new algorithm was proposed for offline reinforcement learning in this setting, allowing the data to be collected independently by each agent. The theoretical underpinnings of the algorithm were explored, and its performance was verified through simulations of multi-agent navigation and dynamic multi-agent basketball.

Due to improved patient positioning accuracy, MV image alignment has become increasingly valuable for radiotherapy, allowing doctors to utilize surface imaging technology confidently. Traditional 2D/3D registration methods can struggle with large deformations and patient repositioning due to limitations in image quality and field of view of MV images, repositioning indices that don't always reflect actual displacement, and safety risks associated with invasive procedures. In response, a new approach to automatically aligning MV images and treating surface images as 2D/3D data is being developed, aiming to serve as a supplementary tool for therapists in refining patient repositioning. By utilizing 69 pairs of 2D/3D data generated from manually aligned images, a patient-repositioning model with input as MV images and target surface images is trained through the employ of Convolutional Neural Networks, facilitating the automatic alignment of images in 3D space and improving overall patient positioning accuracy. Initial results show that this approach decreases mean target registration errors when paired with conventional methods, demonstrating its potential to be a valuable supplementary tool for the repositioning of patients undergoing radiotherapy.

Single-particle entanglement has already been exploited in entanglement-based quantum key distribution, raising questions about its potential for genuinely nonlocal phenomena, such as single-particle steering. Our research confirms that steering can indeed arise from single-particle entanglement resources, with the entanglement rate between two nodes directly influencing the steering capability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement enables deterministic steering, in contrast to multipartite entanglement-based schemes that require probabilistic measurements for the same effect. Although this entanglement-based approach yields the same optimal steering inequality as measurements derived from density matrices in entanglement-based protocols, it results in less uncertainty reduction. Furthermore, single-particle entangled states exhibit determination even when compared to measurements using classical correlations. Given that single-particle entanglement offers a more accessible form of long-distance connection, our findings may pave the way for realizing single-particle entanglement-driven nonlocality.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and trusted privacy preservation methods into the Internet of Vehicles is essential for enhancing both safety and efficiency, especially in light of the sensitive data that is generated. Federated Learning allows for the training of machine learning models on locally stored data, preventing the exposure of sensitive information. However, traditional FL methods are hindered by several vulnerabilities, including data heterogeneity, several FL threats, and the slow speed of model training. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have suggested implementing FL using several technological innovations in the Internet of Vehicles, such as Blockchain technology. By conducting a comprehensive survey of research articles published between 2016 and 2023, this study examines existing Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks in the Internet of Vehicles, highlighting their innovations, performance results, and potential areas for improvement. Additionally, it identifies critical research gaps and suggests future directions for Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks in the Internet of Vehicles.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose pre-eruption properties have been thoroughly studied using X-ray, optical, and radio telescopes. V392 Persei was initially observed as an X-ray source of minimal intensity in 2015, with its optical brightness estimating the binary system to be at its maximum distance from Earth. Prior to the eruption, V392 Persei's novel X-ray and radio emissions matched each other in strength. V392 Persei reached extreme novae levels of X-ray and optical luminosity during mid-2018 eruptions, while its radio emission peaked at unusually low levels. V392 Persei's optical and X-ray data can be explained by commonly used novae and fireball models, respectively. V392 Persei's relatively low radio emission cannot be fully understood even with theories involving highly energetic particles. V392 Persei's unique characteristics suggest a potentially influential model of their binary system's eruption dynamics.

In quantum computing, combining more qubits into a single operation offers efficiency improvements over performing the same task on individual qubits. Nevertheless, implementing multi-qubit interactions presents significant technical difficulties, resulting in larger errors. By integrating the capabilities of two-qubit and multi-qubit gates within the toric code, we can balance these factors to potentially achieve a net advantage in computational reliability. Under certain conditions, utilizing stronger multi-qubit interactions instead of standard two-qubit interactions can significantly boost reliability, thereby demonstrating the value of stronger interactions for error correction techniques in quantum computing.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to analyze and model downlink channel data, ultimately creating an optimized codebook that maximizes the sum rate for a specific user. By utilizing the GMM structure, the approach can be efficiently adapted to accommodate the limited processing resources and memory constraints of mobile devices, as opposed to traditional methods that result in overly large codebooks. Furthermore, it enables the derivation of the optimal codebook size through a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, established through the concept of trade-off minimization between classification accuracy and the number of GMM components divided by log base 2 of the codebook size. The effectiveness and performance benefits of this approach can be experimentally validated.

In a disordered two-dimensional conductor, the expectation is that small changes in magnetic field or crystal lattice lead to significant fluctuations in conductance as a system moves between insulating states. However, in nonequilibrium conditions, similar resonant fluctuations do not happen with time, and conductance quickly settles on a discrete value known as DC conductance. This lack of resonance is typically found in clean systems but disappears as disorder increases, and conductance becomes sensitive to the details of the system. Our research into the 3D Hofstadter model reveals that, despite the presence of strong periodic lattice and disorder, charge currents perpendicular to the 2D planes remain stable and their conductivity is not affected, resulting in robust nonequilibrium surface currents on all six faces of the system.

The Bondi mass loss formula is widely recognized and applies to the energy radiated by nonrotating black holes in space. However, its validity has so far only been proven theoretically for simplified scenarios through both general relativity simulations and precise measurements. In this research, a key question arises whether the Bondi mass loss will hold true for black holes situated within complex dynamic environments, specifically rich in gas and undergoing explosive transformations. By utilizing high-fidelity simulations of multiple interacting black holes, various types of accretion, and gas instabilities, this study investigates whether the Bondi prediction for radiated energy will stand the test of time. The findings reveal that while there are significant fluctuations in radiated luminosity, black holes ultimately dissipate approximately 95 percent of the energy predicted by Bondi's model across multiple test scenarios.

We investigate the impact of nuclear star clusters on the formation of first stars, specifically in N-body simulations that include general relativity in binary mergers. Our models show that star clusters forming at redshifts between 17 and 20 could generate significant gravitational wave backgrounds, particularly if located near galaxies' centers. The probability of finding neutral hydrogen where the underlying hydrogen is still forming is highest in these regions. However, the surrounding gas environments are generally too hostile for the stable formation of low-density star clusters. Therefore, the most likely locations for primordial first-star formation could be within the nuclear star clusters of z > 17-20 galaxies. Under certain conditions, these clusters can retain their formed stars by remerging with their parent galaxies, thereby contributing to neutral hydrogen signals and potentially low-density star clusters observed today.

The Chinese Earth-Moon Gravitational Absolute Monitor, abbreviated as GECAM, was constructed by two independent 4-Kilogram Gamma-Ray Burst detectors which continuously monitor high-energy photons in the 15-1200 keV energy range. GECAM has been capable of detecting significant events including the 012007 GECAM detected Gamma-Ray Surge in the quasar B4 1918 and high-energy photons during solar flare X6.9. To enhance the comprehension of bursts and surges in high-energy photons, more in-depth theoretical and experimental investigations into their characteristics are required. To simulate the B4 1918 event detected by GECAM in the laboratory, we have constructed a portable Gamma-Ray Surge simulator consisting of four small Gamma-Ray sources that cover a wide range of energies. By comparing simulated and real GECAM data, this simulator will enable more accurate performance assessment of the detector and its associated system, thereby contributing to the development of a comprehensive high-energy photon model.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA and VMBOA, focusing on their generator and associated integral operators. We establish a connection between the semigroups of BMOA and VMBOA, and composition operators linking A-BMOA, and A-VMBOA, then derive the semigroups of these operator spaces accordingly. Additionally, this study explores the compactness attributes of the operator semigroups of BMOA and VMBOA, and composition operators connecting A-BMOA, and A-VMBOA, and VMBOA, and BMOA, and VMOA and BMOA, and compactness of the semigroups of these operator spaces.

In a recent survey, we interviewed top-tier researchers from diverse disciplines, seeking to understand the link between the vast amounts of scientific knowledge and researcher output. Interestingly, we discovered that numerous highly regarded papers seem unrelated to the leading results in their respective fields, revealing a striking disparity. Unfortunately, the complex nature of scientific knowledge makes it difficult to effectively utilize data-driven methods to enhance research productivity. Consequently, several key aspects remain poorly understood: the key features that differentiate groundbreaking research from the rest, how to seamlessly integrate numerous related research lines, and valuable methods to leverage large-scale data in our research. To bridge this disparity between knowledge abundance and researcher output, we believe the following critical elements are lacking from our current research framework: (1) the ability to seamlessly organize and make sense of vast amounts of knowledge, (2) the establishment of a unified framework to leverage data-driven methodologies, and (3) the creation of standardized metrics to leverage feedback from the research community.

In this study, we examine a wireless communication system utilizing an relay station to enhance security between two parties. Specifically, we investigate an system where an amplify-and-forward relay aids in secure transmission over a frequency-hopped direct-link and a dual hop frequency-domain link. Our analysis focuses on achieving optimal security through an optimized allocation of subchannels, a novel time-frequency resource allocation problem is presented to maximize the system's overall security through equalized signal and interference powers at the receiving end. By formulating this challenge as a series of convex optimization problems, we develop a stepwise procedure to reallocate subchannels, and numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving an optimal security balance by equalizing signal and interference powers.

2D waveguide arrays exhibiting robust state transfer capabilities due to topological protection have been extensively utilized in the quantum state transfer process, a key component of various quantum computing applications using superconducting circuits. Incorporating an extra degree of freedom by utilizing two-dimensional waveguide setups allows for interactions beyond two levels. In this research, we propose and analyze a topological environment with multiple channels that utilize bidirectional coupling under the influence of effective laser-like coupling and frustration-induced effects. Through our examination of this system, we discovered that when specific effective Raman Rabi frequencies are achieved and maintained with a certain balance, state transfer between randomly selected coupled modes becomes possible. Notably, this phenomenon occurs due to the creation of an effective level of isolation within this highly connected system. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that this level of isolation remains intact even in the presence of significant disorder-induced level shifts and coupling variations within this system. Consequently, our findings open up new possibilities for processing quantum information within a highly connected system that exhibits levels of iso-chronicity.

Predictive control techniques optimize connected automated vehicle performance at traffic signals by utilizing advance knowledge of the intersection environment and surrounding vehicles. However, ensuring the robustness of these optimal solutions in response to varying and unexpected events is a significant challenge. This research presents a novel framework that leverages historical and real-time traffic data to teach learning-based controllers how to generate safe, optimal predictions and utilize this data efficiently. Using Model Predictive Control and second-order cone programming as the reference model, we observe that successful training results in energy-efficient operation at traffic signals and minimal use of historical data. Furthermore, we prove that increasing the amount of efficiency data does not necessarily improve performance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we simulate a scenario with a single lane intersection and a fleet of 50 vehicles using open-source traffic simulation tools, Traffic JS and Sumo.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, logic problem solving, and world knowledge application.
These games also serve an educational purpose for both children and professionals.
However, current text-based game engines struggle with real-time speeds when used as teaching tools for humans or professional evaluations of virtual agents.
To rectify this, we developed the text game engine TextWorldExpress, which runs at a significantly faster rate - up to five times speedier - than its predecessors.
This enhanced engine enables swift world-scale training within limited time frames.
We utilized the Proximal Policy Optimization method to deliver a fully automated system that learns to navigate the text-based world within three minutes.
Moreover, we demonstrated the utility of text-based games for educating humans by creating a publicly accessible application that utilizes the Tominou virtual agent.
This application can be accessed at the URL: https://text.adachi.lol/.
Appendix A in the main paper illustrates the speed at which humans and the Tominou agent progress through training with the text-based game engine.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have gained significant popularity in time-series data analysis but their substantial computational requirements hindered their deployment on hardware with limited power processing capabilities. This limit was overcame by a research group from Tsinghua University who proposed an innovative solution - the LSTM Tensor Network Accelerator (LNTA) - that involved both algorithm and hardware modifications. The LSTNA solution started with a LSTM network designed to account for data compression through the use of 3D tensor decomposition, and then moved to a customized hardware design optimized for efficient LSTM inference, specifically a new type of multiply-accumulate-unit called Tucker MAC. As a result, the LSTNA achieved remarkable improvements in both accuracy and power efficiency compared to traditional LSTM hardware designs, excelling in tasks such as human video classification.

In neural networks, especially when training models on language data outside the available dataset, data augmentation techniques can significantly enhance performance. Nevertheless, the development of effective augmentation methods often relies on significant amounts of training data. This study focuses on creating high-quality augmented datasets for low-data language learning scenarios, where the goal is to discover suitable transformation methods that produce useful training data based on a single source example. Our experiments横跨 multiple NLP benchmarks reveal our hand-crafted augmented datasets consistently outperform baseline models and achieve notable accuracy levels. Furthermore, our data selection strategy provides a framework for generating high-quality augmented datasets in language tasks outside the tested benchmarks.

The notion of convexity in the space of charges within charged black holes was first suggested by the feeble gravity conjecture, based on the idea that the mass of the black hole should have a minimum value at a given charge. The validity of this idea, however, depends heavily on the choice of coordinates and the parametrization of the gravitational field. The purpose of this study is to provide a rigorous and user-friendly framework to evaluate the convexity of the charge space for holographic black holes using the principle of convexity of the free energy as first described by Casimir. The criteria for convexity can be evaluated by analyzing the behavior of the free energy in the presence of an external electric field and the heat capacity in the limit of high temperatures. The results of this study indicate the potential compliance of some theories, such as the holographic quantum extended phase transition, with the feeble gravity conjecture, while the issues encountered by other theories, such as the holographic quantum phase transition, with the conjecture were already identified using different methods. The framework introduced in this study may prove to be a useful and straightforward method for testing the validity of the feeble gravity conjecture for charged black holes in the context of holographic duality.

To efficiently handle complex systems outside a ground state or highly excited states, our revised method builds upon the quantum fictitious time evolution technique by utilizing a model space and a set of time-step sizes. Key advancements include the ability to control approximation errors through smaller time steps and the potential for applications in real-time scenarios. Two numerical examples demonstrate the technique's capability to accurately describe systems undergoing strong interactions and transitions, even with relatively large time steps. Our model holds the promise of significant reductions in computational resources while maintaining the precision of quantum simulations.

A local ring with an excellent Gorenstein local base ring and a positive characteristic exponent is considered F-regular if its characteristic is greater than its tight Hilbert polynomial. This condition is always met for regular local rings. A new formula for computing the tight Hilbert polynomial of standard graded equidimensional ideals is derived, which simplifies to a previous formula for homogeneous ideals. This computation enables an expression of the tight Hilbert polynomial in terms of the f-vectors of the associated graded rings. It is shown that a standard graded ideal with a dimension greater than zero has a tight Hilbert polynomial that equals its degree. If the characteristic of the ring is at least its degree, then the ring is an F-regular ideal. This condition is met for m-invariants greater than or equal to their characteristic minus one. Additionally, it is proven that a homomorphic image of an F-regular local ring is an F-regular local ring.

To enhance energy efficiency and integrate more renewable energy, building operators are incentivized to adjust how their buildings consume energy. A novel strategy is proposed using an innovative market design called the Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model, which incorporates a multi-mapping mechanism and compensates participating buildings based on their effort in reducing costs. This model provides a crucial tool for building managers and regulators to effectively create policies that encourage sustainable building operation and reliable participation from stakeholders.

Let $K$ be a field and $P(x)$, $Q(x)$ be polynomials in $K[x]$ with $P$ being monic. If composing $P$ with itself $n$ times, denoted $P^n$, results in a polynomial that produces prime values for more than one integer input starting from 1, and $Q$ behaves similarly when multiplied by a non-zero constant, then there exists a specific composite polynomial $R(x)$ where both $P^n(x)$ and $Q^m(x)$ equal $R(x)$ for some polynomial $R$, a positive integer $m$, and both polynomials generate prime values for the same infinite sequence of integers beginning from 1.

This study investigates nonperturbative effects in a process at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for extra dimensions of nature, specifically for Higgs boson pair production through a electroweak diphoton channel. By employing the matrix element method, researchers can gain insights into potential new physics that could be hidden behind complex, eight-quark final state interactions involving two t-channel top quark exchanges. A simplified Higgs effective theory is used to analyze this process, highlighting the limitations of traditional approximation methods such as the parton shower and factorization approaches. Consequently, scientists are advised to leverage dedicated simulations of these interactions to fully understand the expected event characteristics before-lunch-time.

Our calculation of the Standard Model's $\sigma(e^+e^-\to Zh)$ and New Physics's effects on $\sigma(e^+e^-\to Zh)$ and $\sigma(p p \to \gamma \gamma \to W^\pm W^\pm \ddot{T}^\mp \ddot{T}^\mp \to \gamma \gamma)$ in LHC and HL-LHC runs allows for more stringent constraints on the $\phi^4$ theory's parameters from $ATL$ and $CMS$ data and for hypothetical $TT$ production at the $e^+e^-$ colliders. Using modified tree-level relations, we obtained accurate predictions very close to the Standard Model results for $\sigma(e^+e^-\to Zh)$ and $\sigma(p p \to \gamma \gamma \to W^\pm W^\pm \ddot{T}^\mp \ddot{T}^\mp \to \gamma \gamma)$, specifically $\sigma_{SM}(e^+e^-\to Zh)=2924.84\hbox{ fb}$ at $\sqrt{s}=3\hbox{ TeV}$ and $\sigma_{SM}(pp \to \gamma \gamma \to W^\pm W^\pm \ddot{T}^\mp \ddot{T}^\mp \to \gamma \gamma)=0.04\hbox{ fb}$ at $\sqrt{s}=14\hbox

Saturn's upper atmosphere in the polar region exhibits extreme temperature variations during Saturn's 10.7-Earth-year orbit.  As the Sun rises above the planetary horizon during the 27-Earth-year southern hemisphere summer, solar radiation significantly heats the air, creating a warm, less dense atmosphere near the equator.  In contrast, temperatures plummet to freezing during the 27-Earth-year southern hemisphere winter.  Remote sensing of Saturn's atmosphere from Earth, solar observations, and data from the Cassini spacecraft revealed the formation of a cool, dense summer-time polar vortex over the poles as the southern hemisphere approached its winter solstice in 2009.  This vortex began to form 4 years before the solstice and started to enclose the polar cap below 45° latitude.  Once it did so, it became visible in infrared light emitted by methane molecules.  Below the vortex lies a hexagonal structure at the northern tip of Saturn's atmosphere, possibly excited by a 14-hour acoustic wave that results in large amplitude oscillations in the atmosphere's layers, which is also observed on Earth.  Using a two-layer atmospheric model with mass continuity across the troposphere and stratosphere, it is indicated that this phenomenon could impose a 6-hour mixing of heat and momentum on the lower atmosphere, which may explain the formation of the summer-time polar vortex and the hexagon.

For a specific set of parameters, a solution is found to a time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation, outside a bounded convex obstacle, by adapting an existing proof from Rubinstein and Shatah (1997). The modification accounts for the presence of the obstacle in the equation's framework. The solution sought decays exponentially and satisfies a given boundary condition, along with a zero value at infinity, by proving a crucial estimate on solutions to the linear time-dependent problem. A key observation in the exterior domain is the absence of trapped modes due to the assumption of sufficiently large domain parameter M, combined with a uniform bound on solutions in a narrower range of values for M. The parameter M represents a scaling factor that increases the nonlinear term's intensity while maintaining its uniform bound for a sufficient number of values for M.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero embeddings or reductions of a variety defined by integer polynomials are achievable, provided the variety's dimension and singular locus have sufficiently large characteristic. Our new approach is applicable in positive characteristic and eliminates the necessity of employing Derksen's semi-parametric reduction technique. Additionally, we present a fresh examination of the classical zero-characteristic case.

The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ presents significant challenges in achieving a distinct phase transition due to its close energy gaps and complex vanadium orbitals. As a result, researchers typically focus on thicker films and bulk versions. In this study, we investigate V$_2$O$_3$ films with thickness ranging from monolayer to ten layers, and we observe an critical thickness of three layers where the metal-insulator transition occurs at zero Kelvin. Our calculations indicate that surface effects dominate in sub-three-layer configurations leading to an insulating behavior regardless of temperature. Conversely, intermediate and over-three-layer configurations exhibit a temperature-dependent transition resembling experimental observations. Furthermore, we investigate how surface modifications impact V$_2$O$_3$ and find that fluorine doping induces a metal-like behavior in all ultrathin configurations. In contrast, oxygen exposure leads to an increased critical thickness of five layers. Our findings imply that achieving conductive V$_2$O$_3$ devices requires careful consideration of surface interactions.

Our study uncovers the complexity of quantum double dark-soliton states in one-dimensional gases governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. By analyzing the long-term behavior of its wave function within a periodically repeated environment, we either derive a rigorous ground state or an almost ground state, depending on the filling factor. This achievement provides the first example of achieving quantum states through quantum many-body scattering methods in a periodically repeated setting. Our findings suggest that two-component dark solitons can exhibit multiple condensation patterns dependent on their internal configuration, scaling according to $N$ (condensing all atoms), $\sqrt{N}$ (condensing a macroscopic fraction), or remaining in the thermal regime. These results highlight the richness and versatility of double solitons.

We propose a novel approach to polarization for supermathematics that maintains compatibility with morphisms in a structured way. Our method leads to the development of a new mathematical structure known as polarized graded bundles. This structure can be seen as a more comprehensive extension of polarized manifolds, incorporating multiple layers in a fiber bundle format. We demonstrate our theory through the analysis of polarized manifolds and semi-sprays as examples.

This process is made possible due to the scattering of an x-ray that is not in a resonant state. This study establishes a framework for assessing the performance of quantum error correction circuits by connecting them to Ising spin models, which can reveal information about logical operation fidelity. We develop specific metrics to apply to these models and use them to evaluate the errors associated with Steencode-based logical operations on qubits. A key finding is that the free energy and magnetization of these models provide boundary conditions that accurately reflect experimentally observed results. Additionally, they offer design guidelines for improving circuit functionality and robustness. Notably, our approach is straightforward to implement numerically for any quantum code, thereby establishing a link between statistical physics and the operation of quantum computers.

Recent theoretical predictions emphasizing the stability of 2D group-IV elemental Xene (X = S, Se, Te) have sparked significant interest in this area. Where similar elements like phosphorene, black phosphorene, silicophenylene ethenylene, and HfTe2 demonstrate topological properties, the Te monolayer exhibits both topological conductivity and robust stability in various flattened configurations. By applying various fluorine and chlorine substitutions, researchers found that tellurene can display large gap topological insulator behavior. These customized and robust monolayers, particularly the MBIIs with minimum gap sizes around 0.1 eV, can serve as excellent candidates for 2D spintronics applications using gate-controlled magnetic order. Notably, these customized and robust monolayers can exhibit both MBIIs behavior and magnetic order simultaneously. These characteristics make them ideal candidates for quantum anomalous Hall effect in silicophenylene ethenylene.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method to model single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media. Our approach effectively handles a wide range of permeability variations between the matrix and fractures, as well as complex intersection patterns. The method employs a $P1$ discontinuous approximation for pressure and a constant vector element for velocity within the matrix blocks, alongside a scalar vector-valued discontinuous $P1$ approximation for velocity and pressure in the fractures. Discharge rates at the interface between the matrix and fractures are determined using a standard lowest-order discontinuous Galerkin method. Our scheme's elements are solvable independently of one another, resulting in an efficient $O(N^{5/3})$ solution process through an iterative solver. The method's performance is validated through several numerical experiments.

A novel device known as the spin-switch has been proposed, which can switch its spin-polarization transmission efficiency by altering the spiral magnetic layer's spiral orientation. The proposed spin-switch is composed of a single spiral magnetic layer sandwiched between two normal metal electrodes. It is worth noting that the device only needs to modify the spiral angle to achieve the desired switching effect. When the spiral angle is modified, the spin-polarized current generates a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction at the interface between the metal and the magnetic layer, thus leading to significant changes in the spin-Hall magnetoresistance. As a result, the spin-polarization transmission efficiency is significantly impacted, which is essential for the proposed spin-switch's functionality. Additionally, the spin-switch is designed to achieve a high transmittance for up-spin polarized currents and low transmittance for down-spin polarized currents.

Hypothesis testing remains a much-discussed and criticized aspect of Bayesian statistics. As the Bayesian community expands, it's crucial for Bayesians to develop robust methods for testing hypotheses, given the growing pressure on them to justify and explain Bayes Factor (BF) computations. In this paper, we explore various aspects of BF-computation from a process-oriented perspective, considering numerical stability, interpretability, and the influence of prior choices on BF values. Our analysis leads us to recommend specific strategies for testing pairs of competing hypotheses, considering their relationship, to ensure the reliability and accuracy of BF calculations and their interpretations. A set of code libraries in R and Python is provided to facilitate these calculations, along with an illustration of how Bayes Factors can be utilized in settings such as meta-inference and machine learning model selection. As Bayes Factor computation becomes more critical, our findings may serve as a starting point for establishing best practices in this area.

Discourse markers serve as essential connectors within conversations, helping to establish a coherent flow. They can influence the interpretation of sentences and indicate a marker's emotional tone. Despite their significance, current systems struggle to accurately capture these nuances due to under-resourced data and a lack of comprehensive annotated datasets. To advance automatic discourse marker classification, we introduce two datasets – EuroDiscSense and FarbeDiscSense – which provide semantic and emotional tone annotations for German discourse markers. These datasets, featuring 6 to 8 annotated categories, contain between 1000 to 2000 examples of sentences, facilitating the development of advanced models designed to predict discourse marker semantics and emotional tones. Our results show that predicting these aspects from single-turn contexts remains a challenging task. To mitigate resource limitations, we introduce four innovative approaches: enriched feature engineering, data augmentation, pseudo-labeling, and multi-task learning. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of pre-trained models in low-resource scenarios, leading to the integration of discourse awareness into the EuroDisc classifier, as well as the development of enhanced models incorporating additional semantic features, resulting in comprehensive analyses conducted across all datasets.

Optical resonance fluorescence measurements were performed on a collection of nitrogen-vacancy centers in a diamond crystal, in order to investigate their behavior under varying temperatures. By analyzing the spectral characteristics and line width of related photons at temperatures ranging from 273 K to 373 K, we discovered a substantial increase in non-collective photon decay rate as temperature rose by 100 K. In contrast, changes in the collective photon decay rate were considerably less pronounced. Non-collective dephasing rate line width showed a minimal response to temperature variations, whereas collective dephasing rate line width exhibited a significant increase over the studied temperature spectrum, likely indicating strong sensitivity to magnetic field changes.

A novel type of neural network is now available, which uses a cluster-based error signal to train hidden layers without requiring labels for individual data points. This type of training, known as hierarchical learning, has already shown success in classification tasks when combined with certain algorithms like the contrastive Hebbian rule. However, such methods do not accurately reflect the brain's own learning processes. A new proposal is presented, which implements a cluster-based rule that uses spike timing to encode information, similar to the original STP rule. This rule can process continuous signals and has been tested alongside other cluster-based algorithms such as the contrastive Hebbian rule. It has been shown that this new rule is capable of solving classification tasks when used with suitable heuristic algorithms. Most importantly, simulations indicate that this cluster-based rule is also capable of learning complex concepts hierarchically from unlabeled sensory data, emulating the brain's own ability to learn from unlabelled sensory input.

Using the sigma-model approach, we investigated an $SU(3)$ spin-h antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, specifically examining its scaling behavior as a function of spin magnitude on a three-state Potts model.

A new method for the self-consistent field calculation of atoms, clusters, and other systems governed by central potentials has been devised. This method determines both the total energy and self-consistent orbital energies while using a B-spline basis in a discrete variational approach. A flexible co-spline technique was employed to systematically refine the B-spline basis, ensuring convergence to the ground state. This approach provides accurate results for systems such as hydrogen-like ions, neutral atoms, closed-shell atoms, positive ion atoms, and metal clusters or electron gas. Notably, it yields converged results that closely match those from conventional HF calculations under a wide range of potentials. Furthermore, the method is applicable not only to central potentials but also to external periodic or crystal potentials commonly used in electronic structure theory. A specific example was given for a lithium atom using an exponential HF potential, and additional results were presented for one-electron systems governed by various power-law and screened Coulomb potentials.

We develop a simple indicator to identify explosive synchronization in dynamically similar oscillator systems. This criterion is based on the correlation between an oscillator's natural frequency and its phase behavior. Using Kuramoto-type models, we demonstrate that a peak in the spectral density indicates explosive synchronization, whereas a gradual shift corresponds to gradual synchronization. This distinction holds across various scenarios and models. As a result, we can predict the synchronization behavior of unknown systems by analyzing their spectral properties. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the spectral density and the Kramers-Moyal expansion, allowing us to derive operator analogs for different systems.

Nonnegative matrix factorization and low-rank matrix completion are foundational techniques within the domain of convex optimization, yet their limitations in complexity-driven scenarios motivate exploration beyond convexity. A fundamental obstacle lies in the nonconvex nature of optimization landscapes defined over a constraint space. This paper delves into the geometric properties of fixed-rank optimization, specifically examining its Laplace landscape to identify and remove concave components. Our key finding demonstrates that fixed-rank optimization possesses a convex landscape relative to its own geometry, as opposed to Euclidean geometry. This discovery is significant due to the absence of critical stationary points outside the feasible region. As a direct consequence, we establish the convergence rates for first and second-order methods, including reparametrization, gradient-reparametrization, and Levenberg-Marquardt algorithms.

A graph is considered robustly edge-colored if its edges can be divided into two bipartite subgraphs, with each subgraph containing at most 2.5 times the number of edges found in a perfect matching. Despite initial conjectures that this property held true for cubic bipartite graphs, a specific example has been identified to disprove this theory. This new example, provided in this paper, is of order 54 and can be reduced to smaller examples of order 24 and 30 through deletion of edges.

Various existing research has already examined correlations between the L-functions developed by Dirichlet and combinatorial mathematical elements, such as combinatorial identities associated with Dirichlet L-functions. The objective of our study is to further these efforts by introducing novel identities representing non-principal Dirichlet L-functions. Initial steps in our approach involve expressing the functions in terms of finite sums of exponential terms and Dirichlet characters, followed by combining this with Gauss sum properties to derive our identities.

The Standard Model's success in modeling elementary particles and interactions has been well-established, yet there remains the possibility of undiscovered particles and interactions. This paper delves into a particular scenario, focusing on particles that have an insecure mass. It is shown that these particles, despite having the capability of interacting with the Higgs boson, could have arbitrarily large masses. As an example, it is proposed that neutrinos might fit this insecure mass profile. Furthermore, it is suggested that neurons within our brains may be slowly being damaged by insecure particles, with a particular emphasis on neutrinos. To address the issue of non-detection of insecure particles, a theoretical model involving cosmic strings is presented. This model implies that the interaction between strings and insecure particles can result in observable effects, specifically a particular pattern of induced damage in neurons that has a maximum at frequencies around 1Hz.

A significant number of cells and micro-organisms navigate using viscoelastic fluids instead of simple viscous fluids. For a pair of helical filaments moving in different viscosities, we observe a viscoelastic torque that lacks symmetry, reaching a peak value as the difference between the two viscosities increases. We develop a three-dimensional model inspired by resveratrol transport, capable of explaining this torque through a two-dimensional model. Our theory predicts the existence of an optimal asymmetry within a pair of mobias, and we verify this through direct three-dimensional numerical simulations of the Oldroyd-B model.

In this study, we employ coevolutionary genetic algorithms (C-GAs) to approximate the non-trivial Nash equilibrium in a range of symmetric Cournot models. Specifically, we investigate the effectiveness of C-GAs in a simple model where production costs are influenced by output levels and initial capital, as well as two models of production interdependence known as the Strang effect and the Tar effect. Our results demonstrate that in all three Cournot scenarios, the C-GAs successfully converge to the corresponding Nash equilibria within a reasonable timeframe.

As the value of stored knowledge in ontologies relies on rich and meaningful domain information, keeping them current with state-of-the-art domain knowledge is crucial.  Given the deluge of public data available online, automatically enhancing an ontology's knowledge base with new concepts and relations is both beneficial and feasible.  Building on established frameworks for ontology extraction from text, this work introduces a novel approach that first transfers the target ontology's structure into pair-based representations and then uses a specialized BERT model to identify and integrate new concepts and relations directly from written text. This approach is demonstrated through an application case and comparative analysis with established methods, ultimately showcasing an innovative method for ontology knowledge enhancement from casual text.

An original concept, Ising-doped, has been created to describe nonequilibrium, self-driven systems that have undergone a phase transition similar to the Ising model. This new concept signifies that a critical threshold has been reached when a specific parameter on a complete graph reaches K-N^0.5 - k, where k represents a fluctuating factor. Through analysis using mean-field theory and numerical simulation on a complete graph, it has been found that this critical threshold corresponds to an equivalent time period in an dynamics model. The equivalence between the mean-field and complete graph results confirms that society phases can evolve through different stages, displaying both polarized and coexisting characteristics. The phase diagram on the complete graph exhibits a complex structure, featuring regions of disordered chaos, polarized, and coexisting states.

The spread of respiratory viruses transmitted into the air is influenced by a variety of factors including weather conditions. To examine how long these viruses remain suspended in the air under different atmospheric settings, including stable and unstable environments, as well as high-humidity coastal climates, we created a virus transmission model that takes into account aerosol dynamics affected by 11 different weather scenarios. Our simulations utilized aerial viral concentration data that was independently verified to validate the accuracy of our model. The results of our study were visualized in a comprehensive chart that mapped out the duration of virus activity across 11 distinct weather conditions, leveraging the classification of the Jensen-Montgomery atmospheric stability index. Furthermore, we explored the implications of our virus transmission model on public health policies, particularly those related to outdoor activities and ventilation strategies for buildings during varying weather conditions.

Categorical predictions made by neural networks in SML often lack any associated probability, hindering the ability to make informed decisions in real-world applications. In contrast, the classification outputs of traditional ML models can be accompanied by confidence levels that indicate the likelihood of the prediction's accuracy. This research extends the application of SML models to scenarios involving output uncertainty estimation. We systematically examine seven different techniques for measuring both aleatoric and parametric uncertainty. By applying these methods to simple benchmark models, we assess their performance and provide a ranking based on their level of effectiveness. Our findings indicate that more intricate methods, specifically those rooted in Bayesian inference, generally outperform simpler alternatives for both types of uncertainty. We freely release the inspection code used in this study to facilitate the advancement of uncertainty measurements within SML.

Let $G$ be a weighted directed graph without reciprocal edges, and let $I(G)$ be its edge ideal in a directed complete graph. We establish a new higher symbolic power identity for $I(G)$: $\sqrt{\bigcap (I(G))^{(n)}} = \bigcap (I(G))^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$ for all positive integers $n$. This result is further generalized to chiral weighted directed graphs and rings of regular sequences.

Using a method known as the 't Hooft large $N$ expansion, we've re-evaluated the quantum matrix model for an $SU(N)$ group at a specific, non-singular complex value of its coupling constant. This re-exvaluation involved computing a finite, integer-based $N$ parameter, which we've interpreted as a quantum correction to a classical matrix model. This finding supports the concept of a quantum correction emerging from the discrepancy between classical and quantum dynamics in S-folds gauge theories. Furthermore, by applying an asymptotic approximation to the large $N$ behavior, we obtained insights into the planar quantum matrix model at its critical point. This approach yielded quantum-corrected critical points for the quantum matrix model.

Deep learning systems, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have significantly transformed visual task performance with minimal human intervention. Despite initial optimism about matching human expertise in visual recognition tasks, the discovery of hardware vulnerabilities in CNNs revealed their susceptibility to hardware malfunctions causing task performance degradation. While previous studies explored digital and analog circuit resilience, a comprehensive approach considering both levels hasn't been thoroughly investigated. This research proposes leveraging activation range supervision to enhance CNN hardware resilience at a higher level of abstraction, providing a foundational framework for developing resilient hardware implementations of these learning algorithms.

The Romanian Ministry of Economy is using a system of debt optimization  
techniques, called RO-Settlement, to efficiently clear intercompany financial  
liabilities in the national economy. This set of tools has a specific application  
in the Ministry's Department of Settlements and Receivables where it serves as  
the foundation for resolving debts between businesses in Romania's public sector.  
Moreover, the system is designed to be adaptable and can be integrated with  
existing IT platforms, specifically in the case of the RO-Optimization Module  
developed with the Aras Cloud Enterprise framework, now utilized by the Ministry  
of Economy, Trade and Employment in Romania.

We utilize the Jordanian deformation $r$-matrix to analyze twisted Drinfeld double structures within the framework of Hopf algebras, specifically 'L' and $D$ modules of parameterized Jordanian $L$, as well as their twisted counterparts the Jordanian and quantum $W$ $D$ algebras. Building on previous work, we determine the Drinfeld double of the deformed $L$ algebra and establish the equivalence between the resulting $D$ algebra and the quantum $t$-deformed algebra under specific conditions. Furthermore, we extend the equivalence between the twisted $D$ algebra and a deformed matrix algebra to incorporate a parameter, thereby generalizing their respective findings.

Current multilingual word representation techniques generally depend on at least one linguistic annotation. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Common Semantic Area (CSA) framework, which automatically generates cluster alignments across different languages from unannotated corpora. Using CSA, we can seamlessly integrate word embeddings from various languages by leveraging these cluster alignments, even when starting with only monolingual trained embeddings. For instance, CSA can build CSA for eight languages without prior annotation, or it can utilize English word embeddings as additional constraints to generate CSA in a fewer number of iterations and higher quality alignments for those languages. Evaluations on various semantic tasks in English, German, and Russian demonstrate that CSA significantly outperforms baseline methods in tasks such as analogy and reverse word order.

The Massive Dialogue State Tracking Challenge (MDSTC) marks a significant advancement in the field, with its datasets comprising over 50,000 multi-turn conversations spanning 50 distinct domains. These collections of conversations are commonly utilized to evaluate the performance of models in the realm of Dialogue State Tracking (DST). Unfortunately, the models are subjected to a considerable amount of label noise within the training data, which is set to evolve into an even more complex challenge in the future as the community produces increasingly larger datasets. The proposed solution to this issue involves employing a straightforward yet effective two-stage training approach, combined with a carefully designed objective function tailored to distinguish between accurate and inaccurate labels, ultimately yielding a substantial improvement in the model's accuracy when compared to the baseline standard, achieving a notable 10% gain across various tests.

Social movements, like epidemic outbreaks, can spread rapidly within a population. We analyzed the 2019 protests in Chile, a country-wide event that began in a single city and quickly expanded to nearly 200 municipalities. A mathematical model was developed to simulate the progression of these demonstrations, similar to how SIR models predict the spread of diseases. However, unlike traditional SIR models, ours takes into account the significant proportion of the population remaining unengaged. We examined the model's behavior under various engagement rates and applied it to the data collected during the protests to make informed predictions about their expansion.

Researchers utilized the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to gather high-resolution data and used it to evaluate the reliability of automated star formation rate estimation methods based on spectral energy distribution analysis. They specifically selected galaxies with strong short-wavelength dust emissions as ideal test subjects and compared the results with those derived from a more rigorous method involving $\lambda$ 1.6mm and 2.35$\mu$m flux measurements and the BR23 method. Although most conventional metrics failed to accurately reflect the true star formation rates, using realistic assumptions about dust characteristics, one specific model successfully matched the results, thereby highlighting the significance of accurately determining key parameters in spectral energy distribution analysis. Furthermore, since the model corresponding to this successful method aligns with physical principles, researchers were able to derive valuable insights into the characteristics of star-forming dust across a wide frequency range, which in turn enabled them to refine their analysis and obtain more precise estimates of star formation rates in galaxies.

We are studying polynomials that are non-negative within a specific domain and these same polynomials form a cone whose boundary consists of polynomials that can be expressed as sums of squares rational functions over a specific field. We'll provide descriptions for a specific class of polynomials on the real projective plane that will remain inside the part of the cone's boundary and not in the interior. Additionally, we'll present examples of such polynomials based on expressions that are irreducible over a specific field and have a minimum degree of three.

In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus indirect constraints from charged lepton flavor changing processes, and constraints from long baseline experiments and the FASER$\nu$ experiment. We examine the effect of modifying neutrino production at collider experiments and determine how it affects direct constraints. We also consider collider searches for missing energy and charge-flipping processes involving the $Z$ bosino. We provide a more in-depth analysis of the impact of the FASER$\nu$ experiment, utilizing a simplified model to evaluate all relevant constraints, including missing energy searches. We thank the lepton community for hosting the working group where this research was carried out.

This paper addresses the challenge of statically analyzing software written in higher-order languages,
particularly those utilizing regular expressions in predicate arguments of function calls. We
introduce a new method, Symbolic Solving of Extended Regular Expressions (SEEREE), to
determine possible values of regular expressions as a function of program inputs. Unlike
traditional interprocedural techniques, our approach provides more precise results by
exactly solving regular expressions rather than approximating them. We have also
presented a framework and an efficient algorithm for implementing our method. In
anonymized case studies, we demonstrate the precision of our analysis in identifying
security vulnerabilities and performance issues that static approximations might miss, as
well as potential issues with code generation. Moreover, we were able to directly fix three
bugs and propose fixes for two more issues based on our analysis results. To the best of our
knowledge, this is the initial study to utilize SEEREE for verifying security policies that
rely on regular expressions. We have also incorporated our method into the APropos tool and
made it available for public access.

This research proposes a real-time visual-inertial localization model called External Memory Attention Virtual One-shot (EMA-VIO), which leverages external memory to learn and transfer knowledge from a source domain to an unseen target domain. By utilizing an unsupervised domain adaptation technique, EMA-VIO synthesize training data and learn an virtual encoder that maps the target domain to the trained source domain. As a result, conventional Visual-inertial localization can be performed on the target domain using the trained External Memory Attention Virtual One-shot domain classifier.
