A music generation challenge called Pied Piper has been announced by Facebook, specifically targeting the area of speech and music. Participants in this challenge will focus on creating immersive, interactive virtual reality experiences that music and speech can enhance. Using a virtual reality platform, users will be able to interact with the content through music, while also utilizing Pied Piper's approved virtual reality hardware for efficient use of Facebook's Quest meta hardware. Successfully completing the project within the specified timeframe and meeting all requirements could lead to awards starting at $200,000.

This work delves into various structural elements of Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks, which serve as sophisticated tools for analyzing smoother variations within families of smooth objects. These objects can be found in applications ranging from theoretical physics to topology. The discussion focuses on underlying principles rather than specific instances, with particular attention given to the relationships between Morita equivalence, deformation quantization, foliations, and the study of characteristic classes.

A statistical analysis of 103 massive young stellar clusters in the infrared dark cloud "Dragon" reveals an unusual pattern of core expansion. As mass increases, these cluster cores tend to spread out rather than become more concentrated. This core growth phenomenon is attributed to the dynamic evolution of clusters and their ability to form high-mass stars. 

Dragon has the largest collection of massive star clusters compiled so far, making it an ideal location to study cluster dynamics and star formation processes. Research using remote sensing techniques suggests that cluster expansion and core growth are directly linked to stellar creation. 

Furthermore, regions within the cluster that are most likely to produce massive stars are typically found in outer rings as opposed to the center of the cluster. These stars often appear where the densest material is located, which are usually found in the outer parts of the cluster. 

On a larger scale, star formation in Dragon occurs in two distinct patterns: linear growth within a central elongated region and perpendicular expansion within a western region, both of which are superimposed on the underlying shape of the cluster. 

Therefore, further research indicates that massive star formation often takes place away from the center of a cluster and in directions perpendicular to the main direction of star formation, likely due to feedback mechanisms from already formed stars and expanding HII regions as well as wind and magnetic fields.

Godel modal logics can be extended from basic propositional logic to a type-n variant by incorporating Godel relations into a type-n+1 propositional logic framework. This paper delves into the algebraic and modal algebraic aspects of these n-level Godel systems, specifically those of type m where m ranges from 1 to n. We then explore the implications of adding a dual operator, introducing (n,m)-Godel algebras, and provide a corresponding algebraic framework for these extended logics. Finally, the paper will present the algebraic characteristics of these systems through a series of examples, including a two-level (2,1)-Godel algebra and its associated relational structures, in sections dedicated to algebraic and relational representations.

LiDAR, or Light Detection and Ranging, utilizes laser technology to generate 3D point clouds that accurately map objects and environments in three dimensions. This capability makes it the ideal sensing system for a range of applications, such as self-driving cars, robotics navigation, and spatial analysis. However, working with LiDAR data can be a complex task due to the vast amount of information contained within LiDAR data sets. To tackle this challenge, machine learning techniques, such as neural networks, are being widely used for interpreting and making use of LiDAR data, as the techniques allow for faster and more efficient processing. This report provides an in-depth examination of the different techniques used for classifying, detecting obstacles, and navigating using LiDAR data, as well as the corresponding performance outcomes. It also discusses critical aspects, such as data sets, pre-processing techniques, and feature extraction methods, which are crucial for successful LiDAR-based machine intelligence systems.

Recurrence properties of stochastic processes are typically studied in relation to fixed points or sets. To address this, we examine a stochastic model involving $b$ independent Brownian motions on a sphere, and derive the expected time for this system to transition between two other points. We provide explicit representations for this expected time and demonstrate its applicability to recurrence relationships of a stochastic system on the sphere. Additionally, this approach can be used to derive expected times for random walkers on a spherical surface.

The connection between neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and gamma rays makes these particle types ideal for studying cosmic phenomena. Neutrinos travel in straight lines and can be traced back to their sources with accuracy, but plenty of other experiments are necessary due to limited data. Our research employs image analysis to identify possible links between the directions of the neutrinos and those of the ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, using the data from the IceCube/DeepSky and old IceTop experiments. Over an energy threshold starting at 29 TeCh, our findings show the correlation index for neutrinos and cosmic rays is not less than 0.39 at a 90% confidence level. This value is more restrictive than the best previous limit of 0.50 obtained from combining their spectra. Additionally, our method is also utilized to set a constraint on the association between high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays of 0.39, matching the best prior limit using different methods of analysis.

We measure the friction within liquid foams using creep tests and find it is unaffected by the foam's internal pressure. This constant friction is attributed to a disordered network of bonds between the bubbles, similar to the behavior observed in other soft matter systems like colloidal liquids.

This report focuses on using deep learning to classify images in the ISIC-2017 dataset, which contains images categorized into three classes: melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancer, and normal skin. We utilized a deep learning framework, including the ResNet50 network, to extract features and then employed logistic regression to classify the extracted features. Although the initial experiments yielded high accuracy, precision, and recall scores, a closer analysis revealed issues when dealing with a balanced dataset, exposing the model's tendency to incorrectly label rare classes, particularly the melanoma class. Even after fine-tuning the decision threshold for the melanoma class, the model's performance did not significantly improve. To address this issue, we proposed modifying the entropy calculation method for the extracted features, specifically calculating the probability of features falling within certain ranges. By changing this calculation, the model's output distribution became more uniform, effectively mitigating its bias towards data samples.

As molten material extrudes from a rotating cylinder's gap, it extrudes as droplets due to a pressure drop that also causes the formation of fingers with varying fingering speeds and lengths in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. A theoretical model using a balance of viscous and centrifugal forces predicts flexible fingeral patterns by considering the wall velocity to be proportional to the ratio of the viscous and centrifugal forces. This model accurately mirrors the start and end points of periodic branches in a state diagram but fails to capture the inner branch structure.

The traditional approach of calculating entropy changes via the differential formula dS = dQrev/T faces a significant hurdle when encountering processes, like the free expansion of an ideal gas, that involve phase space volume transformations. Consequently, some scientists have suggested using entropy's equivalence to the logarithm of the accessible phase space volume as a means to circumvent this issue, even for irreversible processes. However, this equivalence necessitates defining a unique reference state and, more importantly, relies on the assumption that systems under and outside of equilibrium share the same density and momentum distribution functions, an assumption that lacks empirical validation. We present a contrasting methodology, centered on entropy's equivalence to the average logarithm of Hamiltonian path weights along the system's evolution from an initial to a final state. This methodology allows for distinguishing between reversible and irreversible entropy production and reduces to the conventional calculation based on thermodynamic variables in the case of a quasi-equilibrium process, as demonstrated with the example of an ideal gas free expansion.

Spectral data from the TMC-1 molecular cloud have revealed the presence of two distinct isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, a complex hydrocarbon cycle containing five membered rings. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers are present at concentrations of $3.8^{+4.4}_{-1.9}\times10^{-11}\times\frac{L_{\rm IR}}{2.1\times10^{11}\rm\,\,erg/s}$ for the CCH isomer and $8.4^{+9.0}_{-3.1}\times10^{-11}\times\frac{L_{\rm IR}}{2.1\times10^{11}\rm\,\,erg/s}$ for the CN isomer. These isomers are among the largest hydrocarbon cycles of their kind and their abundances relative to other species like $CN$ and $CCH$ in small hydrocarbon cycles are unusually high. The relative abundance of the two ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers is puzzling as the CCH isomer is more abundant than the CN isomer, despite the opposite being true for other similar cycles like ethynyl benzene and naphthalene. This discovery expands the known list of large hydrocarbon cycles in the TMC-1 molecular cloud and the relative disparity between the two ethynyl cyclopentadiene

In neural machine translation, current models struggle to accurately predict subsequent words. This problem is rooted in limited capacity to fully process input information and generate each target word. To address this, we introduce an approach that allows the model to anticipate more precise details about the target vocabulary during generation. This is achieved by incorporating an expected cross-entropy loss function guided by a graph which encodes word relationships, enabling the model to utilize structural information when decoding. As a result, the expected cross-entropy loss function encourages the model to predict subsequent words based on more intricate details, thereby improving translation quality. Our approach is particularly effective when combined with the nondeterministic chunking model, which determines the model's output in chunks of consecutive target words. Notably, it outperforms the standard start-to-end generation process. Our method can also be applied to other generation tasks, including sentence segmentation and summarization.

In 2001, a team led to create an adaptable and efficient scheduling system for the Dutch Grid (DutchLinx), with a specific focus on interconnecting national grids. Their solution involved a translation of the Andrew File System (AFS) and the creation of a virtual translation layer, known as the Grid Translation Layer (GTL). By providing a seamless translation service, the team was able to connect users to a grid that functioned as a single, cohesive storage area, despite the underlying differences in systems. This translation approach has been shown to have significant implications for the development of grid computing, as it enabled the creation of efficient storage solutions and influenced the design of future virtualization technologies. Furthermore, the team's experience with the Grid Translation Layer has provided a blueprint for the creation of grid computing systems that are both scalable and efficient, as it demonstrates the value of using a translation layer to connect disparate systems and create a cohesive grid. Ultimately, the work of the team has important lessons for the grid computing community, as it highlights the potential of translation approaches to shape the development of efficient and effective computing systems.

In a unified dark matter-dark energy framework, we examined multiple models featuring dark matter with dissipation and a primordial particle population. By applying a scale-factor derivative method, we derived solutions for these models and compared the results to those obtained through direct integration. A consistent approach was established for the models with dissipation, ensuring the first law of thermodynamics is fulfilled. We then, in particular, investigate the radiation-like solution for the bulk viscous model, showing that it can describe the early era of the universe in a manner aligned with the Big Bang nucleosynthesis data. Ultimately, we derived constraints on the parameters of the model based on current observations of the universe.

Understanding the complex nature of curiosity in small group learning is a significant challenge due to its inherent multimodality. Curiosity in such scenarios can be considered as comprising multiple, interrelated aspects, including individual and social components, as well as emotions and cognition. To tackle this challenge, a novel framework is proposed, which utilizes a range of multimodal data sources, including explicit and implicit indicators. This framework captures curiosity's cognitive and emotional dimensions through data collected from surveys, physiological measurements, and video analysis, while its social nature is captured through multimodal dialogue data. To explore the underlying mechanisms of curiosity in small group learning, a Bottom-Up data-driven approach is proposed, which includes a range of advanced data analytics techniques, including multivariate and multimodal association methods, as well as multilinear tensor decomposition. This framework is demonstrated through its application to real-world data obtained from three small group learning sessions, in which participants were exposed to various stimuli designed to induce curiosity. The results of the analysis reveal patterns of curiosity that align with their intended design, including patterns of individual and social co-regulation, as well as dynamic shifts between curiosity states.

Spatial statistical data are frequently analyzed using a combination of a Mat\'ern covariance function and an Gaussian model. This paper develops a discrete equivalent by creating an on-graph Mat\'ern covariance function that maintains the same characteristic length scale and a corresponding on-graph Mat\'ern model. Unlike traditional approaches which use precision specificity for construction, our method directly defines the covariance structure. A key feature of our approach is the use of the Laplace-Beltrami matrix with a commutator adjustment to ensure positive definiteness while preserving the desired long-range behavior. The development of this matrix leads to an efficient algorithm using the Cholesky decomposition, the sum of which grows at a rate of O(ND^3), where N is the number of nodes, and the average degree is denoted by D. This method's efficiency is further highlighted by numerical results from simulations on random geometric graphs and is available for use on the accompanying website.

Traffic monitoring systems in cities face challenges in accurately detecting all roads due to the continuous change in road layouts. We propose a novel approach to efficient road detection that leverages the fleet of ridesharing companies' vehicles for real-world applications. By formulating this problem to maximize detectable roads with minimum assumptions about vehicle distributions, we developed a continuous model and a corresponding optimization version. In the detect-to-reconstruct phase, we designed algorithms to identify the underlying road network, taking into account the limitations of real-world data where some streets may be under-detected. The effectiveness of our method is validated through successful reconstruction of New York City's road network using a data set of over 100,000 taxis from Newsha et al. (2017).

Neutrino and dark matter interactions are described by effective field theories that utilize a heavy scale as the reference point. This analysis focuses on the process of $J/\psi\to (\gamma + ){\rm invisible}$ to determine the parameters of these active-sterile five-neutrino theories and scalar-mediated dark matter analyses. Specifically, we calculate effective field theory amplitudes for $J/\psi\to \mathrm{invisible}$ and compare them to experimental data, which yield highly constrained values for new physics scale $\Lambda$. These values of $\Lambda$ are then used to derive lower bounds on the mass of sterile neutrinos, which in turn impacts the validity of the effective field theory description. Similarly, we derive lower bounds on the scale of four-body scalar interactions relevant to dark matter stability, which also has implications for the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the order consistency approach, and this study extends that work by directly controlling the local truncation error, following the approach set out in [16]. The development of variable stepsize SDIMSIMs of the form y_{n+1}=y_n+h_nf(x_{n+1},y_{n+1}) is achieved and implementation details, including the handling of missing grid points, are explored. The new methods are evaluated using standard test problems, and their results demonstrate improved efficiency when applied to standard initial value problems.

The singular spectrum analysis (SSA) has proven to be a useful nonparametric
method for processing complex, multi-dimensional time series of significant real-world
importance. In this study, we explore the behavior of multi-dimensional (nD) singular
spectrum analysis (nSSA) as both the data dimensions (d) and sample size (r) increase.
Our examination utilizes empirical evidence from synthetic data to illustrate how
nSSA performs in this scenario, revealing a notable level of eigenvalue instability
when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. Furthermore, we suggest a revised
version of nSSA designed to mitigate this instability, and its effectiveness is
validated through additional synthetic data analysis.

Deep learning-based event detection systems, commonly employed in security applications, suffer from high false positive and false negative rates due to their vulnerability to subtle, unseen differences between legitimate and malicious events. Researchers have developed event classification models using large datasets of deliberately altered event data, yet these models struggle to accurately distinguish genuine events from malicious ones. The primary issue lies in the fact that such data does not reflect the genuine event distribution, hindering the model's performance. To address this problem, we investigate the underlying cause of this problem and reveal that security-critical event detectors are particularly sensitive to both event entropy and boundary conditions. As a result, model decisions are extremely overconfident in response to event data that has been preprocessed to remove unnecessary metadata but still contains hidden entropy and boundary conditions embedded within the event data. The overconfident decision-making leads to high rates of false positives and false negatives. Our experiments validate this hypothesis and demonstrate that it accounts for the high error rates observed in recent security studies. The overall movement of a random walk in one dimension, particularly in a confined space, shows interesting patterns when examining its spent time in a particular state. For a walk inside a confined area formed by two moving boundaries, this time, denoted as $L_t$, can be modeled by a Skew Brownian motion. We have a sequence of random walks in one dimension and their corresponding $L_t$ variables. We prove that as these walks approach a continuous process, the $L_t$ variables consistently avoid developing discontinuities jump-by-jump. Our result fills a gap in existing research, which only established the occurrence of such avoidances on a set of full probability, rather than everywhere.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Cadarache site in France requires a powerful and plasma control capable source, which has been characterized as a helicon source with input power of 100kW.  To facilitate plasma control, this helicon source was redesigned with addition of matching system, load coil bypass and improved plasma dump, resulting in startup times under 50ms.  Using a theoretical model validated by local probes and spectroscopic measurements, a simplified method for plasma density control has been implemented, which has been effective in reaching desired plasma densities within 1ms.  This method has also enabled the source to operate in helicon mode, which has a positive density exponent greater than 0.5, critical for efficient plasma heating.  Furthermore, a novel plasma dump design has been introduced to facilitate plasma density regulation, while ensuring the integrity of the source's inner components against sputtering.  However, this design has limitations due to its reliance on an optimal balance between plasma dump area and power load deposited on the dump, which must account for different plasma densities and powers to prevent damage to the source's load coil.  A fully operational helicon source with plasma dump has been designed and will be employed in future H-mode discharges requiring sustained plasmas under 10ms.  A theoretical model has been developed to predict the performance of this design and can guide the selection of optimal parameters.  However, this model has limitations due to its reliance

In order to accelerate the degradation of microbial pesticides, UV light is utilized for their delivery, which negatively impacts their effectiveness by encouraging the multiplication of beneficial organisms through the release of enzymes, hormones, and volatile substances. This process is modeled through a microbial pesticide model that incorporates a competition component, and mathematical analysis reveals that increased interaction leads to reduced pesticide density but prevents microbial extinction. A detailed study of stability conditions and optimal suppression effects is performed through matrix analysis and graphical representations. Furthermore, our model takes into account the U-shaped life cycle of the pesticide, leading to more intricate dynamics that include the influence of self-sustaining pesticides on multiple equilibrium states and limit cycles, as demonstrated in various scenarios.

Gland and nucleus segmentation from histopathology images is a challenging task with numerous applications in medical image analysis. While historical research has utilized various techniques, including deep learning models, there's still room for improvement in accuracy. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel end-to-end framework called Nucleus Identification Network (N-I.D.), which integrates global context information from texture features and histopathology images to enhance performance. In N-I.D., we employ a pre-trained ResNet as a feature extractor and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for classification, with only the MLP being trainable. To adaptally weigh the significance of two inputs, we incorporate a lightweight dual-branch structure to modify the hidden states of both the image and feature data. Furthermore, to efficiently utilize limited histopathology data, we propose a second stage that replaces the MLP with two convolutional blocks and adds a fully connected layer, effectively making it equivalent to a two-stage model with enhanced efficiency. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a F1 score of 0.974 on the DuKE-MAP dataset. Our project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Chengqi-Zhang/N-W.

In the context of finite classical groups, a key property is that two groups sharing the same genus are typically locally isomorphic, meaning they have identical maximal tori (up to fusion). However, this rule doesn't apply to odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups in positive characteristic because they have distinctly different maximal tori. To resolve this, we develop a method to construct maximal tori in these types of groups that are applicable across most characteristics. Our method involves using a method devised by Borei-Spradlin and Brueckner for constructing maximal tori in special linear and unitary groups, as well as applying a technique from Brueckner for constructing maximal tori in various other types of linear groups. Ultimately, our approach enables us to demonstrate that two odd special orthogonal or symplectic groups in positive characteristic of sufficiently large order are locally isomorphic.

Xiong and Liu previously defined two concepts: a graph G is considered n-hamiltonian path index if G's repeated line graph Lk(G) contains a hamiltonian path for all k≥k≥n, and a graph G is a hamiltonian path cover if each vertex in G is part of a hamiltonian path in G. This research expands on previous work by providing a condition for a graph G to have a hamiltonian path in its repeated line graph Lk(G) as k grows indefinitely, and also examines the relationship between a graph's hamiltonian path index and n-hamiltonian path. Additionally, a condition for a graph G to be traceable in its repeated line graph Lk(G) as k grows indefinitely is also established.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory process, can cause conditions like a cytokine storm during infection with SARS-CoV-2. This process is triggered by the activation of caspase-1, which then leads to gasdermin E processing and release of inflammatory substances. Pyroptosis in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells can be regulated by the ACE2 protein, which facilitates cell death but also protects against other viral components. In this study, a single-cell SARS-CoV-2 pyroptosis model was created to analyze the interactions between various factors including the viral entry, replication, and release mechanisms, as well as the effects of anti-inflammatory medication on cell death. By using adaptive stepsize integration, researchers were able to estimate unobservable states and infer the optimal dosing of luciferase inhibitors to minimize the release of GSDMD-N fragments, a byproduct of pyroptosis. Results from the model suggest that reducing the inhibitory effects of the virus on ACE2 mediated apoptosis can substantially lower pyroptotic cell death, with some scenarios producing better outcomes than others. Additionally, applying the inhibitor after gasdermin E processing begins yields more significant reductions in pyroptotic cell death. Ultimately, these findings highlight the importance of understanding the dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 pyroptosis and the potential effectiveness of anti-inflammatory treatments in preventing cytokine storm conditions.

External influences can hinder reinforcement learning agents by exposing them to irrelevant state information and reward information outside their control. This paper aims to formally define and offshoot the concept of latent variables in state and reward information that are external to the agent using the Markov decision process framework. We then explore methods to remove these hidden variables through a new framework that extends the MDP to account for these variables. The proposed methods include mathematical proofs and practical applications demonstrated through landmine avoidance training in simulation and in a real-world setting.

The blockchain platform of smart contracts enables contracts to be executed under predefined conditions and with designated inputs. Although popular blockchain projects like Ethereum provide these platforms, their default type systems, based on unrefinement, pose a significant risk of security breaches by allowing any potential input. To mitigate this risk and prevent common errors in contract development, we have created HELMHOLTZ, a refinement type-based validator for contracts developed on the Refinement Monadic Parser Combinator (RFPC) framework in the Tezos blockchain project. This tool ensures the proper functioning of contracts by providing a reliable validator, and it has been put to use in developing and testing the HELMHOLTZ DAO project in France.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have been widely employed in various applications, yet their complexity, particularly when using graph-based methods, often lacks an transparent and interpretable component which limits broader adoption due to significant security concerns and difficulties in refining the model through iterative processes. This issue poses a common challenge in the development of Deep Learning models, as the lack of clarity in how these networks function hinders their widespread use. Researchers have previously addressed this problem, but existing solutions fail to address a critical requirement for preserving node degrees during the training process, thereby compromising the effectiveness of GCNNs, especially in scenarios involving dynamic and evolving graphs. In response, this study introduces a novel, intuitive framework known as 'matched filtering', a concept that provides a detailed explanation of the underlying mechanisms of GCNNs, including graph classification and node embedding techniques. The matched filtering theory has been utilized to identify specific flaws in existing graph-based methods, providing a specific example of over-smoothing in GCNNs and suggesting the need to preserve node degrees during the training process. Building on this framework, a novel approach called Degree-Matched Filtering (DMF) has been devised to enhance the performance of GCNNs and mitigate over-smoothing issues, resulting in state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks and significantly improved performance in dynamic graph classification tasks.

Start from a three-dimensional Chern-Simons-like action where the elements of an $SU(2)$ algebra are decoupled, and incorporate a complex scalar field with both kinetic terms and covariant derivatives. In the process, identify and discard specific decoupled pieces in the algebra to obtain a consistent set of equations of motion. By employing the Hamiltonian-Holst formalism with the inclusion of the scalar field, we find the corresponding first-order non-diffusive master action in the form of a topologically heavy BF theory with a non-trivial Chern-Simons coefficient. Leveraging the topological nature of this Hamiltonian dynamics, we construct rotating black hole solutions as well as supersymmetric hairy solitons from the master action through topological transformations. These objects exhibit extensive properties aligned with those of uncharged black holes in Einstein gravity with a negative cosmological constant and a scalar hair, specifically showing that the mass of the hairy black holes equals the sum of the Casimir charges of both the topological and Chern-Simons sectors.

Theories that integrate branes equivalent to the dual of the fundamental string, such as D1/FP systems in type II theories, can exhibit the exchange of left and right-moving components. This  L/R- symmetry allows for an increase in supercharges through a process known as a BPS jump. The corresponding Lagrangian systems can be viewed as being associated with certain mathematical structures called sigma models over specific manifolds that possess a rich set of symmetries. The key feature of these manifolds is the presence of subgroups within their T-duals that permit for an involution, which is then mapped to a corresponding subgroup in the algebraic structure of the Kac–Moody Lie algebras. This allows us to derive a set of equations that relate the generators of these algebras, which in turn can be utilized in the construction of non-commutative generalizations of affine Weyl group actions. These actions can be applied to expand the algebra and introduce additional branes, such as D3-branes, into brane configurations, such as D1/D5/D3 systems.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, enables the non-invasive visualisation and assessment of tumour stiffness in patients. The reliability of elastography images is compromised by a lateral shift estimation error exceeding 0.5 pixel. Synthetic aperture synthetic elastography, a related technique, provides higher resolution in the ultrasound imaging. However, its limited beam angle and synthetic beam estimation error exceedingly hinder its application. The proposed method, Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture Ultrasound Elastography, introduces a new beam estimation approach that mitigates these shortcomings. By calculating the actual propagation distance and angle between transmit and receive beams, our algorithm precisely estimates the beam lateral shift. Moreover, it compensates for the beam-related distortion in elastography. The method's lateral shift estimation precision is confirmed to be within 0.3 pixel through simulations and in vivo experiments. Moreover, its capability to recover distorted elastography images is validated. The method's superior performance is evident when compared to traditional algorithms, offering enhanced beam processing and elevated spatial resolution. Overall, we present a highly accurate beam processing algorithm that improves elastography image assessment.

Algorithms and proofs are fundamentally connected, as every algorithm implicitly contains a proof of correctness for its desired output, while there is no analogous proof theory for liquidating an asset at an optimal price. This paper introduces a framework to examine algorithms through their associated proofs, thereby integrating the best pricing an asset can achieve. We propose a pseudocode language based on Coq, which leverages the explicit proof structure to ensure the consistency and optimality of an algorithm's result. We illustrate the potential of this approach by presenting the liquidation algorithm's implicit result as a pseudocode statement, while exploring the concepts of consistency and optimality within the pseudocode framework.

The classic result by Perles in 1955 shows that any $r$-coloring of the Boolean lattice $2^d$ guarantees the presence of monochromatic points forming a specific poset structure. We extend this result to consider posets formed by taking the disjoint union of two such posets and then identifying their greatest lower bound, effectively creating a new poset within a single chain product. Our main contribution is a demonstration that this new poset is also a Ramsey poset in $2^d$, a result that aligns with earlier standalone findings while providing a more efficient bounding of dimension $f(r)$ than its predecessors. Our analysis specifically focuses on determining suitable values for $f(r)$ when applied to a poset representing an 'V' shape in the Boolean lattices.

In the context of dynamic data processing, we investigate the challenge of maintaining an effective solution for the $k$-centers clustering problem. Our primary focus is on providing a clear and efficient approach to solving this problem in a dynamic setting, especially when working with data that has many dimensions. By using a technique known as dimensionality reduction based on Johnson-Lindenstrauss, we can develop a highly effective algorithm that excels in scenarios with high-dimensional spaces. This algorithm, whether it's for one-time updates or more complex changes, allows us to center our $k$ clusters within a minimal distance of $O(\sqrt{\log k}\cdot \log^{3/2}d))$ from the cluster points, using an efficient amount of memory. The efficiency of the algorithm is further showcasing in its use of $O(k\log^{2}k \log^{5/2}d)$ memory, essentially giving it an unparalleled effectiveness in situations where the number of dimensions far surpasses the number of desired clusters.

Multi-agent cooperative games, such as those involving teams pursuing and capturing targets, often pose difficult problems due to their high dimensional and non-convex nature, which can result in complex solutions that require agents to track and mimic each other's behavior through a hierarchical approach. This research explores the potential of decomposition methods to simplify these games into smaller, more manageable parts that can be solved independently and then combined, maintaining clarity in the solution while preserving performance. A specific two-level hierarchical framework based on maximize-min principles and smooth approximations of value functions is proposed, allowing for efficient computation of near-optimal solutions. Moreover, a theoretical analysis proves convergence to an equilibrium in cooperative games, and the effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in a numerical case study involving multiple predators pursuing a prey, yielding results comparable to state-of-the-art techniques.

Probability is often associated with intuition, but the Feller-Luckhardt example from the 1960s shows that some combinations of observed events can lead to counterintuitive conclusions, such as A being more likely than B, B being more likely than C, yet C being more likely than A. This phenomenon is called nontransitive likelihood, and until now, no studies had explored whether such occurrences could happen in cycles. In this paper, we introduce the concepts of cyclicity and nontransitivity to describe the properties of nontransitive events, and we demonstrate through a mathematical framework that it is indeed possible for likelihood events to occur in cycles, providing multiple examples of such cycles. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which cyclicity can happen and the nature of events that are capable of forming cycles.

Recently, deep learning techniques have significantly enhanced low-dose CT image quality, allowing for high-resolution scans with minimal radiation. However, current methods face challenges in real-world applications due to frequent updates in scanner technology and scanning protocols. A single trained model often fails to deliver optimal results for multiple types of low-dose CT data due to these variations. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel AdaSwitch architecture based on the CycleGAN framework, which employs AdaIN layers and is designed for efficient training. This model allows the generator to create high-fidelity low-dose to paired high-res reference images while the discriminator uses multiple channels to distinguish the different high-res high-dose images. Our method offers the benefits of both AdaIN's adaptability to diverse low-dose data and the CycleGAN's ability to process unpaired high-high data. Experiments show that our approach achieves superior low-dose to high-dose restoration results and outperforms the standard CycleGAN model.

Recent advances in dialog understanding through pre-trained large-scale BERT models have achieved remarkable success, primarily attributed to the use of contrastive training that effectively aligns utterances with identical intent labels. However, the availability of sufficiently large labeled datasets is frequently constrained, necessitating the incorporation of additional unlabeled data for improved performance. In this work, we introduce SPACE-2, a novel pre-training framework that combines contrastive training with self-supervised hierarchy. To bridge the gap between local utterance representations and global dataset statistics, we employ a multi-stage process involving the construction of a hierarchical taxonomy from unlabeled data and the development of hierarchical contrastive pairs. Initially, we perform contrastive pre-training on labeled data to secure a strong baseline, then expand the training dataset with unlabeled data using a hierarchical multi-class contrastive loss, and finally refine the models at each taxonomy node through an efficient two-stage process. Our comprehensive evaluations on multiple dialogs corpus demonstrate the superiority of SPACE-2 over both singular and composite baselines in several dialog tasks including end-of-dialog judgment, task completion rate, and multi-task evaluation.

This research explores a conformal Ricci-Yamabe transformation on an ideal fluid spacetime that is geometrically consistent. We demonstrate that under this transformation, the vector field involved must be a Killing vector field, and the scaling factor involved is determined to be the Laplacian of the Yamabe function, while having a specific value of -1. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the energy function involved has a minimum value that is equal to the sum of the Yamabe function and a specific ratio, and this ratio is determined to be the minimum value of the energy function. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the scalar curvature and the Yamabe function, showing that their difference has a specific ratio, and this ratio is determined to be either zero or a value of -1/4 when the spacetime has a certain symmetry. However, if the spacetime has a different type of geodesic consistency, no solution exists. Finally, a geometric interpretation is provided for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe transformation on the ideal fluid spacetime that is geometrically consistent.

To study the spin effects in rotated, distorted rotated halos, we used the relativistic distorted-wave approach to calculate decay properties of one-proton neutrinolysis. We examined cases where the target is in a ground rotational state or excited rotational states, considering total angular momentum decoupling. Notable differences were found in calculated spectrum shapes and decay one-proton energy depending on target rotation and decoupling. Specifically, significant shifts in decay one-proton energies were found in rotated distorted halo nuclei compared to static ones. These shifts can provide valuable information about the intrinsic structure of these unusual nuclei.

A common strategy in video super-resolution involves using information from adjacent frames to fill in the detailed variations across frames, nevertheless, this approach tends to introduce inaccuracies when applied to large motion displacements. Although the sequential application of convolutional layers can effectively recover lost spatial information, it often fails to fully erase the introduced inaccuracies due to misalignment of the remaining adjacent frames' motion. To address this issue, we introduce an upgraded version of the BasicVSR network, specifically BasicVSR++, which incorporates two main innovations: an improved propagation branch and a refined cross branch alignment module. Furthermore, we utilize a large-scale video super-resolution dataset, Video-Super-Resolution-Next (VideoSR-Next), for more rigorous evaluation and comparison, resulting in the following outcomes: (1) the proposed Enhanced Propagation Branch significantly boosts performance over the original network by 0.5-0.8 dB in FSIM on four distinct datasets, (2) the Cross Branch Alignment Module yields substantial improvements of 0.2-0.4 dB in Lpfsim on four datasets, and (3) the proposed network achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art video super-resolution methods, surpassing them in metrics such as Lpfsim and FSIM on VideoSR-Next.

We employ the vector boson approximation to examine the characteristics of second-order scattering processes involving same-sign W bosons and top quarks at a muon collider. By considering initial states consisting of either $(\mu^{+}\mu^{+})$ or $(\mu^{-}\mu^{-})$, we consider two distinct scenarios: fully reconstructed final states for the $W$ bosons and measurements solely of the top quark. Through explicit calculations and studies of parton distribution functions, we find that the $\mu^{+}\mu^{+}$ initial state exhibits significantly enhanced sensitivity to signal cross-sections, particularly for $\mu^{+}\mu^{+}t\bar{t}$, when compared to the $\mu^{-}\mu^{-}tt$ process. Additionally, we observe that detecting only the top quark yields detector efficiencies akin to those of full final state reconstructions. Furthermore, we find that, after accounting for detector efficiencies and theoretical uncertainties, a $\mu^{+}\mu^{+}t\bar{t}$ analysis can distinguish signal from background with a signal-to-background ratio exceeding 10, in contrast to a ratio of approximately 1 achieved in a $\mu^{-}\mu^{-}tt$ analysis.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, later tasks can overpower the network during fine-tuning due to catastrophic interference. To mitigate this, we propose an innovative approach in this paper. We present a modular network structure that isolates each task within its own module in an model-based MBML framework. This isolation prevents the network from experiencing catastrophic interference by keeping each task separate. Furthermore, we introduce a task-embedding mechanism that seamlessly integrates these modules by learning task-specific features and guiding the flow between them. Our method delivers superior performance on the MuJoCo locomotion benchmark, outperforming existing MBML approaches and often requiring significantly fewer neural network parameters.

The paper provides derivations of prior L^p-type and Cauchy-Schwarz type estimates for solutions to the equation $u_t=\Delta_\infty u + \Delta(u^m)$ on a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. It also includes derived pointwise estimates for the infinite Laplacian equation with the $\Delta(u^m)$ term and the infinite diffusion equation, $u_t=\Delta_\infty u$. These estimates are particularly useful in understanding long-term behavior of solutions. A key method involves modifying existing comparison arguments to accommodate the nonlinearity of the equations. Notably, all results are applicable to a large class of spaces that comprise complete, non-compact manifolds with specific curvature constraints and metric measure spaces with $\rho$-compact boundary conditions.

We explore the Godel-Carnap Theorem, a comprehensive theory of recursion that encompasses and extends classical results. This framework enables the development of expanded systems of enumeration with corresponding proof systems. These systems have the capacity to generate basic arithmetic operations within any given number. Furthermore, we examine several distinct notions of provability relative to gathering systems, proving the existence of unprovable statements that signify the absence of gathering in both single and non-single systems. This research extends previous work by Rosser and Tennenbaum on directed quasi-recursive systems.

In complex analysis, solving holomorphic functions involves using analytic tools, whereas in Clifford analysis, the situation is already partially determined by algebraic operations on Clifford variables. This allows us to expand on a "three-balls conjecture" from complex analysis for functions belonging to a specific class, defined as monogenic functions.

In many data collection scenarios, the goal of egalitarianism equates to giving each individual an equal chance of being selected. This principle is commonly seen in voter selection for jury trials, survey participants, and job applicants reviewed by hiring committees. Our research introduces a new algorithm, which gives each eligible candidate the same expected number of equitable views based on a known population distribution. The method surpasses previous approaches, notably the running pool system, in achieving accuracy while using a significantly smaller active pool. The performance of the equal opportunity sampler can be further improved as more history data becomes available.

Robust eye-in-hand camera calibration typically requires taking test images of known scene features under various conditions. However, this process is time-consuming and impractical for real-world applications like robotics. As an alternative, researchers have explored using machine learning to predict camera parameters from distortion images. This approach was initially presented in the context of unsticking suction cups by training a regression model on a synthetic dataset. Despite achieving good results, such models are usually tailored to specific tasks and datasets, which limits their applicability. In a more general study, a machine learning-based camera uncalibration approach is presented, which requires only the robot to capture test images of a known feature, such as a checkerboard, in a controlled environment. A deep neural network is then used to predict the camera's internal parameters from these images. To gather a sufficiently large and varied dataset, the real robot is intentionally exposed to environments that enhance data diversity. A particularly efficient data acquisition method is introduced, which significantly reduces the size of the required dataset while maintaining high accuracy. The proposed approach yields precise predictions of camera parameters, as evidenced by the model's performance in practice.

In disciplines such as biomedical imaging and electrical engineering, solving inverse problems is crucial for determining unknown inputs from measurable output signals.  This process often yields multiple possible solutions and is typically unstable.  Our research aims to restore a well-posed and conditional posterior distribution in inverse problems by inputting measured data and specific conditions.  We propose a novel regularization approach that employs a stochastic discriminative network to model the conditional posterior distribution.  This approach is theoretically proven to restore the posterior distribution as the number of training samples and network capacity increases.  However, training such an approach is computationally expensive.  We introduce a contrastive objective function to efficiently distinguish between real and simulated data.  This method reduces the need for a large number of training data by leveraging a contrastive loss.  Our approach is applied to magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) temperature estimation and image super-resolution tasks and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods such as VAEs and normalizing flows in terms of accuracy and speed.
We investigate fractional order dynamical systems with symmetry, specifically proving that certain algebraic curves in R^2 cannot be invariant under the application of a Adomian polynomial method.

Next-generation wireless networks will utilize terahertz frequencies to significantly boost data transfer rates, yet certain terahertz channels may struggle with signal loss over longer distances. To address this issue, multi-hop short-distance links are utilized, although the extensive beam training required for these connections can be challenging to manage. To overcome this challenge and lower the required beam training, we developed a reinforcement learning approach that selectively conducts beam training to minimize interference and pinpoint optimal beam pairs for each link in the network. Simulation results show that our approach not only achieves lower latency and interference but also delivers more stable performance compared to random beam training methods.

Our team utilized high-cadence observations of the pulsar B1133+16 by the Cherenkov Telescope Array, conducted in collaboration with the Very Large Array, to obtain very precise scintillation patterns around the pulsar. These patterns revealed an orientation of the interstellar medium structures in front of the pulsar that deviates from the expected alignment with the cosmic microwave background structure grain. Furthermore, by analyzing the scale of scintillation patterns, the rotation of the scintillation grating, and the changes in the rate of scintillation over time, we were able to infer the physical properties of the surrounding environment. However, our analysis also revealed inconsistencies in the derived properties when using different methods, which may be a result of the structures being located at various distances between the Earth and the pulsar. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of using scintillometry as a tool for investigating the interstellar medium in the vicinity of the Milky Way, which may have significant implications for future observations with the Cherenkov Telescope Array.

This paper presents a novel generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limitations of noise-based synthesis models in preserving pitch information. Unlike these models, QPNet generates signals directly, enabling it to capture periodic information effectively. By utilizing a specific expansion factor and a quasi-periodic mask, QPNet can efficiently process long-range dependencies and manage the reconstruction of spectral repetitions. Additionally, QPNet incorporates an asymmetric network structure to accelerate training and reduce computational costs. The results show that QPNet outperforms previous models, including Multi-Periodic WaveAutoencoder (MP-WaveAutoencoder) and Multi-Periodic WaveNet (MP-WaveNet), in both objective and subjective evaluations.

This study introduces a novel annotation and correction tool for Standard and dialectal Arabic that can be used online.  Since Arabic has a rich morphological system, automatic processing of the language is particularly difficult.  Consequently, a reliable annotation scheme is crucial for training accurate machine learning models, which requires human input for a significant amount of annotated data.  To facilitate the creation of high-quality annotated and corrected data, a new online application called MADARi was created.  By incorporating a reliable annotation format, user-friendly features, and access to pre-processed datasets, this system streamlines the annotation and correction process for both standard and dialectal Arabic, thus enabling several improvements to be made to the existing web platform for a more efficient workflow.

This paper provides an overview of current research on the photochemistry and spectral characteristics of temperate, gas-rich exoplanets. As we have limited observational data on these planets in their habitable zones, our primary solar system reference points are gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, which are significantly less affected by stellar radiation. In contrast, temperate worlds experience intense photochemical processes driven by host star UV radiation that can significantly alter atmospheric composition and thermal structure. Our discussion encompasses possible photochemical models for these planets, an exploration of their thermal structure using radiative-convective modeling, and their potential observational detection methods. Furthermore, we have limited our analysis to hydrogen-rich atmospheres common in super-Earth and Neptune-class exoplanets.

Differentiating between zero-energy Majorana peaks and ordinary peaks in tunneling spectra is an ongoing challenge in topological superconductivity experiments. A proposed experiment involves measuring tunneling density of states with an Ohmic environment, where the conductance is linearly related to capacitance. In this setup, the environment's resistance matches the quantum resistance, and charge and voltage are coupled through a Cramer-Rao lower bound. Using non-equilibrium Green's function theory, we simulate tunneling spectra and observe how dissipation influences peak positions and shapes. For ordinary tunneling, the peaks shift to higher energies due to charge and voltage fluctuations, while in topological tunneling, the peaks remain at zero energy due to self-orthogonality. These results can help distinguish between Majorana and ordinary peaks in tunneling experiments.

The rising intensity of urban networks worldwide, particularly in developing nations, accelerates road flaw incidents such as potholes and uneven surfaces, posing safety risks and hindering traffic flow. While numerous research studies and existing systems have tackled this problem, the vast number of roads makes the task of identifying defects on all streets impossible without the support of a comprehensive and user-friendly system. To address this challenge, we present RoadAtlas, an innovative platform designed to facilitate the efficient detection of road flaws and streamlined management of assets across entire urban areas. By providing a data source for all streets within a municipality, this system streamlines the scope of detection tasks and facilitates the integration of cutting-edge technologies, including deep learning models, into flawed road detection projects.

This informal exploration focuses on advanced mathematical concepts, specifically those related to higher-dimensional categories and their applications in linear algebra and topology. We will discuss the notion of shadows and marks in the context of semi-simplicial categories and their functors, and explore the concept of bicategorical signs as their orthogonal complements. Moreover, we will demonstrate how the Smashing Lemma arises from the interaction between shadows and marks through an n-labelling map, and ultimately show how this relationship can be seen as a manifestation of duality in mathematics.

Recently, noise2noise models have shown remarkable success in image restoration by learning to copy images. These models are particularly effective due to their minimal requirement for labeled data. In this work, we investigate a more difficult scenario in visual noise localization, which is also known as noise classification. Our research is centered on developing a method to accurately classify a new and more challenging type of visual noise called "mismatched compression artifacts". To achieve this, we design a method to locally classify these artifacts at a very granular level, specifically down to the block-block pattern. Our approach is highly efficient as it only requires the use of pre-trained detection models and does not rely on trained customization. To showcase its effectiveness, we develop a comprehensive dataset consisting of 210,000 images with compression artifacts in the range of 2-10% and cover a wide variety of real-world scenes. Our experiments reveal that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in localizing this new and complex type of visual noise called "mismatched compression artifacts".

Recent years have seen a significant advancement in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which have proven effective in various applied areas. The success of these models relies heavily on the property of Isomorphism Invariance in graphs. Most research has focused on Euclidean space where graphs exist, overlooking graphs that are positioned in non-Euclidean, specifically Lorentzian metric spaces. We present an initial framework for a new type of GNN, the Lorentzian Graph Neural Network (L-GNN), that operates on graphs in Lorentzian metric spaces. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of L-GNNs, demonstrate their practical applications in tasks such as node classification and graph classification, and compare their performance to existing Eucledian GNNs. The results show that L-GNNs outperform their Euclidean counterparts, particularly in challenging classification scenarios.

The primary objective of this research is to pinpoint a source of sound within a limited frequency range, given an audio signal measured further away from the source. The setup for the experiment involves a limited number of acoustic sources confined to a small area, a large measurement region beyond the source region, and a single sensor that records sound at a specific point in the measurement region. The goal of the experiment is to reconstruct the sound sources from the measured data. A key challenge in this experiment is the ambiguous nature of the forward process, which does not provide enough information to accurately pinpoint the source location. To address this, a novel approach based on regularized time reversal will be introduced and implemented using data generated on a 2D surface. The results of this approach include the successful localization of sound sources using only a single sensor in the measurement region. Furthermore, this technique allows the source image to be obtained using only real data in the simulation. The novel algorithm introduced in this research involves a time-reversed application of a regularizing operator that mimics the acoustic system's dynamics. This differs significantly from traditional time reversal methods, which seek the closest solution in a limited energy space. Replacing the time reversal with a surface time reversal in the algorithm leads to a more precise result, which outperforms the traditional method. The theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of this approach are explored in the study.

In complex systems, linking disparate areas of study, we investigate a situation in optomechanics where squeezed light enters system and leaves in a compressed state. This study focuses on steady-state scenarios and calculates the exact matrix values for both quantum mechanics and thermodynamics. Our findings contradict previous beliefs that such conditions are impossible to achieve with thermal environments. Moreover, our work extends beyond quantum mechanics to thermal physics, and we propose experimental methods that can be implemented with current optical resonator technology.

We examine the basic characteristics of a specialized form of modal $\mu$-calculus, known as scalar and vectorial mu-calculus, which expands traditional modal $\mu$-calculus to handle structured data in trees. This enhanced version of the calculus allows for the creation of programs that transform these data trees. We establish a connection between the scalar version and modal $\mu$-calculus with program variables, making it possible to convert one into the other. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the extended capabilities of the vectorial version can be harnessed to transform modal $\mu$-calculus formulas into normal forms.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 1999 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by T. S. Sotirakopoulos. Our model is based on the 1998 Tsallis
probability theory reformulation by A. Tsallis, and incorporates the concept of
nonextensivity as a measure of uncertainty and nonstationarity. By doing so, we
demonstrate the versatility of the Tsallis probability theory and reformulate key
economic and psychological variables, such as market prices, impulsive behavior,
and delayed decision making, in line with the nonextensivity of a market. We also
derive an immediate implication, presenting a delayed version of the Fisher's
equation, and discuss potential applications and limitations of our model.

In the context of hefty gravity, which is a type of higher-order derivative theory, we examined its gauge symmetries in the harmonic gauge. Despite previous studies claiming the existence of a harmonic gauge in this theory, we contend that such a gauge is actually impossible, except possibly in a singular $d$-dimensional case. Additionally, we introduce a new gauge symmetry specific to the harmonic gauge, and show that the theory can be harmonically reduced to a well-defined model with four degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space.

A signed graph is considered expandable if its edge graph has a property allowing a homomorphism from another graph while maintaining the same cycle orientations. This concept is related to Teng's work on oriented graphs and their restrictions. Your research explores sufficient conditions for a signed graph to be expandable, focusing on homomorphism bounds to other signed graphs. Specifically, you examine whether certain cycles with specific orientation patterns allow a homomorphism, relating to 5-cycles and their edge-directed cycles. You also discuss the implications of these findings and their relevance to oriented graphs.

We suggest using Weyl-Wigner functional methods and operational quantum language to create a robust, general formula for normal forms of Weyl-Wigner states, representing canonical quantum equilibrium conditions. Notably, our approach bypasses the use of density matrices. Instead, we express the normal form as a functional using Weyl-Wigner arguments, with a distinct feature being the identification of unique operator states within this class of functions.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, utilizing both approaches to depict the temperature, or more precisely, the factor $\tau = k_{\rm B}T$. We then discuss the concept of heat flow in terms of the $\tau$ parameter in relation to the negative and positive temperature regimes.

Let G be an abelian group and G' a subgroup of G. For any subset A of G with elements not in G', we prove that the restricted sumset A⁺A has a element that represents at least |A|ⁿ times the number of elements in A⁺A, where n is the difference between the dimension of the smallest real vector space containing a representative set of G'/A and the dimension of the smallest real vector space representing the elements of A. This result leads to an answer to a question posed by Ahmadi and Keshari regarding the minimum size of restricted sumsets A⁺A in Z, where the elements of A have a difference that is a power of 2 and the answer is at least n+1, where n is the largest such number. Furthermore, we derive a representation theorem for a subset of Z,mZ that contains the elements of A⁺A with a certain distance between its consecutive elements that belong to a same coset of mZZ, which in turn gives an exact solution to a question posed by Broderick, Prendiville, and Tolev in their work on a discrete variant of Yuval's polynomial method in Szemeredi-Turan type theorems.

Characterizing histopathological features through microscopic analysis provides the gold standard in pathology, aiding the diagnosis and treatment of diseases. However, manually labeling histopathological characteristics is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Recent studies propose using deep learning techniques to annotate digital pathology slides, but the equipment required for this approach is not commonly available in research laboratories. We introduce UniToPatho, a comprehensive histopathological dataset containing approximately 10K cropped images and corresponding abnormality grades for the entire colorectal polyp. This dataset will facilitate the evaluation of innovative methods that utilize histopathological features to classify polyps and annotate digital pathology slides with the aid of automatic deep learning tools.

A novel numerical approach is presented for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around determining the scattered acoustic field when an incoming plane wave interacts with a nonlinear scattering object and determines the field in the exterior space. This method is developed within a variational framework and results in a homogeneous scattering equation set in $L^2$ for all frequencies. The approach utilizes an adaptive finite element method that strategically refines the computational mesh to ensure high-frequency problems can be solved within a problem-mesh ratio range typical of the Monge-Ampere equation. The approach's theoretical underpinnings are grounded in asymptotic analysis, allowing for the development of reliable error estimates both inside and outside the scattering object's boundary. The approach's success hinges upon the application of an outstanding approximation property for spherical Hankel functions by piecewise piecewise linear functions. Furthermore, the approach includes a newly developed type of boundary projection operator that facilitates accurate representation of the multiple scattering process. The approach' validity and performance are supported by multiple numerical experiments.

A theory proposing that the early inner solar disk was accreting due to processes like photoevaporation or viscous friction is presented. According to this model, the disk was generating heat and radiating it in the form of x-rays and infrared light. Viscous heating resulted in the inner disk becoming ionized and affecting the growth of planetary embryos through a process called aerodynamic drag. As a result, the embryos did not effectively accrete dust due to the Rayleigh-Taylor instability being suppressed, which limited the mass of the largest planetesimals to about 10 km in diameter. Models based on this accretion disk model were adjusted until their predictions about the age distribution of radiogenic $^{182}Hue$ matched the age distribution of whole meteorites, in particular the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites, to about 350 million years old and 2.1 billion units of $^{10}Be/^{9}Be$ ratio in about 4 meters of the meteorite respectively. Based on these matches, the authors suggest that an actively accreting disk is responsible for the age distribution of the meteorites, in contrast to the standard solar nebula model, which predicts a different, inconclusive metric about billions years old and an insufficiently old ratio in less than a million years, which conflicts with the Chelyabinsk meteorite data.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we apply the affine quantum-group symmetry to simplify scalar products and compute eigenvalues for a wide range of higher-spin XXZ chains. This is achieved by extending the B-ansatz method to cover an infinite number of spin types. Key calculations include determining the vacuum and Gelfand-Tsetlin module eigenvalues for the XXZ chains with an odd number of sites, as well as their thermodynamic limits, by leveraging the affine quantum-group symmetry. Furthermore, using the flat-fusion relations and evaluating the residues of the transfer matrix at its affine quantum-group zero-eigenvalues, we derive the complete, universal expression for the full spectrum of the XXZ chain's Hamiltonian, regardless of the specific spin values.

Previous work on voice translation heavily relied on a large number of person-specific training samples, resulting in a significant gap between laboratory tests and real-world applications. To bridge this disparity, our study explores zero-shot voice translation, achieving this without the need for target language data or speaker-specific training. Utilizing transfer learning and two novel models - Cycle-GAN Voice Morphing and a Multi-domain Proximity Network - we successfully demonstrate voice translation to a new language and accent. Interestingly, our studies revealed that while the MDPN delivered better results in English to Spanish translation, the ZSGC excelled in English to Mandarin translation. Furthermore, listeners found our voices to sound more natural and easier to understand.

We examine the interaction of time-varying electromagnetic fields with matter in an enclosed space or on a surface over any frequency range. This interaction is analyzed by expanding into multiple components based on geometry alone, which is valid for any wavelength in comparison to the shape of the object or area. By using a different approach than traditional methods, we achieve an accurate and efficient way to calculate the average scalar energy and complex power for each component based on a mathematical transformation, which includes effects up to higher-order multipole interactions. Our method is made simpler and faster by utilizing an algorithm called Fast Multipole Method, which enables accurate calculations of total energy and optical force on objects or surfaces with complex shapes in real-time or over time-varying configurations.

This study introduces two new concepts: double Young-Capelli bitableaux and the Schur shifted symmetric expressions algebra. Notably, the Schur shifted symmetric expressions algebra is isomorphic to a specific two-sided ideal within the algebra of quantum Young-Capelli algebras, characterized by an n^2 by n matrix unit ideal. Furthermore, we establish a connection between double Young-Capelli bitableaux and shifted Young tableaux that predate this discovery.

In this study, we examine the easiest implementation of the scoto-seesaw model, which offers a suitable WIMP dark matter candidate, neutrino mass generation through the radiative type-II seesaw mechanism, and ensures the stability of the Higgs vacuum. We examine the impact of non-zero dark sector parameters on the neutron-proton oscillation rate and its ability to detect WIMP dark matter. In addition, we establish the limits for the right-handed neutrino mass parameter, the right-handed Majorana mass, and the dark sector parameters. Furthermore, taking into account the one-loop corrections to the Higgs self-energy, we assess the effect of these parameters on the vacuum stability.

The concept of orbitally hybridized electrons, known as blending, is thoroughly explained for transition metal compounds. Despite its fundamental significance, this idea lacks a clear, widely accepted definition when it comes to identifying distinct spectral features. Using a combined theoretical and experimental approach, this study explores the distinctive signs of blended electrons as seen in X-ray absorption and photoemission spectra. By contrasting this with purely orbitally overlapping electrons, we seek to clarify the complex relationships between electrons and their surrounding environment, as well as their impact on the interpretation of these spectra for transition metal compounds. Through case studies such as LaIrO$_3$, we illustrate how electrons can be identified and their unique features explained.

The Stiefel-黎氏 bundle associated with a complex vector bundle possesses a natural Riemannian structure, yet this geometry does not remain invariant as we apply a rational transformation, transforming the Stiefel manifold into its counterpart, $F_n$, and altering its metric properties. Notably, the resulting geometry of the transformed manifold collapses into a degenerate form. Through an in-depth investigation into the geometry of the transformation map, we discover a subset of the original Stiefel manifold that maps onto the entire transformed manifold in a one-to-one manner. This sub-set, equipped with its own geometry, sees its degenerate metric split into distinct components through the transformation map, revealing rich and structured characteristics in each component.

Advances in medical image analysis have primarily utilized conventional deep learning techniques, with few instances of combining them with generative adversarial networks for accurate and interpretable diagnostic results. This research aims to fill that knowledge gap by proposing a novel deep learning framework, called MedGAN, which integrates medical image diagnosis with medicine-related image generation. The framework adapts a generator that can generate chest X-rays depicting specific medical conditions, allowing for the exploration of latent representations and the incorporation of medical image enhancement techniques. Experimental results on a large dataset of chest X-rays show that MedGAN's components can achieve competitive diagnostic performance, indicating its effectiveness as a viable approach for generating illness-aware medical images.

ViDaExpert is an advanced tool for exploring and analyzing complex data sets. It boasts a unique capability to visualize data in two and three dimensions, while also featuring an innovative nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique called Variational Isometric Projection. By incorporating this technique, ViDaExpert sets itself apart from other tools, providing a tailored solution for even non-technical users to easily customize and optimize data representation. Additionally, ViDaExpert's source code is freely accessible, enabling both researchers and developers to further develop or integrate its techniques into other graphical interfaces.

The task of computing Newtonian potentials for functions defined on a two-dimensional area can be broken down into a complex formula, consisting of a two-dimensional and a line integral component. The study utilizes adaptive versions of Fast Multipole Methods to efficiently calculate the integral part, either by applying methods directly or indirectly for specific cases. The study's results show a significant improvement in computational time for potential calculations on regular polygons, achieving a 10 to 125-fold decrease in time compared to existing methods, including the use of Special Function Packages. The proposed approach has a simple and adaptable framework, which can be broken down into the following steps: (a) representing the density function as a series of basis functions, (b) deriving computational formulas for potential components based on the series, and (c) obtaining the potential value by evaluating the series. The study demonstrates the proposed approach's effectiveness through a comparison of two methods for a classic problem, consisting of calculating the potential generated by a uniformly distributed unit disk.
